Behold, they will come up by the ascent of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the valley, east of the wilderness of Jeruel.<sup>17</sup>You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf, O Judah and Jerusalem.' Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the LORD will be with you."<sup>18</sup>Then Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell down before the LORD, worshiping the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And the Levites, of the Kohathites and the Korahites, stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.<sup>20</sup>And they rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa. And when they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, "Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will succeed."<sup>21</sup>And when he had taken counsel with the people, he appointed those who were to sing to the LORD and praise him in holy attire, as they went before the army, and say, "Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever."<sup>22</sup>And when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come against Judah, so that they were routed.<sup>23</sup>For the men of Ammon and Moab rose against the inhabitants of Mount Seir, devoting them to destruction, and when they had made an end of the inhabitants of Seir, they all helped to destroy one another.<sup>24</sup>When Judah came to the watchtower of the wilderness, they looked toward the horde, and behold, there were dead bodies lying on the ground; none had escaped.<sup>25</sup>When Jehoshaphat and his people came to take their spoil, they found among them, in great numbers, goods, clothing, and precious things, which they took for themselves until they could carry no more. They were three days in taking the spoil, it was so much.<sup>26</sup>On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, for there they blessed the LORD. Therefore the name of that place has been called the Valley of Beracah to this day.<sup>27</sup>Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, and Jehoshaphat at their head, returning to Jerusalem with joy, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies.<sup>28</sup>They came to Jerusalem with harps and lyres and trumpets, to the house of the LORD.<sup>29</sup>And the fear of God came on all the kingdoms of the countries when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.<sup>30</sup>So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around.<sup>31</sup>Thus Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.<sup>32</sup>He walked in the way of Asa his father and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>33</sup>The high places, however, were not taken away; the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers.<sup>34</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, from first to last, are written in the chronicles of Jehu the son of Hanani, which are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel.<sup>35</sup>After this Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly.<sup>36</sup>He joined him in building ships to go to Tarshish, and they built the ships in Ezion-geber.<sup>37</sup>Then Eliezer the son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, "Because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made." And the ships were wrecked and were not able to go to Tarshish.
20.overview: A coalition is already at Engedi, and Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD, calling a national fast (vv. 1-4). His prayer establishes God's jurisdiction, recalls the land given to Abraham your friend, quotes Solomon's dedication prayer back to him, points out that the invaders are nations Israel had been forbidden to touch, and ends: we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you — with the children standing there (vv. 5-13). The Spirit comes on Jahaziel, a temple singer: the battle is not yours but God's, stand firm and watch (vv. 14-19). At dawn the king tells them to believe, and sends the choir out in front of the army (vv. 20-21). When they began to sing, the coalition destroys itself; the spoil takes three days, and the fourth is spent blessing God in a valley that keeps the name (vv. 22-30). The reign is summed up — and then he allies with Ahab's son and his ships are wrecked (vv. 31-37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — We Do Not Know What to Do
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A coalition of Moab, Ammon and the Meunites is already at Engedi (vv. 1-2). Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah, and the whole country comes up to seek him (vv. 3-4). His prayer begins with who God is — are you not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations (vv. 5-6) — moves to what he has done for the descendants of Abraham your friend (v. 7), and then quotes the dedication of the temple back to him (vv. 8-9). The invaders are the very nations Israel was forbidden to touch at the Exodus (vv. 10-11). And it ends: we are powerless ... We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you (v. 12) — with all Judah standing there, with their little ones, their wives, and their children (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 8 and 9 are Solomon's dedication prayer used for the case it was written for. A hundred and twenty years earlier a king had asked God to hear when disaster came and his people cried toward this house; now a king stands in that house and reads the clause back.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 is three admissions and one direction. Powerless, and we do not know what to do — and then, instead of a plan, our eyes are on you. It is the shortest honest prayer a person in trouble can make.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Moabites and Ammonites, and with them some of the Meunites, came against Jehoshaphat for battle. Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, "A great multitude is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the sea; and, behold, they are in Hazazon-tamar" (that is, Engedi). Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah. And Judah assembled to seek help from the LORD; from all the cities of Judah they came to seek the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The news arrives late. A coalition out of Moab and Ammon and the Meunites has already crossed and is at Engedi, on the western shore of the Dead Sea, which is a day and a half from Jerusalem up a wadi.

And verse 3 says two things about the king in a single breath that most people would put in separate sentences.

Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD.

He was afraid. The Chronicler writes it down without embarrassment, of a man he approves of, in a chapter that will end in total victory. And the fear did not disqualify the seeking; it produced it. Set his face is a phrase of deliberate turning — a man frightened out of his ordinary routine and pointing himself somewhere on purpose.

Then he proclaims a fast through the whole country, and verse 4 uses the book's own verb twice more: Judah assembled to seek help from the LORD; from all the cities of Judah they came to seek the LORD.

From all the cities. These are the towns Jehoshaphat had sent officials and Levites round with the Book of the Law in his third year. The teaching has been going on for two decades, and this is what it turns out to have produced: when a coalition crosses the border, the villages empty toward Jerusalem instead of toward the armoury.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of the LORD, before the new court, and said, "O LORD, God of our fathers, are you not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. In your hand are power and might, so that none is able to withstand you. Did you not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham your friend? And they have lived in it and have built for you in it a sanctuary for your name, saying, 'If disaster comes upon us, the sword, judgment, or pestilence, or famine, we will stand before this house and before you— for your name is in this house—and cry out to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer is built in the order a good prayer is built, and it takes a long time to get to the request.

Where he stands is given precisely: in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of the LORD, before the new court. Somebody had built a new court — an extension to the temple precinct, added at some point in the century and a half since Solomon, and mentioned here as though every reader would know which one. The building has been maintained and enlarged; a king who repaired a neglected altar had a son who added a courtyard, and the nation is now packed into it.

It starts with who God is. O LORD, God of our fathers, are you not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. In your hand are power and might, so that none is able to withstand you.

Every clause is about jurisdiction. God in heaven; ruling over the kingdoms of the nations — including the three that are marching; power and might in his hand. Jehoshaphat is establishing that the invasion is happening inside God's territory before he mentions it. It is his great-great-grandfather's prayer at the end of his life, where David said that greatness and power and glory belonged to God and that he ruled over all.

Then what God has done. He drove out the inhabitants of this land and gave it forever to the descendants of Abraham your friend.

Your friend. Only one other place in the Old Testament calls Abraham that, and the New Testament picks it up when James says that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness, and he was called a friend of God. Jehoshaphat is not naming a distant founder. He is reminding God of somebody they both knew.

And then verses 8 and 9, which are the reason this prayer works.

And they have lived in it and have built for you in it a sanctuary for your name, saying, If disaster comes upon us, the sword, judgment, or pestilence, or famine, we will stand before this house and before you — for your name is in this house — and cry out to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.

He is quoting Solomon. That is the fourth petition of the dedication prayer, almost clause for clause: if there is famine, pestilence, blight, siege, whatever plague, whatever sickness, and they stretch out their hands toward this house — then hear from heaven your dwelling place and forgive.

A hundred and twenty years earlier a king knelt on a bronze platform and asked God to receive prayers made toward that building in exactly this kind of trouble. Now a great-great-grandson stands in the same courtyard, in exactly that trouble, and reads the clause back. The building is being used for the case it was dedicated for, and the man using it knows the paperwork.

verseByVerse.quote: And now behold, the men of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came from the land of Egypt, and whom they avoided and did not destroy— behold, they reward us by coming to drive us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit. O our God, will you not execute judgment on them? For we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you." Meanwhile all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the situation, and there is a bitterness in the way he puts it.

And now behold, the men of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came from the land of Egypt, and whom they avoided and did not destroy — behold, they reward us by coming to drive us out of your possession.

Every one of those three nations is a people Israel was specifically forbidden to attack. God had told Moses not to contend with Esau's descendants in Seir, because he had given Seir to Esau; not to harass Moab, because he had given Ar to the sons of Lot; and not to harass Ammon, for the same reason. Israel came round them, at some cost, four centuries ago.

And now they are on the road to Jerusalem. Jehoshaphat's complaint is precise: we obeyed you about these people and this is the return on it. He is not accusing God; he is putting the obedience into the record and asking God to notice what it produced. O our God, will you not execute judgment on them?

Then the last line of the prayer, and there is nothing else like it in the book.

For we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.

Three admissions and one direction. We have no strength. We have no plan — a king saying that in public, in front of his own commanders, about an army already inside the border. And then, instead of a strategy, a posture: our eyes are on you.

It is the shortest honest prayer available to somebody in real trouble, and it is available to anybody, because it requires nothing except telling the truth about your own position and then looking in the right direction.

And verse 13 shows who was standing there while he said it. Meanwhile all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.

The toddlers are at the prayer meeting. Somebody carried them up from the villages and stood holding them in the temple court through the whole of that prayer. A nation that believed the danger was real and believed the answer was here brought the babies to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Battle Is Not Yours but God's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the middle of the assembly (v. 14). His word is do not be afraid ... for the battle is not yours but God's (v. 15), with the route and the position given (v. 16) and the instruction: You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf (v. 17). The king goes face-down and the Levites stand up to praise with a very loud voice (vv. 18-19). At dawn Jehoshaphat charges them, Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established (v. 20), and appoints singers in holy attire to go before the army saying Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The man the Spirit falls on is a chorister. Chronicles had already described the temple singers as men who prophesied with lyres and harps; here one of them stands up in a national emergency and delivers the word that decides it.
verseByVerse.examples: The singers went in front. Not behind the shields, and not in armour — in holy attire, vestments, at the head of the column, singing the line that had been sung when the ark came home and when the fire fell.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly. And he said, "Listen, all Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem and King Jehoshaphat: Thus says the LORD to you, 'Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God's. Tomorrow go down against them. Behold, they will come up by the ascent of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the valley, east of the wilderness of Jeruel. You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf, O Judah and Jerusalem.' Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the LORD will be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel the son of Zechariah ... a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly.

He is a chorister. Four generations of his family are given, and the last identification is the one that matters: of the sons of Asaph — the guild of temple singers David appointed, whose founder had stood east of the altar with cymbals when the ark came home.

The previous book described that guild in a word most readers pass over: the sons of Asaph and Heman and Jeduthun prophesied with lyres and harps and cymbals. It sounded like a way of speaking. Here a man from that choir stands up in the middle of a national emergency and the Spirit of the LORD comes on him, and what he says decides the war.

Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God's.

Not yours. The king had said we are powerless and God's answer is that powerlessness was never the relevant fact, because the fight was not theirs to be strong for. The ownership of the battle changes hands in one clause, exactly as Asa had asked it to when he prayed let not man prevail against you.

Then the orders, and they are specific: tomorrow, the ascent of Ziz, the end of the valley east of the wilderness of Jeruel. God gives a map. And then the strangest military instruction in Scripture:

You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf.

Those words have been said once before, on the shore of a sea, by a man with six hundred chariots behind him and water in front: fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. Judah is being put back at the Red Sea, and told to turn up, form a line, and watch.

And notice the frame around the orders, because Jahaziel says it twice — once at the beginning of the word and once at the end. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde ... Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the LORD will be with you.

Those are not general words of comfort. They are the formula Moses used when he handed Israel to Joshua at the Jordan, and the formula David used twice when he handed the temple to Solomon — be strong and courageous, do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. They are commissioning words, given to a man at the start of a job too big for him.

Here they are given to an army that has just been told it will not have to fight. The same sentence that sent Joshua over a river and put Solomon to work on a temple is used to send Judah down a wadi to stand still, which suggests that standing still in the right place is a job of the same order and takes the same nerve.

Note that they are still ordered out. Stand firm is not stay home. They have to walk twenty miles into a wilderness and stand in front of an army that outnumbers them, and do nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell down before the LORD, worshiping the LORD. And the Levites, of the Kohathites and the Korahites, stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice. And they rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa. And when they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, "Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will succeed." And when he had taken counsel with the people, he appointed those who were to sing to the LORD and praise him in holy attire, as they went before the army, and say, "Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response to the word is worship. The king goes face-down on the ground, the whole assembly falls with him, and then the Levites — Kohathites and Korahites — stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.

Everyone else is on the floor and the choir is on its feet, shouting. The battle is tomorrow and nothing has happened yet.

They rise early and go out to the wilderness of Tekoa, and Jehoshaphat stops the column to say one sentence.

Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will succeed.

In Hebrew the first half is a play on a single root: believe, and you will be made firm. The word behind believing is the word behind reliability — the root we say at the end of a prayer when we say amen. Trust the God who is solid, and you will be made solid. Isaiah would use the identical construction on a later king of Judah who did not take it.

And the second half is remarkable coming from a king: believe his prophets, and you will succeed. Two chapters ago he stood in a gateway in Samaria and heard four hundred men tell a king what he wanted, and one man tell him the truth, and he marched with the four hundred. He has learned something, and he says it out loud to an army.

Then the order of march. He appointed those who were to sing to the LORD and praise him in holy attire, as they went before the army, and say, Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever.

The singers go first. Not behind the shields — in front of the whole column, dressed in vestments rather than armour, unarmed, walking toward a coalition army.

And the words they sing are the words this book cannot stop quoting. David appointed them the afternoon the ark came into Jerusalem. The choir sang them when the glory filled the house and the priests could not stand. The whole nation said them face-down on the pavement when fire came down. Now they are a marching song, sung by men with nothing in their hands, going down a wadi in front of an army that has been told it will not need to fight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush, and the coalition turns on itself until none is left (vv. 22-24). The spoil takes three days to carry (v. 25), and on the fourth they assemble to bless the LORD in a valley that keeps the name Beracah to this day (v. 26). They come home with joy, into Jerusalem with harps and lyres and trumpets, to the house of the LORD (vv. 27-28). The fear of God falls on the surrounding kingdoms when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel (v. 29), and the realm is quiet, for his God gave him rest all around (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The timing in verse 22 is exact: when they BEGAN. Not when they finished, not when the army engaged. The ambush was set while the first line of the song was still going up.
verseByVerse.examples: They went out singing and came back singing, to the same building they had prayed in — harps, lyres and trumpets, into the house of the LORD. The march out and the march home use the same instruments.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come against Judah, so that they were routed. For the men of Ammon and Moab rose against the inhabitants of Mount Seir, devoting them to destruction, and when they had made an end of the inhabitants of Seir, they all helped to destroy one another. When Judah came to the watchtower of the wilderness, they looked toward the horde, and behold, there were dead bodies lying on the ground; none had escaped. When Jehoshaphat and his people came to take their spoil, they found among them, in great numbers, goods, clothing, and precious things, which they took for themselves until they could carry no more. They were three days in taking the spoil, it was so much. On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, for there they blessed the LORD. Therefore the name of that place has been called the Valley of Beracah to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush.

When they began. Not when the singing was finished, not when the two lines met. The first verse was still going up out of the wadi when it started.

What happened is described without any attempt to explain it. The men of Ammon and Moab turned on the men of Seir and destroyed them, and then turned on each other, and they all helped to destroy one another. Three allies in a narrow valley, in the dark or the dust, and something went through them.

By the time Judah reaches the watchtower over the wilderness there is nothing to fight. They looked toward the horde, and behold, there were dead bodies lying on the ground; none had escaped.

Then the spoil, and the detail is domestic: goods, clothing, precious things, which they took for themselves until they could carry no more. They were three days in taking the spoil, it was so much. An army that was told it would not need to fight spent three days carrying property home.

And on the fourth day they did not go home. They assembled in the Valley of Beracah, for there they blessed the LORD. Therefore the name of that place has been called the Valley of Beracah to this day.

Beracah means blessing. They stopped, in the field, with the carts loaded, and held a service — and the name stuck to the ground so hard that people were still calling it that when the Chronicler wrote. Three days collecting, one day thanking, and the day of thanks is the one the map remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, and Jehoshaphat at their head, returning to Jerusalem with joy, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies. They came to Jerusalem with harps and lyres and trumpets, to the house of the LORD. And the fear of God came on all the kingdoms of the countries when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel. So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The homecoming is described in terms of its soundtrack. Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, and Jehoshaphat at their head, returning to Jerusalem with joy, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies. They came to Jerusalem with harps and lyres and trumpets, to the house of the LORD.

They went out singing and they came back singing, with the same instruments, into the same building they had prayed in four days earlier. The march out and the march home are the same procession, and the only thing that changed in between is that God did something.

And the fear of God came on all the kingdoms of the countries when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.

What frightened the neighbours was not Judah's army. The report that travelled was about who had done the fighting, which is precisely what Jahaziel had said would be on display: see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf.

That sentence has appeared once before in this reign. In his third year, after he sent officials and Levites round every town in Judah with the Book of the Law, the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat. The same result, twice, from two entirely different causes — once because a king taught his own villages, and once because God destroyed an army nobody in Judah had touched.

And the chapter's last word on the reign is the word that opened Asa's: So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–37 — And He Did It Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reign is summed up: twenty-five years, and he walked in the way of Asa his father and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD (vv. 31-32). The high places, however, were not taken away; the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers (v. 33), and the record is kept in the chronicles of Jehu the son of Hanani (v. 34). Then, after all of it, he joins Ahaziah of Israel who acted wickedly in a shipbuilding venture, and Eliezer prophesies against him: because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made — and the ships are wrecked (vv. 35-37).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 33 gives the reason the high places stood, and it is not the king. The people had not yet set their hearts. A ruler can pull down an altar; he cannot set a nation's heart, and Jehoshaphat had spent a reign sending the law round the towns trying.
verseByVerse.examples: He had been rebuked by name for exactly this — should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD — and after the greatest deliverance of his life he went into partnership with the house of Ahab again.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. He walked in the way of Asa his father and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD. The high places, however, were not taken away; the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, from first to last, are written in the chronicles of Jehu the son of Hanani, which are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The summary is generous. Twenty-five years; he walked in the way of Asa his father and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD.

Then the qualification, and its reason is not what the reader expects. The high places, however, were not taken away; the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers.

Chapter 17 said he took the high places and the Asherim out of Judah, and the two statements are usually reconciled by supposing the shrines came back, or that some were never reached. What is more interesting is the reason this verse gives, because it does not blame the king at all.

The people had not yet set their hearts.

That is the phrase this book has been using since Rehoboam's reign — the northerners who set their hearts to seek the LORD and emigrated, the king who did not set his heart and was judged for it, and Jehoshaphat himself, of whom Jehu said that he had set his heart to seek God. Here it is applied to a whole nation, in the negative, after twenty years of a king sending the law round every town in the country.

He did everything a ruler can do. He taught them, judged them justly, prayed for them publicly, and led them out with singers in front. He could pull down an altar. He could not set their hearts, and the Chronicler says so without suggesting he should have been able to.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly. He joined him in building ships to go to Tarshish, and they built the ships in Ezion-geber. Then Eliezer the son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, "Because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made." And the ships were wrecked and were not able to go to Tarshish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, after all of it, the chapter ends like this.

After this Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly.

After this. After the fast and the prayer and the toddlers in the temple court, after Jahaziel and the ambush and the three days of spoil and the Valley of Blessing and the harps coming home. After a prophet met him at his own gate and asked whether he should help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD, and told him that wrath had gone out against him for it.

He joins the house of Ahab again. The son this time — Ahaziah, whose reign the book of Kings sums up in two years and a fall through a lattice — and the venture is commercial rather than military, a merchant fleet built at Ezion-geber for the Tarshish run.

Eliezer of Mareshah says the sentence: Because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made. And the ships were wrecked in harbour and never sailed.

The Chronicler puts this at the end of the chapter that contains the best day of Jehoshaphat's life, and offers no reflection on it whatever. He does not withdraw verse 32, which says the man did what was right in the sight of the LORD and did not turn aside. Both sentences stand about the same person.

Some faults are not cured by their consequences. This one had already cost him a battle he should never have been in, a rebuke delivered at his own door, and a marriage that would shortly put Ahab's daughter on the throne of Judah with a knife in her hand. He knew all of it. He liked them anyway, and the ships were built, and God broke them up in the harbour.

20.theology:
Verses 8-9 are Solomon's dedication prayer used for the case it was written for. The fourth petition had asked that when famine or pestilence or siege came and the people stretched out their hands toward that house, God would hear. A hundred and twenty years later a king stands in the same courtyard, in exactly that trouble, and reads the clause back. A building dedicated with a prayer is being used according to its own terms.

And verse 12 is the whole chapter in one line: we are powerless ... we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you. God's answer does not supply the missing strength; it removes the premise — the battle is not yours but God's — and orders them out to stand still and watch, in the words Moses used at the Red Sea.

Verse 33 then declines to blame the king for the high places: the people had not yet set their hearts. He taught them, judged them, prayed for them and led them out behind a choir. A ruler can pull down an altar. He cannot set a nation's heart.
20.examples:
He was afraid, and the text says so in the same breath as the seeking. Fear did not disqualify him; it turned him round.

The toddlers were at the prayer meeting. Families carried them up from the villages and stood holding them through the whole prayer, because they believed the danger was real and believed the answer was there.

The singers walked in front of the army in vestments rather than armour, singing the line that had been sung when the ark came home and when the fire fell — and the ambush was set while the first verse was still going up.

Three days were spent collecting the spoil and the fourth was spent blessing God, and it is the fourth day the map remembered.

21.title: He Departed with No One's Regret
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah; all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.<sup>3</sup>Their father gave them great gifts of silver, gold, and valuable possessions, together with fortified cities in Judah, but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn.<sup>4</sup>When Jehoram had ascended the throne of his father and was established, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.<sup>8</sup>In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own.<sup>9</sup>Then Jehoram passed over with his commanders and all his chariots, and he rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and his chariot commanders.<sup>10</sup>So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. At that time Libnah also revolted from his rule, because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers.<sup>11</sup>Moreover, he made high places in the hill country of Judah and led the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom and made Judah go astray.<sup>12</sup>And a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father, 'Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah,<sup>13</sup>but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel and have enticed Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom, as the house of Ahab led Israel into whoredom, and also you have killed your brothers, of your father's house, who were better than you,<sup>14</sup>behold, the LORD will bring a great plague on your people, your children, your wives, and all your possessions,<sup>15</sup>and you yourself will have a severe sickness with a disease of your bowels, until your bowels come out because of the disease, day by day.'"<sup>16</sup>And the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the anger of the Philistines and of the Arabians who are near the Ethiopians.<sup>17</sup>And they came up against Judah and invaded it and carried away all the possessions they found that belonged to the king's house, and also his sons and his wives, so that no son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest son.<sup>18</sup>And after all this the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease.<sup>19</sup>In the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of the disease, and he died in great agony. His people made no fire in his honor, like the fires made for his fathers.<sup>20</sup>He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he departed with no one's regret. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
21.overview: Jehoshaphat is buried and his eldest son takes the throne. The Chronicler names the six brothers and the estates their father settled on them, and then reports that once Jehoram was established he killed every one of them (vv. 1-4). Eight years; Ahab's ways; and the reason set down in a subordinate clause — for the daughter of Ahab was his wife (vv. 5-6). Against that stands verse 7: God will not destroy the house of David, because of the covenant. Edom and Libnah break away, he builds high places, and a letter arrives from Elijah with two charges and a sentence in two parts (vv. 8-15). Philistines and Arabians strip the palace and carry off his sons and his wives until one is left; the disease comes after all this and takes two years (vv. 16-19). The regnal formula is printed a second time so that one line can land: he departed with no one's regret (v. 20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Six Brothers, and a Lamp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoshaphat is buried with his fathers in the city of David and Jehoram takes the throne (v. 1). The Chronicler names the six brothers and the estates their father settled on them (vv. 2-3), and then: When Jehoram had ascended the throne of his father and was established, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel (v. 4). Eight years, Ahab's ways, and the cause stated in a subordinate clause — for the daughter of Ahab was his wife (vv. 5-6). Then the hinge: Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Kings tells verse 7 in almost the same words but says God was unwilling to destroy JUDAH (2 Kgs 8:19). The Chronicler writes the house of David, and adds a word Kings leaves out here: covenant. Not a fondness for the family, not a policy under review. A sworn bond, holding over a man who has just murdered six brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 is a good father providing for his younger sons, and verse 4 is those same estates becoming a list of addresses. Nothing Jehoshaphat did there was foolish. The one thing he did that was foolish, the marriage of 18:1, he never undid — and it is standing in the palace in verse 6 with a crown on.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place. He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah; all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel. Their father gave them great gifts of silver, gold, and valuable possessions, together with fortified cities in Judah, but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn. When Jehoram had ascended the throne of his father and was established, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.

Buried with his fathers. Hold that phrase for twenty verses, because the chapter ends on a burial that is carefully not that one, and the distance between the two graves is the story.

Then the Chronicler does something he did not have to do. He names the dead man's other sons: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah; all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel. Six names. The list is here so that verse 4 cannot be read as a number. (King of Israel, he says, of a king of Judah — his usual way of speaking. For him the true Israel is wherever the temple stands and David's son sits.)

Their father had provided for them, and provided well: great gifts of silver, gold, and valuable possessions, together with fortified cities in Judah. Rehoboam had done the same for his own sons, spreading them through the walled towns with abundant provisions (11:23). It is what a wise king does — the throne to the eldest, a living and a place to the rest, so that no brother is left with nothing and nothing to do.

Verse 4 turns that provision into a list of addresses.

When Jehoram had ascended the throne of his father and was established, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.

Some of the princes as well, which means the sword went past the family and into Judah's own nobility. But it is the word established that this book has used before. Turn back nine chapters: When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD (12:1). Twice now the sentence has turned at the moment the king stopped being afraid.

Insecurity did not make Jehoram a murderer. Safety did. He waited until the succession was past challenging and then removed everyone who could have challenged it, and the question that puts to the rest of us is not a comfortable one. What did you do with the year when nothing could touch you? Hard times keep a man on his knees whether he likes it or not. The settled years — money in the account, the job secure, nobody asking questions — are the ones that show what he wanted all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife.

There is the cause, dropped into a subordinate clause as though it were a detail of genealogy. For the daughter of Ahab was his wife.

Trace it back three chapters. Now Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab (18:1). That alliance nearly killed him at Ramoth-gilead. A prophet met him at his own gate afterwards and told him wrath had gone out against him for it (19:2). He went into partnership with Ahab's son anyway and watched his fleet break up in harbour (20:35-37). Every warning landed. The one thing he never reversed was the wedding.

Jehoshaphat is one of the better men in this book. He sent teachers round the towns with the Book of the Law, he seated judges in every fortified city and told them they judged for the LORD and not for man, and he stood in the temple court with the toddlers in front of him and prayed we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you. And his one unreversed policy put Ahab's daughter in the palace, where she is still standing in the next chapter, over the bodies of her own grandchildren.

A pet compromise does not stay private and it does not stay yours. It outlives you and it goes on working in people you will never meet.

Then verse 7, and the chapter changes altitude in a single word.

Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.

Kings tells this in nearly the same words, but Kings says God was unwilling to destroy Judah (2 Kgs 8:19). The Chronicler writes the house of David, and he puts in a word Kings does not use here: covenant. Not a preference. Not a policy that could be reviewed in the light of the king's conduct. A sworn bond.

And the image is chosen with care. Not a throne, not a fire, not a dynasty — a lamp. One flame, small enough to carry in the hand and small enough to pinch out between two fingers, kept alight over a man who had just murdered his brothers, and kept alight because of a promise made six generations back to a shepherd. The house of David comes through this chapter for exactly one reason, and the reason is not in the house of David.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom revolts and sets up its own king (v. 8); Jehoram takes the chariots out and ends the night surrounded, cutting his way clear in the dark (v. 9); Edom stays free to this day, and Libnah goes too, because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers (v. 10). He builds high places and leads Jerusalem into whoredom (v. 11). Then a letter arrives from Elijah: two charges — the fathers he would not walk with, and the brothers who were better than you (vv. 12-13) — and a sentence in two parts, a plague on his household and, for the king himself, a disease until your bowels come out ... day by day (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The letter comes before any of it does, and that gap is where this book usually puts its mercy. Rehoboam heard a prophet, humbled himself, and the sentence was cut down (12:6-7); Manasseh will be dragged to Babylon and humble himself there and be brought home (33:12-13). Humbled is the verb 2 Chronicles turns on, and it does not occur once in this chapter. Jehoram had the word in his hand and there is no record that he read it aloud.
verseByVerse.examples: The charge sheet is a family tree. You have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah, but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel. Two working models inside living memory, in his own house, and he went shopping in Samaria for a third.

verseByVerse.quote: In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own. Then Jehoram passed over with his commanders and all his chariots, and he rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and his chariot commanders. So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. At that time Libnah also revolted from his rule, because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers. Moreover, he made high places in the hill country of Judah and led the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom and made Judah go astray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reign now comes apart at the edges, and the Chronicler lets it happen on a map.

In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own.

Verse 9 reports the campaign that followed, and it repays a slow reading. Then Jehoram passed over with his commanders and all his chariots, and he rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and his chariot commanders. He rode out to put down a rebellion and finished the night surrounded, cutting his way clear in the dark. Verse 10 gives the result without softening it: So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. He survived the battle and lost the country.

Set that beside his father, one chapter back. Jehoshaphat faced an invasion, prayed in the temple courtyard, sent the choir out in front of the army, and then spent three days carrying the plunder home because there was more of it than they could lift in one (20:25). His son takes out the chariots and brings back nothing but himself.

Libnah goes as well, a Levitical town on the Philistine border, and here the narrator stops narrating and states the cause: because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers. Forsaken is this book's word. It was the charge against Rehoboam when the rule was established, it was in the prophet's mouth to Asa, and it will be the epitaph of the whole nation in chapter 36. A man does not usually announce that he is leaving God. He simply stops going where God is, and one day the map is smaller.

Verse 11 says what moved into the space. Moreover, he made high places in the hill country of Judah and led the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom and made Judah go astray. Asa had pulled high places down (14:3); Jehoshaphat pulled more down (17:6) and the record still admits that some stood (20:33). Jehoram builds them. And the word for what he leads the capital into is the marriage word. Judah is not charged with a policy error. She is charged with adultery, which is how God has always spoken of this, because that is what it feels like from his side.

verseByVerse.quote: And a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father, 'Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah, but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel and have enticed Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem into whoredom, as the house of Ahab led Israel into whoredom, and also you have killed your brothers, of your father's house, who were better than you, behold, the LORD will bring a great plague on your people, your children, your wives, and all your possessions, and you yourself will have a severe sickness with a disease of your bowels, until your bowels come out because of the disease, day by day.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet.

Elijah appears once in this book, and this is it. Not on Carmel with the fire falling, not under the broom tree, not at Horeb in the silence — a document, delivered to a king in Jerusalem. The prophet who spent his ministry in Ahab's face writes to Ahab's son-in-law in the south. How the letter squares with the whirlwind of 2 Kings 2 is not told us, and the honest thing is to leave the gap open rather than fill it with a guess.

The letter names God as the LORD, the God of David your father, and then builds the charge sheet out of fathers. Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah, but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel. Two working models inside living memory, both of them in his own house, and he went to Samaria for a pattern instead.

Then the second charge, and it should stop the reader dead. And also you have killed your brothers, of your father's house, who were better than you.

God has read the list in verse 2. He has an opinion about those six men and he states it out loud: they were better than the man who killed them. Jehoram did not merely break a commandment; he removed from Judah six men heaven rated above him.

The sentence comes in two parts and both are exact. Behold, the LORD will bring a great plague on your people, your children, your wives, and all your possessions — and then, for the king himself, you yourself will have a severe sickness with a disease of your bowels, until your bowels come out because of the disease, day by day. Day by day. Not a stroke but an itinerary.

Everything in that letter arrives before any of it happens, and the gap between the word and the blow is where this book keeps its mercy. Rehoboam heard a prophet, humbled himself, and the sentence was cut down to a part of itself (12:6-7). Manasseh will be dragged to Babylon with hooks in him, humble himself there, and be brought home (33:12-13). Humbled is the verb 2 Chronicles turns on — and it does not occur once in this chapter. Jehoram had the word in his hand for two years. There is no record that he ever read it out loud, or tore his clothes, or asked one person to pray.

One more thing waits in that charge, once its weight is felt. The accusation God brings against Jehoram is that he killed a brother better than himself. It is the accusation that lies against us all, for there was a brother better than every one of us, of our own father's house, and we killed him. The difference is what the blood says afterwards. Abel's blood cried out of the ground for justice on the man who spilled it; this brother's blood speaks a better word, and the word it speaks is pardon (Heb 12:24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD stirred up the Philistines and the Arabians, who strip the palace and carry off his sons and his wives until one son is left (vv. 16-17). And after all this the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease (v. 18); two years later it kills him, and his people made no fire in his honor, like the fires made for his fathers (v. 19). The regnal formula is printed a second time so that the addition can land: And he departed with no one's regret. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Both halves of the covenant are working in the same chapter and neither cancels the other. The judgment is specific, announced, and carried out to the letter. The promise is also specific, and it holds — the lamp of verse 7 comes out of this reign still lit, down to one boy, and out of the next chapter down to a baby under a nurse's arm in a bedroom.
verseByVerse.examples: They made a fire for Asa — spices, a bier, a very great fire in his honor (16:14) — and Asa had jailed a prophet and died with diseased feet. Even he got the bonfire. Jehoram got a cold hearth and an address without a room, buried in David's city and kept out of the kings' tombs.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the anger of the Philistines and of the Arabians who are near the Ethiopians. And they came up against Judah and invaded it and carried away all the possessions they found that belonged to the king's house, and also his sons and his wives, so that no son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest son. And after all this the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease. In the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of the disease, and he died in great agony. His people made no fire in his honor, like the fires made for his fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the anger of the Philistines and of the Arabians who are near the Ethiopians.

Those two peoples have stood together in this book once before, and it was four chapters ago. Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents and silver for tribute, and the Arabians also brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats (17:11). The same two nations, one generation apart, on the same roads. Under the father they came up with tribute. Under the son they come up and empty the palace.

The emptying is itemised in the letter's own order. They came up against Judah and invaded it and carried away all the possessions they found that belonged to the king's house, and also his sons and his wives. Possessions, sons, wives. The plague on his household did not arrive as an illness. It arrived on horses, in daylight, through the gate.

Then the chapter's arithmetic closes on him: so that no son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest son. He had put six brothers to the sword to make a throne safe. He ends with one boy left, the last one anybody would have counted. And the dynasty he purified by murder will be down to a single baby under a nurse's arm before the next chapter is out.

And after all this the LORD struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease.

After all this. The disease comes last. It is not the opening move of a short-tempered God but the closing one, after a marriage, a massacre, two rebellions, a letter and a raid have all gone by without a word of repentance out of him.

Two years, exactly as the letter said, and he died in great agony. Then a line the Chronicler could have left out and did not: His people made no fire in his honor, like the fires made for his fathers. They had made one for Asa — spices prepared by the perfumer's art, and a very great fire in his honor (16:14) — and Asa was a man who jailed the prophet who told him the truth and died with diseased feet. Even he got the bonfire. Jehoram got a cold hearth, and everybody in Jerusalem knew what the cold hearth meant.

verseByVerse.quote: He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he departed with no one's regret. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.

We were told that in verse 5, in the same words. The formula is printed twice on purpose, so that the second time through we are listening for what gets added.

And he departed with no one's regret.

The Hebrew is blunter than the English: he went without being wanted. Not howled at from the gate — simply not missed. Eight years on the throne of David, and when the throne emptied what the city felt was relief.

That yields a question with a real answer, and most people know theirs before they finish reading it. If the news went round your street tomorrow, who would be relieved? Not who would be sad; that one is easy and it flatters us. Who would breathe out?

They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings. He got the address and not the room. He lies a few hundred yards from the man whose covenant is the only reason his family still exists, and outside the chamber where the kings were laid.

There is one more grave to set beside that one. The word behind no one's regret is built on the root Isaiah uses of the Servant: he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isa 53:2). Jehoram had nothing anyone wanted, and he had earned every inch of it. The Son of David had nothing anyone wanted, and had earned none of it — despised, rejected, condemned outside the city, and buried in a grave that was not his own. The lamp that verse 7 refused to let go out was being kept for him. It was not kept for the sake of the men who carried it; not one of them deserved it, and this one least of all. It was kept because God had sworn, and because the small flame at the end of that long dark corridor was the light of the world.

21.theology:
Verse 7 is the chapter's spine, and the Chronicler has sharpened it. Kings says God was unwilling to destroy Judah (2 Kgs 8:19); this says the house of David, and supplies the ground — the covenant that he had made with David. The promise is not being kept because the current holder is bearable. It is being kept because it was sworn, and the man it is being kept over is the worst king Judah has had.

Both edges of that covenant cut in the same twenty verses. The judgment is announced before it falls, itemised, and carried out to the letter — possessions, sons, wives, and then the king's own body, day by day. The promise is equally specific and it holds. What comes out of this reign is a lamp, not a blaze: one surviving son, and then one hidden baby.

The verb this book turns on is missing here, and its absence is the verdict. Kings in 2 Chronicles humble themselves and are answered — Rehoboam under Shishak, Manasseh in a Babylonian prison, Josiah over an open scroll. Jehoram received the clearest warning any of them got, in writing, with two years to act on it, and never bent.
21.examples:
Six men had names, households and towns of their own, and their father's careful provision for them is what made them worth killing.

A good king's one unreversed compromise walked into the palace in a wedding dress and was still giving orders two reigns later.

A king rode out to crush a revolt and spent the night cutting his way out of an encirclement, and the territory was gone anyway; his father had spent three days collecting plunder he had not fought for.

Under one king the Philistines and the Arabians came up the road with rams and goats and silver. Under his son they came up the same road and took the queen and the princes.

They lit a great fire for Asa, who had jailed a prophet. For this king they lit nothing.

22.title: Hidden in the House of God
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And the inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, his youngest son, king in his place, for the band of men that came with the Arabians to the camp had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah reigned.<sup>2</sup>Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri.<sup>3</sup>He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly.<sup>4</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done. For after the death of his father they were his counselors, to his undoing.<sup>5</sup>He even followed their counsel and went with Jehoram the son of Ahab king of Israel to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. And the Syrians wounded Joram,<sup>6</sup>and he returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that he had received at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was wounded.<sup>7</sup>But it was ordained by God that the downfall of Ahaziah should come about through his going to visit Joram. For when he came there, he went out with Jehoram to meet Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab.<sup>8</sup>And when Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab, he met the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, who attended Ahaziah, and he killed them.<sup>9</sup>He searched for Ahaziah, and he was captured while hiding in Samaria, and he was brought to Jehu and put to death. They buried him, for they said, "He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." And the house of Ahaziah had no one able to rule the kingdom.<sup>10</sup>Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family of the house of Judah.<sup>11</sup>But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were about to be put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, because she was a sister of Ahaziah, hid him from Athaliah, so that she did not put him to death.<sup>12</sup>And he remained with them six years, hidden in the house of God, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
22.overview: One son is left alive, so Jerusalem crowns him (v. 1). Ahaziah reigns a year, and the Chronicler names the cause of the disaster twice: his mother counselled him and Ahab's household counselled him, to his undoing (vv. 2-4). On their advice he rides to Ramoth-gilead, the town that nearly killed his grandfather, and then goes down to Jezreel to sit with his wounded cousin (vv. 5-6). It was ordained by God that the visit would finish him: Jehu is there, executing judgment on Ahab's house, and Judah's princes go down with him (vv. 7-8). He is buried for his grandfather's sake (v. 9). Then Athaliah destroys the royal family, and a priest's wife steals one baby into the temple, where he is hidden six years while she reigns (vv. 10-12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — His Mother Was His Counselor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The raiders have left one son, so the inhabitants of Jerusalem make Ahaziah king (v. 1). Twenty-two years old, one year on the throne, and his mother is Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri (v. 2). Then the diagnosis, given twice: his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly (v. 3), and after the death of his father they were his counselors, to his undoing (v. 4). Following that counsel he goes to war alongside Ahab's son at Ramoth-gilead, and when Joram is wounded he goes down to Jezreel to see him (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler does not say Ahaziah was wicked by temperament. He says the boy's counsel came from one house and it ruined him. Rehoboam at least had two sets of advisers in front of him and chose the worse (10:6-8); Jehoshaphat took trouble over who sat on his benches (19:8-11). This court has one board, and every seat on it belongs to Samaria.
verseByVerse.examples: Ramoth-gilead is where his grandfather went with Ahab and was nearly killed, after a prophet had told the whole council what would happen (ch. 18). Two reigns later the family is back at the same town with the same allies. Some roads a household keeps driving down until one of them does not come home.

verseByVerse.quote: And the inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, his youngest son, king in his place, for the band of men that came with the Arabians to the camp had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah reigned. Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri. He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done. For after the death of his father they were his counselors, to his undoing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, his youngest son, king in his place, for the band of men that came with the Arabians to the camp had killed all the older sons.

The city has to do it. There is no orderly succession left to run, because the raid of the last chapter went through the royal nursery, and the only son above ground is the youngest. This is the same boy called Jehoahaz at 21:17; the two halves of the name have simply been turned round. Either way it means the LORD has taken hold of him, which is a heavy name for a man with twelve months to live.

His mother's name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri.

At 21:6 she was the daughter of Ahab. Here she is Omri's granddaughter, which reaches back another generation and names the whole northern dynasty. What came into Judah through one wedding was not a wife. It was a house.

Then the Chronicler gives his diagnosis, and he gives it twice so that nobody can file it under bad character. He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly. And again: For after the death of his father they were his counselors, to his undoing.

Counselor is a job title. The man had an advisory council, and every chair at that table was occupied by Ahab's family. Rehoboam at least had two sets of advisers to choose between and chose the flatterers (10:6-8). His great-grandfather Jehoshaphat had gone to real trouble over who sat on which bench and who answered for what (19:8-11). Ahaziah has one board, and it is staffed out of Samaria.

Which puts a plain question to anyone reading. Not who do you admire, and not whose books are on the shelf. Who do you actually ring at eleven at night when the decision has to be made by morning? Those people are your council, whatever you would have said if asked. The voices whose approval you want are the voices that govern you.

verseByVerse.quote: He even followed their counsel and went with Jehoram the son of Ahab king of Israel to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. And the Syrians wounded Joram, and he returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that he had received at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was wounded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He even followed their counsel and went with Jehoram the son of Ahab king of Israel to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead.

Ramoth-gilead. Look at where this family keeps going.

Four chapters ago his grandfather Jehoshaphat sat in a robe beside Ahab at the gate of Samaria, heard four hundred prophets say go up, heard one prophet say he had seen Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd, watched that prophet slapped and jailed, and rode out to Ramoth-gilead anyway. He came home alive only because he screamed and God turned the chariots off him.

Now the grandson rides to the same town with the same family against the same enemy. The warning is on file. It was given publicly, in front of two kings, and it was proved right within a day. Two reigns later nobody in the palace can remember why the name of that town ought to make them hesitate.

The Syrians wound Joram, and he goes back to Jezreel to recover. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was wounded.

That is the sentence that kills him, and there is nothing wicked in it. It is a family visit. A man goes to sit with a wounded relative, which is a decent thing to do and would be commended anywhere else in Scripture. The trouble is not the visit. The trouble is that this was his family, and he had spent his one year in office making sure of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — It Was Ordained by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But it was ordained by God that the downfall of Ahaziah should come about through his going to visit Joram (v. 7). He arrives just as Jehu, anointed to destroy Ahab's house, arrives; Jehu kills the princes of Judah and Ahaziah's nephews in Ahaziah's own retinue (v. 8), then hunts him down in Samaria and executes him. And they bury him, for they said, He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 says the visit was ordained, and verses 3-5 say he followed wicked counsel of his own free choosing. The Chronicler prints both within five verses and does not treat them as rivals. God's hand is not an excuse offered on Ahaziah's behalf; it is the reason the reader is told the story at all.
verseByVerse.examples: The one kindness in his death is borrowed. He is not buried for anything he did. He is buried because of what an old man two generations back had been — a man who sought the LORD with his whole heart — and the soldiers digging the grave say so out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: But it was ordained by God that the downfall of Ahaziah should come about through his going to visit Joram. For when he came there, he went out with Jehoram to meet Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab. And when Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab, he met the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, who attended Ahaziah, and he killed them. He searched for Ahaziah, and he was captured while hiding in Samaria, and he was brought to Jehu and put to death. They buried him, for they said, "He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." And the house of Ahaziah had no one able to rule the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it was ordained by God that the downfall of Ahaziah should come about through his going to visit Joram.

The narrator steps forward at precisely the point where a reader would reach for the word coincidence. Wrong week, wrong town, wrong cousin. No, says the Chronicler: from God. The sick-visit that looks like the most incidental thing in the chapter is the hinge, and it was set there.

Notice that he says this without lifting a gram of weight off Ahaziah. Four verses earlier the same narrator said the man followed wicked counsel and did evil in the LORD's sight. Both sentences stand in the same paragraph, and the text feels no strain between them. Scripture does not protect God's sovereignty by shrinking human guilt, and it does not protect human responsibility by making God a spectator. The man chose his advisers, kept them, obeyed them, and went where they sent him. And God had appointed the road.

Jehu, anointed to end Ahab's house, finds Judah's princes and Ahaziah's nephews travelling in Ahaziah's own party and kills them (v. 8). A Davidic king had folded his household so completely into an Omride household that when judgment came for the one it swept up the other. He is run down and executed in Samaria, of all cities, hiding.

Then comes the strangest kindness in the chapter. They buried him, for they said, He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart.

He gets a grave, and the reason given has nothing to do with him. Nobody says he was a good king or a brave one or even a young one. They say whose grandson he was, and they describe the grandfather in the language this book keeps for its best men. The single decent thing that happens to Ahaziah after death happens on somebody else's record.

Which is a small, sideways picture of the only hope any of us has. Nothing in the life just ended earned that grave. It was granted because of another man's whole-hearted seeking. Christ sought God with a whole heart from Nazareth to the cross, and the burial of every believer, and the rising after it, is granted on the strength of his record and not our own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — A Baby in a Bedroom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Athaliah sees her son is dead, and she arose and destroyed all the royal family of the house of Judah (v. 10) — her own grandchildren. But Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter, Ahaziah's sister and wife of Jehoiada the priest, steals one baby out of the condemned nursery and puts him and his nurse in a bedroom (v. 11). And he remained with them six years, hidden in the house of God, while Athaliah reigned over the land (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the only place in the book where somebody sets out to end David's line on purpose, and it very nearly works. What stands between the promise of 21:7 and its extinction is one woman, one nurse and one locked room. The covenant does not survive because it is defended by power; it survives because God keeps it, and the means he used that week were two women and a baby who had to be kept quiet.
verseByVerse.examples: Chronicles adds a detail Kings leaves out: Jehoshabeath was married to the high priest (2 Kgs 11:2 names her without it). That is the mechanism. A princess who is also the priest's wife is the one person in Jerusalem with a reason to be in the palace and a key to the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family of the house of Judah. But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were about to be put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, because she was a sister of Ahaziah, hid him from Athaliah, so that she did not put him to death. And he remained with them six years, hidden in the house of God, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family of the house of Judah.

Read that again with the family tree in front of you. The royal family of the house of Judah are her grandsons. She had married into David's line, buried her husband, buried her son, and now she goes through the nursery so that nobody with David's blood can take back the throne she means to sit on.

It is the one moment in this book when somebody sets out deliberately to end the line of David. Jehoram thinned it by murder and a raid thinned it further, but no one before her had aimed at the promise itself. Twenty verses ago God said he would not destroy the house of David because of the covenant he had made. Ahab's daughter is now in the corridor with soldiers, doing exactly that.

But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were about to be put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom.

One woman, walking the wrong way down a corridor full of soldiers, carrying a baby out of a room where children are being killed. And the Chronicler tells us something Kings does not: she is the wife of Jehoiada the priest. There is the mechanism. A king's daughter married to the high priest is the one person in Jerusalem who has a reason to be in the palace and a key to the temple, and she used both inside the same hour.

There is a second woman in that verse and she is never named. The nurse went into hiding with the child and stayed. Six years of keeping an infant fed, and quiet, and out of sight, in a building where hundreds of people came and went. Whatever else the covenant needed that week, it needed somebody willing to be shut in a room for six years with a boy who could not be allowed to cry at the wrong moment.

And he remained with them six years, hidden in the house of God, while Athaliah reigned over the land.

The rightful king is in the temple and the usurper is on the throne. For six years anyone in Jerusalem looking for the king of Judah was looking at the wrong building. It is not the last time that is true. A true King was carried into Egypt by night while a killer held Jerusalem, and grew up in a village nobody rated, and stood among people who did not know who was in the room.

The lamp of 21:7 is down to a wick in a back room behind a locked door, in the arms of a woman whose name most readers have never heard. It has never been closer to going out, and it was never in any danger at all. God had sworn, and the whole armed strength of Ahab's house, with the throne in its hand and no opposition left alive, could not put out one small flame that God had promised to keep.

22.theology:
Verse 7 is the theological centre. The Chronicler puts God's ordaining and Ahaziah's guilt in the same paragraph, five verses apart, and does not soften either. The king chose his counsellors and obeyed them; God appointed the road they sent him down. Scripture never protects the one truth by shrinking the other.
