Verse 9 is the chapter's grace, given sideways. Ahaziah is buried on the strength of a record that is not his — the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart. Nothing in his own year on the throne could have bought that grave.

And verse 12 is the covenant of 21:7 at its narrowest point. The promise to David comes through this chapter reduced to one hidden child, kept alive by two women in a locked room while the woman on the throne hunts the family. God's sworn word is never safer than when it looks finished, because what keeps it is not the strength of the people carrying it.
22.examples:
A young king's advisory board had one household on it, and the historian names that, and not his appetites, as what ruined him.

The family rode to Ramoth-gilead a second time, two reigns after a prophet had told them in open court what would happen there.

He went to sit with a wounded relative, which is a decent thing to do, and it was the last thing he did.

The soldiers who buried him gave their reason out loud, and it was about his grandfather.

A princess married to the high priest carried a baby out of a nursery where children were being killed, and an unnamed nurse kept him quiet in a back room of the temple for six years.

23.title: The King's Son Shall Reign
23.text: <sup>1</sup>But in the seventh year Jehoiada took courage and entered into a covenant with the commanders of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, Azariah the son of Obed, Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri.<sup>2</sup>And they went about through Judah and gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, and the heads of fathers' houses of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And all the assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God. And Jehoiada said to them, "Behold, the king's son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David.<sup>4</sup>This is the thing that you shall do: of you priests and Levites who come off duty on the Sabbath, one third shall be gatekeepers,<sup>5</sup>and one third shall be at the king's house and one third at the Gate of the Foundation. And all the people shall be in the courts of the house of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>Let no one enter the house of the LORD except the priests and ministering Levites. They may enter, for they are holy, but all the people shall keep the charge of the LORD.<sup>7</sup>The Levites shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever enters the house shall be put to death. Be with the king when he comes in and when he goes out."<sup>8</sup>The Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men, who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, for Jehoiada the priest did not dismiss the divisions.<sup>9</sup>And Jehoiada the priest gave to the captains the spears and the large and small shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of God.<sup>10</sup>And he set all the people as a guard for the king, every man with his weapon in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house.<sup>11</sup>Then they brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king, and Jehoiada and his sons anointed him, and they said, "Long live the king."<sup>12</sup>When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she went into the house of the LORD to the people.<sup>13</sup>And when she looked, there was the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and the singers with their musical instruments leading in the celebration. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!"<sup>14</sup>Then Jehoiada the priest brought out the captains who were set over the army, saying to them, "Bring her out between the ranks, and anyone who follows her is to be put to death with the sword." For the priest said, "Do not put her to death in the house of the LORD."<sup>15</sup>So they laid hands on her, and she went into the entrance of the horse gate of the king's house, and they put her to death there.<sup>16</sup>And Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and all the people and the king that they should be the LORD's people.<sup>17</sup>Then all the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars.<sup>18</sup>And Jehoiada posted watchmen for the house of the LORD under the direction of the Levitical priests and the Levites whom David had organized to be in charge of the house of the LORD, to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, as it is written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and with singing, according to the order of David.<sup>19</sup>He stationed the gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD so that no one should enter who was in any way unclean.<sup>20</sup>And he took the captains, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the upper gate to the king's house. And they set the king on the royal throne.<sup>21</sup>So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword.
23.overview: In the seventh year Jehoiada moves. He binds five named commanders by covenant, gathers the Levites and family heads out of every town in Judah, and presents the hidden boy to the assembly: Behold, the king's son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David (vv. 1-3). The plan is laid out in detail — three divisions on duty, nobody but priests and Levites inside the house, and armed men around the child wherever he moves (vv. 4-7). Both Sabbath shifts are held on duty, David's own weapons come out of the temple store, and Joash is crowned, handed the testimony, anointed and acclaimed (vv. 8-11). Athaliah follows the noise, sees the boy at the royal pillar, cries treason, and is taken out and executed at the horse gate (vv. 12-15). Then a covenant that the people should be the LORD's, the demolition of the Baal temple, the Levitical order restored, and the king brought down to his throne in a city that is finally quiet (vv. 16-21).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But in the seventh year Jehoiada took courage and made a covenant with five named commanders of hundreds (v. 1), who quietly gathered the Levites and the heads of families from every town in Judah (v. 2). The assembly covenants with the boy in the house of God, and Jehoiada presents him: Behold, the king's son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David (v. 3). Then the plan, in detail — three divisions of the Sabbath shift at the gates, the palace and the Gate of the Foundation, the people in the courts (vv. 4-5), nobody but priests and ministering Levites inside the house itself (v. 6), and the Levites ringing the boy with weapons in their hands (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The warrant is not that Joash has the better claim by blood, though he has. It is as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David. A promise made generations earlier is treated as the operative document in a room full of armed men, and everything that happens in this chapter happens because somebody took that promise to be still in force.
verseByVerse.examples: The courage in verse 1 has a date on it, and the date is what makes it costly. Six years Jehoiada had the rightful king under his own roof and did nothing visible, while a woman who had murdered that child's brothers sat on the throne. Waiting is not the opposite of courage. Sometimes it is most of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the seventh year Jehoiada took courage and entered into a covenant with the commanders of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, Azariah the son of Obed, Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri. And they went about through Judah and gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, and the heads of fathers' houses of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem. And all the assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God. And Jehoiada said to them, "Behold, the king's son! Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in the seventh year Jehoiada took courage and entered into a covenant with the commanders of hundreds.

Read the date before the courage. The seventh year. That means six years in which this same man did nothing that anyone could see.

Six years with the rightful king of Judah asleep in his own house. Six years of walking past Athaliah in the corridor, of conducting worship in a city that had a working Baal temple down the road, of watching a woman who had cut the throats of his wife's nephews give orders in David's name. Whatever we mean by courage, it has to be big enough to include those years. He was not waiting because he was frightened. He was waiting because a seven-year-old cannot be crowned at one, and because a coup that fails kills the boy.

Then five names: Azariah the son of Jeroham, Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, Azariah the son of Obed, Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri. Kings tells this story and names none of them. The Chronicler writes down the five men who agreed to risk execution for a child they had never met, and their fathers' names as well, because somebody should know.

They go quietly round Judah and bring in the Levites from every town and the heads of the families. Kings has this coup run by the Carites, foreign mercenaries on the palace payroll. Chronicles tells it from inside the temple, and the men in the corridors are priests and Levites and clan elders. The two accounts stand as they are; this one is interested in the house of God and who serves in it.

And then the boy is produced. Behold, the king's son!

Everyone in that room had spent six years believing the family was finished. Athaliah had gone through the nursery herself. Now a child stands in front of the assembly, and the priest gives the legal ground for what they are about to do, and it is not a claim about blood. Let him reign, as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David.

The document they are acting on is a promise. Not a treaty, not a precedent, not the will of the people, though they have that too. God said something about David's sons more than a century and a half before, and these men have decided to treat that sentence as still binding on a Tuesday morning with soldiers in the courtyard.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the thing that you shall do: of you priests and Levites who come off duty on the Sabbath, one third shall be gatekeepers, and one third shall be at the king's house and one third at the Gate of the Foundation. And all the people shall be in the courts of the house of the LORD. Let no one enter the house of the LORD except the priests and ministering Levites. They may enter, for they are holy, but all the people shall keep the charge of the LORD. The Levites shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever enters the house shall be put to death. Be with the king when he comes in and when he goes out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is a set of orders, and what those orders are made of is the surprise.

Three divisions of the Sabbath shift: one third on the gates, one third at the palace, one third at the Gate of the Foundation, with the people massed in the courts. Then this: Let no one enter the house of the LORD except the priests and ministering Levites. They may enter, for they are holy, but all the people shall keep the charge of the LORD.

Consider the situation. The high priest is running an armed operation against a sitting monarch, in the temple, with the life of the last Davidic heir on the table, and the thing he spends his instructions on is who is allowed through which door. A man in that position has every excuse to say that the rules can wait until Tuesday.

He does not. The holiness of the house is not suspended because the stakes are high. It is one of the quietest and most impressive things in the chapter, and it is exactly what a later king will fail to do: Uzziah, with far less pressure on him, will walk into that same house with a censer in his hand because he is strong and it seems reasonable (26:16).

The last order is the one that tells you what Jehoiada was actually thinking about. The Levites shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand ... Be with the king when he comes in and when he goes out.

Not hold the gate. Not take the palace. Stay with the boy. Every other objective in the operation is negotiable, and one is not: wherever that child goes, a ring of armed men goes with him. God had promised a lamp to David's sons, and on this particular morning the lamp was seven years old and could be picked up in two hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — The Crown and the Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites do exactly as ordered, and Jehoiada keeps both Sabbath shifts on duty at once (v. 8). He arms the captains from the temple store with the spears and the large and small shields that had been King David's (v. 9), and rings the house with armed men (v. 10). Then they brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony; they anoint him and shout Long live the king (v. 11). Athaliah hears the noise, comes into the house of the LORD, sees the boy at his pillar with the trumpeters and the singers, and tears her clothes: Treason! Treason! (vv. 12-13). Jehoiada has her taken out between the ranks — Do not put her to death in the house of the LORD — and she is killed at the horse gate of the palace (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 11 hands a child two things in the same minute: a crown and a copy of the law. The testimony is the document that defines and limits the office he has just received (Deut 17:18-20). Israel's king is not the source of the law but its first subject, and the ceremony says so before he has given a single order.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is where the plan actually turns. The one hour in the week when twice the usual number of Levites can be in the temple without a single question being asked is the Sabbath changeover, and Jehoiada simply does not send the outgoing shift home. The most dangerous half-hour in Judah's history was staged inside the duty rota.

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men, who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, for Jehoiada the priest did not dismiss the divisions. And Jehoiada the priest gave to the captains the spears and the large and small shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of God. And he set all the people as a guard for the king, every man with his weapon in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house. Then they brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king, and Jehoiada and his sons anointed him, and they said, "Long live the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men, who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, for Jehoiada the priest did not dismiss the divisions.

That is the whole plan, and it is beautiful. The temple ran on a rota. Every Sabbath one course of priests and Levites came off duty and another came on, and for a short while both were in the building at once — which is the one hour in the week when twice the normal number of armed-eligible men can be inside the temple precincts and nobody at the palace thinks anything of it. Jehoiada simply did not send the outgoing shift home. The most dangerous morning in Judah's history was staged inside the duty roster.

Then he opens the store. And Jehoiada the priest gave to the captains the spears and the large and small shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of God.

David's own weapons, laid up in the temple, brought out and put into the hands of men standing guard over David's last descendant. They had lain in that store since the day there was a house of God to lay them in. The founder's armoury is issued to defend the founder's promise, and the whole scene says what this book keeps saying: the past is not decoration.

Then they brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony.

Two objects, one gesture. The crown is the power. The testimony is the law — the copy of the covenant document that Deuteronomy required a king of Israel to keep beside him and read all the days of his life, so that his heart would not be lifted up above his brothers (Deut 17:18-20). Judah hands its king authority and the limits of that authority in the same minute, before he has given a single order.

Every ruler wants the crown. This ceremony says you may not have it without the book. And the same holds several rungs further down, wherever anyone is given charge of anything — a department, a household, a class, a congregation. Authority handed over without a standard over it is not a gift. It is a trap with a ribbon on.

verseByVerse.quote: When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she went into the house of the LORD to the people. And when she looked, there was the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and the singers with their musical instruments leading in the celebration. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!" Then Jehoiada the priest brought out the captains who were set over the army, saying to them, "Bring her out between the ranks, and anyone who follows her is to be put to death with the sword." For the priest said, "Do not put her to death in the house of the LORD." So they laid hands on her, and she went into the entrance of the horse gate of the king's house, and they put her to death there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she went into the house of the LORD to the people.

What brought her out was the sound of praise. She had ruled six years without ever needing to enter that building, and the one thing that finally walked her through its gate was a noise she could not account for.

Then the Chronicler shows us the room through her eyes. There was the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and the singers with their musical instruments leading in the celebration.

By his pillar. There was a place in the temple where the king of Judah stood, a fixed station with a fixed name, and it had been empty for six years, and she had known it was empty. Now a child is standing in it, and the trumpeters are on either side of him, and the choir is running the room. Judah's worship and Judah's throne have found each other again in the space of one morning.

And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, Treason! Treason!

It is the last word of a woman who took the throne by killing the children who owned it. She is not wrong that a conspiracy has taken place. She is simply the last person in Judah entitled to be shocked by one.

Then the order that shows what kind of man is in charge of this. The crowd has her. The captains are armed. Nobody in that courtyard would have raised a hand to stop them doing anything at all to her, and everybody there had a personal reason. Jehoiada says two things: take her out between the ranks, and do not put her to death in the house of the LORD.

At the moment of victory, the one instruction he gives is about God's honour and not about her. She is walked out to the horse gate of the palace and executed there — at the seat of the power she seized, and not in the house she despised, which she does not get to defile even by dying in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — And the City Was Quiet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoiada makes a covenant between himself, the people and the king that they should be the LORD's people (v. 16), and the crowd goes straight from the temple to the house of Baal and pulls it down, killing Mattan its priest at his own altars (v. 17). The Levitical order is reinstated as it is written in the Law of Moses ... according to the order of David, with gatekeepers set so that nothing unclean comes in (vv. 18-19). Then the procession: captains, nobles, governors and all the people bring the king down through the upper gate and seat him on the throne (v. 20). So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Three covenants are cut in this chapter and they climb. In verse 1 a priest binds five officers to himself. In verse 3 the assembly binds itself to the king. In verse 16 priest, people and king together bind themselves to the LORD. The politics is settled by verse 15; verse 16 is what the politics was for.
verseByVerse.examples: A functioning Baal temple stood in the city of David, with altars in use and a priest on the staff, and everyone knew the address. The people who tore it down that morning had walked past it for six years.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and all the people and the king that they should be the LORD's people. Then all the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And Jehoiada posted watchmen for the house of the LORD under the direction of the Levitical priests and the Levites whom David had organized to be in charge of the house of the LORD, to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, as it is written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and with singing, according to the order of David. He stationed the gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD so that no one should enter who was in any way unclean. And he took the captains, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the upper gate to the king's house. And they set the king on the royal throne. So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and all the people and the king that they should be the LORD's people.

Count the covenants in this chapter and watch them climb. In verse 1 a priest binds five officers to himself. In verse 3 the assembly binds itself to the king. Here in verse 16 priest, people and king together bind themselves to God. The politics was finished at verse 15. This is what the politics was for.

And a covenant that means anything gets up and walks. Then all the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars.

There had been a house of Baal in the city of David. Not a shrine on a hill outside town — a functioning temple with altars in use and a priest on the staff whose name everybody knew. The people who pulled it down that morning had been walking past it for six years. That is what a national repentance looks like when it is real: it is dated, it is public, and it leaves rubble.

Then the positive half, which matters as much. Watchmen posted, the Levitical order restored under the priests whom David had organized, burnt offerings resumed as it is written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and with singing, according to the order of David, and gatekeepers set so that nothing unclean comes through. Moses and David named in one breath as the two authorities, exactly as at Solomon's dedication. Tearing down Baal's house was one morning's work. Restarting the daily offerings and the singing is the work of every morning after.

The last two verses are a procession. Captains, nobles, governors and all the people bring the boy down from the temple through the upper gate and set him on the throne. He goes from the house of God to the house of the king, escorted by the whole nation, along a route the city could watch.

So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet.

Quiet. Not triumphant, not loud, not even, in that final word, especially joyful. After six years of a woman who came to power over her grandchildren's bodies, the thing the Chronicler chooses to record is that Jerusalem could breathe out.

And there is one more coronation to set beside this one. A priest stood in front of a crowd, pointed at the rightful king and said Behold, the king's son, and the trumpets went and the people shouted Long live the king. Nine hundred years later a governor stood in front of another crowd, pointed at another son of David, bleeding and crowned with something else, and said Behold your King — and that crowd shouted for his blood (John 19:14-15). The first king was hidden in the temple and brought out to reign. The second was brought out to die, and by dying he took a throne no coup will ever touch, and the quiet he purchased for his city is not for six years but forever.

23.theology:
The legal ground for the whole chapter is a sentence God spoke generations earlier: as the LORD spoke concerning the sons of David. Jehoiada does not argue from the boy's blood, from the people's misery or from Athaliah's crimes, though all three would have served. He argues from a promise, and treats it as binding on the morning in question.

Verse 11 sets crown and testimony in one gesture. The king receives the law at the moment he receives the power, as Deuteronomy required (17:18-20), so that the office is defined before it is exercised. Israel's king is the law's first subject, not its author.

And the holiness of the house governs the day from beginning to end. In verse 6, with an armed operation under way, only priests and ministering Levites may go inside. In verse 14, with the usurper in the crowd's hands, the one order given is that she must not be killed in the LORD's house. The reverence does not bend for the emergency at either end of it.
23.examples:
Six years of doing nothing visible came before the sentence Jehoiada took courage, and the waiting was part of the courage, not the alternative to it.

Five officers agreed to risk execution for a child they had never met, and the Chronicler writes down their names and their fathers' names.

The whole operation was hidden inside the Sabbath shift change, the one hour when twice the usual number of Levites in the building raised no questions at all.

A seven-year-old was handed a crown and a law book in the same minute.

The crowd had the woman who murdered the royal children, and the only instruction the priest gave was about where she must not be killed.

A working Baal temple had stood in the city of David for six years, and everybody knew the address; by that afternoon it was rubble.

24.title: As Long as Jehoiada Lived
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba.<sup>2</sup>And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.<sup>3</sup>Jehoiada got for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters.<sup>4</sup>After this Joash decided to restore the house of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And he gathered the priests and the Levites and said to them, "Go out to the cities of Judah and gather from all Israel money to repair the house of your God from year to year, and see that you act quickly." But the Levites did not act quickly.<sup>6</sup>So the king summoned Jehoiada the chief and said to him, "Why have you not required the Levites to bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the tax levied by Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the congregation of Israel for the tent of testimony?"<sup>7</sup>For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken into the house of God, and had also used all the dedicated things of the house of the LORD for the Baals.<sup>8</sup>So the king commanded, and they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to bring in for the LORD the tax that Moses the servant of God laid on Israel in the wilderness.<sup>10</sup>And all the princes and all the people rejoiced and brought their tax and dropped it into the chest until they had finished.<sup>11</sup>And whenever the chest was brought to the king's officers by the Levites, when they saw that there was much money in it, the king's secretary and the officer of the chief priest would come and empty the chest and take it and return it to its place. Thus they did day after day, and collected money in abundance.<sup>12</sup>And the king and Jehoiada gave it to those who had charge of the work of the house of the LORD, and they hired masons and carpenters to restore the house of the LORD, and also workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>So those who were engaged in the work labored, and the repairing went forward in their hands, and they restored the house of God to its proper condition and strengthened it.<sup>14</sup>And when they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, and with it were made utensils for the house of the LORD, both for the service and for the burnt offerings, and dishes for incense and vessels of gold and silver. And they offered burnt offerings in the house of the LORD regularly all the days of Jehoiada.<sup>15</sup>But Jehoiada grew old and full of days, and died. He was 130 years old at his death.<sup>16</sup>And they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house.<sup>17</sup>Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them.<sup>18</sup>And they abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherim and the idols. And wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs.<sup>19</sup>Yet he sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD. These testified against them, but they would not pay attention.<sup>20</sup>Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people, and said to them, "Thus says God, 'Why do you break the commandments of the LORD, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you.'"<sup>21</sup>But they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>Thus Joash the king did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada, Zechariah's father, had shown him, but killed his son. And when he was dying, he said, "May the LORD see and avenge!"<sup>23</sup>At the end of the year the army of the Syrians came up against Joash. They came to Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people and sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus.<sup>24</sup>Though the army of the Syrians had come with few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army, because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. Thus they executed judgment on Joash.<sup>25</sup>When they had departed from him, leaving him severely wounded, his servants conspired against him because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed. So he died, and they buried him in the city of David, but they did not bury him in the tombs of the kings.<sup>26</sup>Those who conspired against him were Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonite, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabite.<sup>27</sup>Accounts of his sons and of the many oracles against him and of the rebuilding of the house of God are written in the Story of the Book of the Kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
24.overview: Joash comes to the throne at seven and reigns forty years, and the verdict on him is dated from the start: he did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest (vv. 1-3). He decides to repair the temple; the Levites are slow, the king rebukes the high priest out of the law of Moses, and it emerges that Athaliah's sons had stripped the house for the Baals (vv. 4-7). A chest outside the gate solves it — public giving, emptied daily and counted by two officials — and the house is restored and the offerings resume (vv. 8-14). Then Jehoiada dies at 130 and is buried among the kings; the princes come and bow, and the king listens to them (vv. 15-17). Judah turns to the Asherim, prophets are ignored, and Zechariah, clothed by the Spirit, is stoned in the temple court by the king's own command (vv. 18-22). Within a year the Syrians kill the princes, Joash is murdered in his bed by his servants, and he is buried outside the tombs of the kings (vv. 23-27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — All the Days of Jehoiada
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joash is seven at his accession and reigns forty years (v. 1), and the verdict on him arrives with a limit built in: he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest (v. 2). The priest arranges his marriages and the line begins to grow again (v. 3). Then the king's own initiative: After this Joash decided to restore the house of the LORD, and he sends the Levites out for the money — but the Levites did not act quickly (vv. 4-5). So he summons the high priest and asks why the levy of Moses has not been required (v. 6), the repairs being needed because Athaliah's sons had broken into the house of God and spent its holy things on the Baals (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Kings says Joash did right all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him (2 Kgs 12:2). Chronicles cuts the clause down to the length of one man's life. It is not a harsher verdict so much as a more exact one, and the rest of the chapter is written to prove it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is one of the most quietly human lines in the book: the king says go and do it quickly, and the Levites do not do it quickly. Verse 6 has a young man rebuking the priest who raised him, and doing it out of the law of Moses rather than out of temper.

verseByVerse.quote: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba. And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest. Jehoiada got for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba.

Zibiah of Beersheba. After Athaliah of Samaria, the Chronicler names a queen mother from the far south of Judah, and the detail does its own quiet work. The northern house is out of the palace.

Forty years is a long reign, the length of David's and Solomon's. And then the verdict, with a clock inside it.

And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.

Kings tells it more warmly: he did right all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him (2 Kgs 12:2). The Chronicler shortens the sentence to the length of one old man's life. He is not being unkind. He is being precise, and the next twenty-five verses are the proof.

Then a domestic note that is easy to read past. Jehoiada got for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters. The priest arranged the marriages. Two chapters ago this dynasty was one baby in a locked room, and the man who carried him there is now deliberately rebuilding a household around him. Somebody has to think about grandchildren before there are any, and in this case it was not the king.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Joash decided to restore the house of the LORD. And he gathered the priests and the Levites and said to them, "Go out to the cities of Judah and gather from all Israel money to repair the house of your God from year to year, and see that you act quickly." But the Levites did not act quickly. So the king summoned Jehoiada the chief and said to him, "Why have you not required the Levites to bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the tax levied by Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the congregation of Israel for the tent of testimony?" For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken into the house of God, and had also used all the dedicated things of the house of the LORD for the Baals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Joash decided to restore the house of the LORD.

It is his own idea, and it is the right one for this particular man. He had been kept alive in that building. For six years the temple was his nursery and his hiding place, and the first great project of his reign is to put its roof back on.

He sends the priests and Levites out to the towns to collect, and adds: see that you act quickly.

But the Levites did not act quickly.

Five words, and anyone who has ever tried to get a fabric appeal moving will recognise them. The professional religious staff of Judah, freshly restored to their courses by Jehoiada himself, were slow about the collection. The Chronicler does not explain and does not excuse; he simply records that the delay was on the clergy's side.

At that the king summons the high priest. Why have you not required the Levites to bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the tax levied by Moses, the servant of the LORD?

Note what he does and does not do. He does not invent a levy, and he does not appeal to his own authority. He asks why an existing statute — the half-shekel of Exodus 30, laid on Israel in the wilderness for the tent of testimony — is not being enforced. A young king rebukes the old priest who saved his life, and does it by opening the law of Moses on the table between them. That is a hard thing to do well and it was done well here.

Verse 7 says why the building needed the money at all: the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken into the house of God, and had also used all the dedicated things of the house of the LORD for the Baals. The gifts that Judah had given to God had been carried down the road and spent on Baal's house. The repair fund is not decorating. It is undoing a robbery.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Chest at the Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A chest is made and set outside the gate of the house of the LORD, with a proclamation of the tax Moses laid on Israel in the wilderness (vv. 8-9). And all the princes and all the people rejoiced and brought their tax and dropped it into the chest until they had finished (v. 10). It fills so fast that it has to be emptied daily, by the king's secretary and the chief priest's officer together (v. 11). Masons, carpenters and metalworkers are hired, and the house is restored to its proper condition and strengthened (vv. 12-13). The surplus is turned into vessels for the service, and the burnt offerings go up regularly all the days of Jehoiada (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The point of the building work is stated in the last verse of the section, and it is not the building. The masonry was for the sake of the offerings; the plaster and the ironwork existed so that a nation could come and meet its God every morning without the roof coming in.
verseByVerse.examples: Two men from two institutions emptied that chest, every day, together. The money was given in public, into a box outside the gate that anyone could watch, and counted by a royal official and a priestly one at the same table. It is a small piece of administrative wisdom and it has not dated: money handled where people can see it, by more than one pair of hands, protects the giver, the work and the man who counts it.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king commanded, and they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of the LORD. And proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to bring in for the LORD the tax that Moses the servant of God laid on Israel in the wilderness. And all the princes and all the people rejoiced and brought their tax and dropped it into the chest until they had finished. And whenever the chest was brought to the king's officers by the Levites, when they saw that there was much money in it, the king's secretary and the officer of the chief priest would come and empty the chest and take it and return it to its place. Thus they did day after day, and collected money in abundance. And the king and Jehoiada gave it to those who had charge of the work of the house of the LORD, and they hired masons and carpenters to restore the house of the LORD, and also workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of the LORD. So those who were engaged in the work labored, and the repairing went forward in their hands, and they restored the house of God to its proper condition and strengthened it. And when they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, and with it were made utensils for the house of the LORD, both for the service and for the burnt offerings, and dishes for incense and vessels of gold and silver. And they offered burnt offerings in the house of the LORD regularly all the days of Jehoiada.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the king commanded, and they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of the LORD.

Outside the gate, where the people are. The Levites had been asked to go and fetch the money and had not gone; so instead of chasing the collectors, Joash puts a box where every worshipper in Jerusalem walks past it, and has a proclamation read through Judah explaining what the box is for.

And all the princes and all the people rejoiced and brought their tax and dropped it into the chest until they had finished.

Rejoiced, and gave until the giving was done rather than until they were tired of it. Then the logistics, which the Chronicler thinks are worth four lines: the chest filled so fast that it had to be emptied every day, and it was emptied by two officials together — the king's secretary and the officer of the chief priest — one from the palace and one from the temple, so that neither institution could be accused and neither man ever handled the money alone.

That is a small piece of administrative wisdom that has not aged a day. Money given in public, into a container people can see, counted by more than one pair of hands from more than one office. It protects the giver, it protects the work, and it protects the man who does the counting, who is usually the person most in need of protecting.

The work then gets done properly: masons and carpenters, workers in iron and bronze, and the repairing went forward in their hands, and they restored the house of God to its proper condition and strengthened it. The surplus is turned into vessels for the service. Nobody pockets the overrun.

And the last line of the section says what all the scaffolding was for. And they offered burnt offerings in the house of the LORD regularly all the days of Jehoiada.

The plaster and the ironwork were never the point. They existed so that a nation could come every morning and every evening and meet its God at an altar that was still standing. That is the only reason to mend a roof over a place of worship, then or now — and the clause that dates it, all the days of Jehoiada, has now been used twice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — Then the King Listened to Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoiada dies at 130 and is buried in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house (vv. 15-16). Then: Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them (v. 17). They abandon the house of the LORD for the Asherim, and wrath comes (v. 18). God sends prophets and nobody listens (v. 19). So the Spirit of God clothes Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, who tells them plainly that they have forsaken the LORD and he has forsaken them (v. 20) — and by the king's own command he is stoned in the temple court (v. 21), with the words May the LORD see and avenge! (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 is not a new doctrine but the family text. Azariah had said it to Asa in this same book: if you forsake him, he will forsake you (15:2). Zechariah preaches his father's theology in his father's temple and is killed for it in his father's court.
verseByVerse.examples: It took a funeral and a bow. The princes did not argue Joash out of forty years of temple religion; they came and paid homage, and the man who had been the ward of a priest since infancy discovered how much he liked being deferred to. The people whose respect we want are the people who end up writing our policy.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jehoiada grew old and full of days, and died. He was 130 years old at his death. And they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house. Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jehoiada grew old and full of days, and died. He was 130 years old at his death.

A hundred and thirty. Moses died at a hundred and twenty and Aaron at a hundred and twenty-three. The Chronicler gives this priest a lifespan longer than either of them, in a book that counts years carefully, and the reader is meant to feel the weight of it: this is a patriarch's death notice.

And they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house.

A priest in the royal tombs. There is no law that allowed it and no precedent for it; the nation simply decided that the man who hid the king, crowned the king, tore down Baal's house and restarted the offerings belonged with the kings, and they gave three reasons — good done in Israel, good done toward God, good done toward his house. Hold that sentence, because the last verses of this chapter will hand the actual king the opposite of it.

Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them.

That is the hinge of the chapter and it turns on a bow. Nobody argued Joash out of forty years of temple religion. There was no crisis, no defeat, no seduction that the text bothers to describe. Men of rank came and did obeisance to a king who had spent his whole life being the ward of a priest, and he found that he liked it, and the ones who bowed lowest got the policy.

The people whose respect we want are the people who end up writing what we do. Knowing who they are before they arrive is most of the defence, because they arrive politely, at a funeral, with excellent manners, and they do not look like a turning point.

verseByVerse.quote: And they abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherim and the idols. And wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs. Yet he sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD. These testified against them, but they would not pay attention. Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people, and said to them, "Thus says God, 'Why do you break the commandments of the LORD, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you.'" But they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD. Thus Joash the king did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada, Zechariah's father, had shown him, but killed his son. And when he was dying, he said, "May the LORD see and avenge!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherim and the idols.

The building he had just repaired is the building he now walks out of. Every beam in it had been paid for by people who dropped coins in a box at the gate while he was king, and the vessels on its tables had been made out of the surplus of his own appeal.

Then the patience. Yet he sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD. These testified against them, but they would not pay attention. Verse 27 will let slip that there were many such oracles. God does not move from the offering to the sword in one step; he sends men to talk, repeatedly, to people who have stopped listening.

Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people.

Clothed him. It is the verb used of Gideon when the Spirit came on him at the winepress (Judg 6:34) — the Spirit put the man on like a garment and wore him. This is Jehoiada's own son, standing above the crowd in the courtyard his father saved.

And what he says is the family text. Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you. Azariah said that to Asa in this same book, in almost those words (15:2). Zechariah is not innovating. He is preaching what his house has always preached, in the place his house has always preached it.

But they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD.

In the court of the house of the LORD. Go back one chapter and stand in that courtyard. It is where a baby was hidden for six years. It is where a crown was put on a seven-year-old's head. And it is where Jehoiada gave one order at the height of his triumph — that Athaliah, who had butchered the royal children, must not be executed inside these walls, because the house of the LORD was not to be defiled with her blood.

Joash has his old guardian's son killed on those very stones. The murderess was walked out to the horse gate for the sake of the place. The prophet was stoned where he stood.

Thus Joash the king did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada, Zechariah's father, had shown him, but killed his son.

He did not remember. The whole of his life was a kindness he had not earned — the arms that carried him out of the nursery, the room that hid him, the covenant that crowned him, the marriages that gave him children. Ingratitude is not a small sin with a mild name. It is the soil that this murder grew in.

And when he was dying, he said, May the LORD see and avenge!

Centuries later another man was stoned in a holy place for saying the same kind of thing, and as he went down he prayed the opposite: Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:60). Both prayers are righteous, and the difference between them is Calvary standing in between. Zechariah asked God to see, and God saw. Stephen could ask God not to charge the sin to the men throwing the stones, because he had watched a better blood than his own be poured out for exactly such men, in a city that had a long habit of killing the people God sent to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–27 — At the End of the Year
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the end of the year the Syrians come up, destroy all the princes of the people and send the spoil to Damascus (v. 23) — a few men given a very great army, because Judah had forsaken the LORD (v. 24). They leave Joash severely wounded, and his own servants kill him in his bed because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest; he is buried in the city of David but not in the tombs of the kings (v. 25). The two assassins are named with their mothers, an Ammonite and a Moabite (v. 26), and the record closes with a note of the many oracles against him (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The book's own military arithmetic is run backwards here. Abijah won because Judah relied on the LORD (13:18); Asa prayed that there is none like God between the mighty and the weak (14:11). Now a small force is handed a great army, and the reason given is the same reason in reverse. The God who is not impressed by numbers is not impressed by Judah's either.
verseByVerse.examples: Set the two graves side by side. A priest lies among the kings because he did good in Israel and toward God and his house (v. 16). A king lies outside the royal chamber in the same city (v. 25). Kings says Joash was buried with his fathers (2 Kgs 12:21); this book will not give him that sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of the year the army of the Syrians came up against Joash. They came to Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people and sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus. Though the army of the Syrians had come with few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army, because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. Thus they executed judgment on Joash. When they had departed from him, leaving him severely wounded, his servants conspired against him because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed. So he died, and they buried him in the city of David, but they did not bury him in the tombs of the kings. Those who conspired against him were Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonite, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabite. Accounts of his sons and of the many oracles against him and of the rebuilding of the house of God are written in the Story of the Book of the Kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of the year the army of the Syrians came up against Joash.

Inside twelve months. The Chronicler dates the answer to that dying prayer and puts it in the first clause.

And look at who dies. They came to Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people and sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus. The princes. The men who came and paid homage in verse 17, whose flattery turned a king, are the men the Syrians single out. The counsel-room that ruined him is emptied in an afternoon.

Though the army of the Syrians had come with few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army, because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.

This book has told us before what God does with numbers. Abijah's men were outnumbered two to one and won because they relied on the LORD (13:18). Asa prayed that there is none like God to help between the mighty and the weak (14:11). The arithmetic has not changed; the side has. A God who is not impressed by a large army is not impressed by Judah's large army either, and the small Syrian force walks through it.

Then the last turn of the knife, and it is precise. When they had departed from him, leaving him severely wounded, his servants conspired against him because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed.

Because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada. The narrator states the motive, which means the prayer of verse 22 is answered by name. And the man who was smuggled as an infant into a bedroom to keep him alive is finished in a bed by his own household staff.

They buried him in the city of David, but they did not bury him in the tombs of the kings.

Set that beside verse 16 and the chapter closes itself. The priest lies among the kings because he did good in Israel and toward God and his house. The king lies in the same city and outside that room. Kings records this burial without the sting — they buried him with his fathers in the city of David (2 Kgs 12:21) — and the Chronicler declines to give him the sentence. Office does not settle the honour. Faithfulness does.

Verse 26 names the two assassins with their mothers, and both mothers are foreign: Shimeath the Ammonite, Shimrith the Moabite. Kings names the men and not the nationalities. The Chronicler adds them, and the addition lands where he means it to. A king who forsook the God of his fathers is put down inside his own house by the sons of the nations his fathers were told to keep out of it.

Forty years, and the good in them all belonged to somebody else's life. That is the warning this chapter exists to give, and it should be taken personally by anyone whose faith has always had a Jehoiada in it — a parent, a pastor, a friend, a church, a marriage. Those gifts are real and God gives them. But the day comes when the scaffolding is buried at the age of a hundred and thirty, and what is left standing is whatever was actually built. The Lord Jesus is not a scaffold. He is the foundation, and he does not grow old and full of days, and he is never buried, and the house that rests on him is still standing when every prop around it has gone into the ground.

24.theology:
The chapter is built on one clause used twice — all the days of Jehoiada (vv. 2, 14). Kings says Joash did right all his days (2 Kgs 12:2); this book measures the good by the life of the man standing next to him. A faith held up entirely by another person's faith is not thereby false, but it is not yet the man's own, and the day it is tested is the day of the funeral.

God's patience is written in before the judgment, as it was with Jehoram. Prophets are sent, repeatedly (v. 19), and verse 27 says there were many oracles. Only after the word has been refused does the sword come, and it comes dated: at the end of the year.

The two burials are the Chronicler's verdict in architecture. A priest is laid among the kings because he did good toward God and his house (v. 16); a king is kept out of the royal tombs in the same city (v. 25). It is not the office that decides where a man is honoured.
24.examples:
The king said act quickly and the Levites did not act quickly, and the historian writes that down without softening it.

A chest stood outside the gate where everyone could see it, and two officials from two institutions emptied it together, every day, so that no one could be accused.

The masonry was for the sake of the morning and evening offerings; that is the only reason given for mending the roof.

The turn of a whole reign was a bow at a funeral. Men of rank paid homage, and the king who had been a priest's ward all his life discovered how much he enjoyed it.

Jehoiada would not let Athaliah be executed inside the temple walls. Joash had Jehoiada's son stoned in that courtyard.

The servants who killed him gave their reason, and it was the blood of the son of Jehoiada.

25.title: Not with His Whole Heart
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart.<sup>3</sup>And as soon as the royal power was firmly his, he killed his servants who had struck down the king his father.<sup>4</sup>But he did not put their children to death, according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not die because of their children, nor children die because of their fathers, but each one shall die for his own sin."<sup>5</sup>Then Amaziah assembled the men of Judah and set them by fathers' houses under commanders of thousands and of hundreds for all Judah and Benjamin. He mustered those twenty years old and upward, and found that they were 300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield.<sup>6</sup>He hired also 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel for 100 talents of silver.<sup>7</sup>But a man of God came to him and said, "O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel, with all these Ephraimites.<sup>8</sup>But go, act, be strong for the battle. Why should you suppose that God will cast you down before the enemy? For God has power to help or to cast down."<sup>9</sup>And Amaziah said to the man of God, "But what shall we do about the hundred talents that I have given to the army of Israel?" The man of God answered, "The LORD is able to give you much more than this."<sup>10</sup>Then Amaziah discharged the army that had come to him from Ephraim to go home again. And they became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger.<sup>11</sup>But Amaziah took courage and led out his people and went to the Valley of Salt and struck down 10,000 men of Seir.<sup>12</sup>The men of Judah captured another 10,000 alive and took them to the top of a rock and threw them down from the top of the rock, and they were all dashed to pieces.<sup>13</sup>But the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back, not letting them go with him to battle, raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon, and struck down 3,000 people in them and took much spoil.<sup>14</sup>After Amaziah came from striking down the Edomites, he brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his gods and worshiped them, making offerings to them.<sup>15</sup>Therefore the LORD was angry with Amaziah and sent to him a prophet, who said to him, "Why have you sought the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand?"<sup>16</sup>But as he was speaking, the king said to him, "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" So the prophet stopped, but said, "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."<sup>17</sup>Then Amaziah king of Judah took counsel and sent to Joash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face."<sup>18</sup>And Joash the king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle.<sup>19</sup>You say, 'See, I have struck down Edom,' and your heart has lifted you up in boastfulness. But now stay at home. Why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?"<sup>20</sup>But Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God, in order that he might give them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought the gods of Edom.<sup>21</sup>So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah.<sup>22</sup>And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home.<sup>23</sup>And Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for 400 cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.<sup>24</sup>And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God, in the care of Obed-edom. He seized also the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria.<sup>25</sup>Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash the son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.<sup>26</sup>Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, from first to last, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel?<sup>27</sup>From the time when he turned away from the LORD they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there.<sup>28</sup>And they brought him upon horses, and he was buried with his fathers in the city of David.
25.overview: Amaziah reigns twenty-nine years, right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart. He executes his father's assassins but spares their sons, citing the Book of Moses (vv. 1-4). He musters 300,000 men, hires 100,000 northerners for 100 talents, and is told by a man of God to send them home; he asks about the money, is told the LORD can give much more than this, and obeys (vv. 5-10). He wins in Edom, throws 10,000 prisoners off a cliff, and comes home to find the discharged troops have killed 3,000 of his people (vv. 11-13). Then he sets up the gods of the nation he has just beaten, and silences the prophet who asks why (vv. 14-16). He challenges Israel, is answered with a fable about a thistle and a cedar, will not listen, and is routed at Beth-shemesh; Jerusalem's wall is breached and the treasuries emptied (vv. 17-24). Fifteen years later he is assassinated at Lachish — and the Chronicler dates the conspiracy from the day he turned away from the LORD (vv. 25-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Right, Yet Not with a Whole Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah reigns twenty-nine years, and the verdict is exact: he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart (vv. 1-2). He executes his father's assassins once his throne is secure, but spares their children, according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses (vv. 3-4). He musters 300,000 men and hires 100,000 more out of Israel for 100 talents of silver (vv. 5-6). A man of God tells him to send the northerners home, for the LORD is not with Israel (vv. 7-8). Amaziah asks the obvious question — what shall we do about the hundred talents? — and is told the LORD is able to give you much more than this (v. 9). He discharges them, and they go home in fierce anger (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Kings says Amaziah did right yet not like David his father (2 Kgs 14:3). The Chronicler drops the comparison and goes to the organ: not with a whole heart. It is the measure this book has been using all along — Asa's heart wholly true (15:17), God's eyes running to and fro for the blameless heart (16:9), judges charged to act with a whole heart (19:9), Jehoshaphat remembered for seeking with all his (22:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 is a king with the power and the motive to wipe out his father's murderers root and branch, and the Chronicler tells us what stopped him: a sentence in a book. He had Deuteronomy open in front of him, and he obeyed it against his own instincts, in an age when a new king cleared his rivals as a matter of routine.

verseByVerse.quote: Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart. And as soon as the royal power was firmly his, he killed his servants who had struck down the king his father. But he did not put their children to death, according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not die because of their children, nor children die because of their fathers, but each one shall die for his own sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart.

Nine words, and they govern twenty-eight verses. Kings puts it as a comparison — he did right yet not like David his father (2 Kgs 14:3). The Chronicler goes past the comparison to the organ. Not with a whole heart.

That is a measurement, not a mood, and this book has been using the same instrument for ten chapters. Asa's heart was wholly true all his days, failures and all (15:17). God's eyes run to and fro through the earth looking for the heart that is blameless toward him (16:9). Jehoshaphat told his judges to act with a whole heart (19:9), and the soldiers who buried his grandson said of him that he sought the LORD with all his heart (22:9). Amaziah is being weighed on Judah's own scales and found light.

And then, startlingly, two good things. As soon as the royal power was firmly his, he killed his servants who had struck down the king his father.

Three times now in five chapters this book has noticed what a man does the moment he is safe. Rehoboam abandoned the law when his rule was established (12:1); Jehoram murdered his brothers when he was established (21:4). Here the king who has just become secure does something lawful: he executes the men who assassinated his father in his bed, which is justice and not revenge, and every court in the ancient world would have said the same.

It is what he does next that is remarkable. But he did not put their children to death, according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, where the LORD commanded, Fathers shall not die because of their children, nor children die because of their fathers, but each one shall die for his own sin.

He had the power, the motive and the custom of the age all pointing the same way. Two chapters back a queen went through the nursery; three chapters back a king put six brothers to the sword. Amaziah has the assassins' sons in front of him and he opens Deuteronomy instead (24:16), and the Chronicler gives the citation so the reader can check it.

A man restrained by a text is a different creature from a man restrained by his temperament, because temperament does not hold when the blood is up. Whatever else is wrong with Amaziah's heart, on this morning the book on the table was stronger than the grief in his chest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah assembled the men of Judah and set them by fathers' houses under commanders of thousands and of hundreds for all Judah and Benjamin. He mustered those twenty years old and upward, and found that they were 300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield. He hired also 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel for 100 talents of silver. But a man of God came to him and said, "O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel, with all these Ephraimites. But go, act, be strong for the battle. Why should you suppose that God will cast you down before the enemy? For God has power to help or to cast down." And Amaziah said to the man of God, "But what shall we do about the hundred talents that I have given to the army of Israel?" The man of God answered, "The LORD is able to give you much more than this." Then Amaziah discharged the army that had come to him from Ephraim to go home again. And they became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He musters the nation: 300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield.

Count that against the figures this book has already given. Abijah fought with 400,000 (13:3). Asa had 300,000 from Judah and 280,000 from Benjamin (14:8). Jehoshaphat's muster comes to more than a million (17:14-18). Amaziah can raise 300,000 from Judah and Benjamin together — the smallest army in Judah since the kingdom divided. The Syrians who came through in his father's last year and killed all the princes are still being paid for.

So he hires. He hired also 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel for 100 talents of silver. A hundred talents is something over three tonnes of silver, paid up front, and it buys him a third again of the men he has.

Then a man of God walks in with a word that is going to cost a fortune. O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel, with all these Ephraimites ... For God has power to help or to cast down.

And Amaziah asks the question anybody would ask, and the Chronicler loves him enough to record it without mockery. But what shall we do about the hundred talents that I have given to the army of Israel?

It is not a sneer. It is an accountant's problem, and a real one. The money is gone. The contract is signed. The troops are camped outside the city eating Judah's food. Obedience at this point does not mean giving up something he might have had; it means writing off something he has already bought.

The LORD is able to give you much more than this.

There is the sentence to take out of this chapter and keep. Notice what it does not say. It does not say the hundred talents were nothing, or that the loss was imaginary, or that Amaziah was wrong to count it. It says God is richer than the mistake. The prophet lets the cost stand at full value and then sets God beside it.

That is the shape of most hard obedience. It is rarely a choice between loss and no loss. It is a choice between a loss you can see on the ledger and a God whose resources are not on the ledger at all, and the deposit you have already paid is the hardest money in the world to walk away from.

He walks away from it. Then Amaziah discharged the army that had come to him from Ephraim to go home again. And they became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger. He obeyed, and it made him a hundred thousand new enemies before breakfast.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — The Gods of the Losers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah took courage, went to the Valley of Salt and killed 10,000 men of Seir (v. 11); another 10,000 prisoners were thrown from the top of a rock (v. 12). Meanwhile the discharged northern troops raided the towns of Judah, killing 3,000 (v. 13). Then the unaccountable act: After Amaziah came from striking down the Edomites, he brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his gods and worshiped them (v. 14). A prophet arrives with one question — Why have you sought the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand? (v. 15) — and the king cuts him off: Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's question is the whole case against idolatry in one line. Amaziah has just watched these gods fail to save their own worshippers from his own army, and he carries them home and builds them altars. Nobody ever chooses an idol because the evidence is good. The decision is made somewhere else and the reasons are supplied afterwards.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 16 is the third reign running in which the word counsel decides everything. Athaliah counselled her son to his undoing (22:3-4); the princes bowed to Joash and got the policy (24:17); Amaziah tells a prophet he is not on the advisory board, and then in the very next verse takes counsel and starts a war.

verseByVerse.quote: But Amaziah took courage and led out his people and went to the Valley of Salt and struck down 10,000 men of Seir. The men of Judah captured another 10,000 alive and took them to the top of a rock and threw them down from the top of the rock, and they were all dashed to pieces. But the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back, not letting them go with him to battle, raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon, and struck down 3,000 people in them and took much spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Amaziah took courage and led out his people and went to the Valley of Salt and struck down 10,000 men of Seir.

Took courage — the same verb used of Jehoiada in the seventh year (23:1). He goes out short-handed, having just sent a third of his force home on the word of a prophet, and he wins. The arithmetic of this book holds again: God has power to help, and he helped.

And then verse 12, which no honest reader can hurry past. The men of Judah captured another 10,000 alive and took them to the top of a rock and threw them down from the top of the rock, and they were all dashed to pieces.

Ten thousand prisoners walked to a cliff edge and pushed off it. The Chronicler reports it and says not one word in its favour; there is no divine command here, no prophet endorsing it, no comment at all. He simply sets it down, the way he sets down Jehoram's brothers and Athaliah's grandchildren, and lets it stand against the man who did it. A victory won in God's strength does not sanctify what the winner does with his prisoners, and a man can be carried by God's help on Tuesday and be a butcher on Wednesday.

Then the bill for obedience arrives, and the Chronicler puts it here on purpose. But the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back, not letting them go with him to battle, raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon, and struck down 3,000 people in them and took much spoil.

Read the sequence. He obeyed the prophet, lost three tonnes of silver, won his battle, and came home to find that the men he had obediently sent away had burned through his border towns and killed three thousand of his people. Nothing in the text tidies this up. The word of God was right, the obedience was right, and the short-term account is a disaster.

Scripture is honest about this in a way that a good deal of preaching is not. Obedience is not a mechanism for producing comfortable outcomes inside the quarter. It is trust placed in the character of a God who has promised to give much more than this, on a timetable he has not shown us, and who is not obliged to make the first consequence of doing right feel like a reward.

verseByVerse.quote: After Amaziah came from striking down the Edomites, he brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his gods and worshiped them, making offerings to them. Therefore the LORD was angry with Amaziah and sent to him a prophet, who said to him, "Why have you sought the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand?" But as he was speaking, the king said to him, "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" So the prophet stopped, but said, "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Amaziah came from striking down the Edomites, he brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his gods and worshiped them, making offerings to them.

Stand in the absurdity of it for a moment. He has just come back from Seir. He has seen what these gods did for their own people: nothing. Their worshippers are dead in the Valley of Salt and smashed at the bottom of a cliff. He loads the carved images onto a cart, carries them a hundred miles to Jerusalem, has altars built for them, and starts making offerings.

The prophet who comes puts his finger exactly on it. Why have you sought the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand?

No idol has ever been chosen because the evidence was good. The evidence is almost always in plain view and almost always against it. The decision is taken somewhere lower down, and the reasons get assembled afterwards to keep the owner respectable. Ask the question about anything that has our confidence: what has it actually delivered, for anybody, under pressure? Money did not save the people who had it. Reputation did not save the people who had it. Health did not save the healthy.

And here the king's answer tells us the whole state of him. Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?

Counsellor. For the third reign running, that word is where this book locates the trouble. Athaliah was her son's counsellor, to his undoing (22:3-4). The princes bowed to Joash and then wrote his policy (24:17). Now Amaziah tells a man carrying God's word that he has no seat at the table, and threatens to have him killed for speaking out of turn — and in the very next verse took counsel and declared war. He had advisers. He had a whole room of them. He simply would not have the one who contradicted him.

So the prophet stopped, but said, I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel.

He stopped, which is its own kind of courage.
