He did not shout, and he did not stay to argue; he said one more sentence and walked out into the street, leaving the king with a verdict he could not unhear. There is a point at which the kindest thing God's servant can do is stop talking and let the silence be the sermon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — A Thistle Wrote to a Cedar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah challenges Joash of Israel: Come, let us look one another in the face (v. 17). The reply is a fable — a thistle on Lebanon asked a cedar for its daughter, and a wild beast came by and trod the thistle flat (v. 18) — with the diagnosis attached: your heart has lifted you up in boastfulness. But now stay at home (v. 19). But Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God (v. 20). At Beth-shemesh Judah is beaten and every man runs home (vv. 21-22). The king is captured and carried to his own capital, where 400 cubits of wall come down between the Ephraim Gate and the Corner Gate (v. 23), and the gold, the temple vessels in the care of Obed-edom, the palace treasury and hostages all go to Samaria (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 holds two things at once without apology: Amaziah would not listen, and it was of God that he would not. The same construction stood over Ahaziah's fatal visit (22:7). Scripture states the man's deafness as his own and states God's purpose in it in the same sentence, and leaves the two standing.
verseByVerse.examples: The man who told Amaziah the truth about his own heart was a pagan king of the northern kingdom, writing to insult him. Judah had prophets for this. It had just had one, and shouted him down. So the accurate word about Judah's king came out of Samaria, in a fable, from a man who did not care whether he repented or not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah king of Judah took counsel and sent to Joash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face." And Joash the king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle. You say, 'See, I have struck down Edom,' and your heart has lifted you up in boastfulness. But now stay at home. Why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?" But Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God, in order that he might give them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought the gods of Edom. So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah. And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home. And Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for 400 cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God, in the care of Obed-edom. He seized also the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Amaziah king of Judah took counsel and sent to Joash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, Come, let us look one another in the face.

A man who has just silenced a prophet picks a fight with the strongest army on his border. The phrase is a duellist's phrase: let us look each other in the eye. He is not defending anything. He has been to Edom and won, and he wants a bigger stage.

The reply is one of the coldest pieces of writing in the Old Testament, and it is a fable.

A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, Give your daughter to my son for a wife, and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle.

A weed on the mountain writes to the great tree of the mountain proposing a marriage alliance between their families. While the letter is being read, something comes through the scrub and flattens the weed without noticing it was there. The insult is not about courage. It is about proportion, and Joash makes it explicit: You say, See, I have struck down Edom, and your heart has lifted you up in boastfulness. But now stay at home.

A lifted-up heart is a phrase to keep hold of, because this book is about to use it twice more: Uzziah, when he was strong, grew proud to his destruction (26:16), and Hezekiah's heart was lifted up after God healed him (32:25). The same words are a commendation at 17:6, where Jehoshaphat's heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD. A high heart is not the problem. A high heart with nothing above it is.

And the man who diagnoses Amaziah correctly is a pagan king writing to humiliate him. Judah had a prophet for this work a few verses ago and shouted him down, so the accurate word about Judah's king arrives from Samaria, wrapped in a joke, from a man with no interest at all in whether he repents. God is not short of mouths.

But Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God, in order that he might give them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought the gods of Edom.

Both halves again, in one sentence, with no attempt to reconcile them for us. He would not listen: that is his deafness and his guilt. It was of God: that is the deafness handed to a man who had already chosen it. This is the same construction the Chronicler used of Ahaziah's fatal sick-visit (22:7). The judgment on a man who will not hear is sometimes simply that he gets his wish.

Beth-shemesh is a rout. Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home. The king is taken prisoner and brought to his own capital to watch what happens next: four hundred cubits of the wall of Jerusalem, some six hundred feet of it, pulled down between the Ephraim Gate and the Corner Gate. The city is left standing and open.

Then the stripping, and one name inside it deserves a pause. The gold and silver and all the vessels that were found in the house of God, in the care of Obed-edom, go north to Samaria. Obed-edom is the man whose house kept the ark for three months in David's day and was blessed for it, and whose sons were given the gatehouse and the oversight of the stores (1 Chr 26:4-8, 15). Two centuries later his family is still minding the temple treasury — and they have to stand and watch it carried out of the door because the king wanted a fight.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–28 — From the Time When He Turned Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah outlives his conqueror by fifteen years (v. 25), and the records are cited as usual (v. 26). Then the Chronicler dates the end: From the time when he turned away from the LORD they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem; he runs to Lachish and is killed there (v. 27), and is brought back on horses and buried with his fathers in the city of David (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The clock on the conspiracy does not start at Beth-shemesh. It starts at the Edomite altars. The Chronicler is not interested in telling us that bad policy has bad consequences; he is telling us that the turn away from God was the event, and everything in the following fifteen years was its working out.
verseByVerse.examples: He gets the grave. Jehoram was kept out of the royal tombs (21:20) and so was his own father (24:25); Amaziah is buried with his fathers in David's city, exactly as Kings records (2 Kgs 14:20). The honours in this book are graded, and a half-hearted king is measured honestly at both ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash the son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, from first to last, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel? From the time when he turned away from the LORD they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there. And they brought him upon horses, and he was buried with his fathers in the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash the son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.

Fifteen more years. He outlives the man who humiliated him, and reigns on over a capital with six hundred feet of gap in its wall and an empty treasury, and the Chronicler tells us nothing about those years at all. There is no recovery narrative. He simply continues.

Then the ending, and look where the clock is started. From the time when he turned away from the LORD they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there.

Not from the time he lost the battle. Not from the time the wall came down or the hostages went north, which is what a political historian would have written. From the time he turned away from the LORD. The Chronicler names the Edomite altars as the real event of the reign, and everything afterwards — the challenge, the rout, the breached wall, the fifteen silent years and the knife at Lachish — as its slow arrival.

And they brought him upon horses, and he was buried with his fathers in the city of David.

He gets the grave. Jehoram was kept out of the royal tombs and so was Amaziah's own father, but this king is carried home and laid with his fathers, exactly as Kings records it (2 Kgs 14:20). This book does not flatten its kings into a single verdict. It weighs them, and a man who was right and not whole-hearted is measured honestly at both ends: the book on the table in verse 4, the Edomite altars in verse 14, and a grave in David's city at the end.

Which leaves the reader with the nine words from verse 2, and they are uncomfortable precisely because most of us recognise them. Right, yet not with a whole heart. Obedient in the public crisis, where a prophet is standing in the room and three tonnes of silver are at stake; quietly fascinated, afterwards, by something that never saved anybody. The only whole heart ever offered to God in this world belonged to the Son of David, who could say I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart (Ps 40:8) and mean every syllable of it, at the Jordan, in the wilderness, in Gethsemane and on the cross. He was never half anything. And the astonishing arrangement of the gospel is that his whole heart is reckoned to people like Amaziah, and to readers like us, who have never once managed it and who are saved not by the wholeness of our love for him but by the wholeness of his for his Father and for us.

25.theology:
Verse 2 is the chapter's instrument of measurement, and the scale is the book's own. Kings says Amaziah was not like David (2 Kgs 14:3); Chronicles says he was not whole-hearted, which is how this book has assessed every king since Asa (15:17; 16:9; 19:9; 22:9). Half a heart will carry a man through a public crisis with a prophet in the room. It will not carry him through the quiet afternoon afterwards.

The prophet's reply in verse 9 is the clearest word on the cost of obedience in these two books. He does not pretend the hundred talents are nothing; he sets God beside the loss and lets both stand at full size. And the chapter then refuses to make obedience look safe: the men sent home in obedience come back and kill three thousand Judeans (v. 13).

Verse 20 puts God's purpose and the king's guilt in a single sentence — Amaziah would not listen, for it was of God — exactly as at 22:7. The deafness is his, and it is also the judgment. A man who shouts down the word he has been given may find that the silence he asked for is granted.
25.examples:
A king with every motive to wipe out his father's murderers root and branch opened Deuteronomy instead, and the historian printed the reference.

Three tonnes of silver were already spent when the prophet spoke, and the deposit is the hardest money in the world to walk away from.

He obeyed, and a hundred thousand discharged soldiers burned their way along his border and killed three thousand of his people. The text does not tidy it up.

He carried the gods of the men he had just beaten a hundred miles home and built them altars.

The prophet said one more sentence and walked out, and left the king with a verdict he could not unhear.

The accurate diagnosis of Judah's king arrived from Samaria, inside an insult, from a man with no interest in whether he repented.

Obed-edom's family, who had kept the ark and then the stores since David's day, stood and watched the temple vessels carried out to Samaria.

26.title: When He Was Strong, He Grew Proud
26.text: <sup>1</sup>And all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah.<sup>2</sup>He built Eloth and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers.<sup>3</sup>Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.<sup>5</sup>He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper.<sup>6</sup>He went out and made war against the Philistines and broke through the wall of Gath and the wall of Jabneh and the wall of Ashdod, and he built cities in the territory of Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.<sup>7</sup>God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabians who lived in Gurbaal and against the Meunites.<sup>8</sup>The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah, and his fame spread even to the border of Egypt, for he became very strong.<sup>9</sup>Moreover, Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate and at the Valley Gate and at the Angle, and fortified them.<sup>10</sup>And he built towers in the wilderness and cut out many cisterns, for he had large herds, both in the Shephelah and in the plain, and he had farmers and vinedressers in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.<sup>11</sup>Moreover, Uzziah had an army of soldiers, fit for war, in divisions according to the numbers in the muster made by Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer, under the direction of Hananiah, one of the king's commanders.<sup>12</sup>The whole number of the heads of fathers' houses of mighty men of valor was 2,600.<sup>13</sup>Under their command was an army of 307,500, who could make war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy.<sup>14</sup>And Uzziah prepared for all the army shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and stones for slinging.<sup>15</sup>In Jerusalem he made machines, invented by skillful men, to be on the towers and the corners, to shoot arrows and great stones. And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong.<sup>16</sup>But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense.<sup>17</sup>But Azariah the priest went in after him, with eighty priests of the LORD who were men of valor,<sup>18</sup>and they withstood King Uzziah and said to him, "It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have done wrong, and it will bring you no honor from the LORD God."<sup>19</sup>Then Uzziah was angry. Now he had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead in the presence of the priests in the house of the LORD, by the altar of incense.<sup>20</sup>And Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked at him, and behold, he was leprous in his forehead! And they rushed him out quickly, and he himself hurried to go out, because the LORD had struck him.<sup>21</sup>And King Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death, and being a leper lived in a separate house, for he was excluded from the house of the LORD. And Jotham his son was over the king's household, governing the people of the land.<sup>22</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, from first to last, Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz wrote.<sup>23</sup>And Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the burial field that belonged to the kings, for they said, "He is a leper." And Jotham his son reigned in his place.
26.overview: The people crown a sixteen-year-old after his father's assassination, and he rebuilds Eloth (vv. 1-2). Fifty-two years follow — the second longest reign in this book — under a verdict with a limit in it: he did right as his father Amaziah had done, and he sought God in the days of Zechariah, prospering as long as he sought the LORD (vv. 3-5). Philistine walls come down, tribute comes in, and God helped him (vv. 6-8). Then the inventory: towers, cisterns, herds, vinedressers for he loved the soil, an army of 307,500 fully equipped, and engines on the walls to throw arrows and stones (vv. 9-15). But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction: he takes a censer into the temple, eighty priests stand him down, and leprosy breaks out on his forehead (vv. 16-20). He lives out his days in a separate house, excluded from the house of the LORD (v. 21), and is buried in the burial field rather than the tombs, for they said, He is a leper (vv. 22-23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — As Long as He Sought the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people put the sixteen-year-old on the throne after his father's murder (v. 1), and he rebuilds Eloth, the Red Sea port Judah lost two generations back (v. 2). Fifty-two years in Jerusalem, and a verdict with a shadow in it: he did right according to all that his father Amaziah had done (vv. 3-4). Then the sentence the chapter turns on — He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper (v. 5). Philistine walls come down at Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod; God helped him against the Arabians and the Meunites; the Ammonites pay tribute and his name reaches the Egyptian border (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 measures him by his father, and this book has just measured his father: right, yet not with a whole heart (25:2). The commendation is real and it has a ceiling printed on it.
verseByVerse.examples: For the second time in three reigns the Chronicler dates a king's seeking to the lifetime of the man who taught him. Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest (24:2); Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God. Good teachers are a gift and they are not a substitute, and both these men were still standing when their teacher was buried.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah. He built Eloth and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers. Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done. He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah.

The people do it again. They installed Ahaziah when the raiders had emptied the nursery (22:1), and now, with Amaziah's body just brought back from Lachish on a horse, the nation puts a sixteen-year-old on the throne. Judah has learned how to survive its own kings.

And the first thing recorded of him is a repair to the map. He built Eloth and restored it to Judah. Eloth is the port at the top of the Red Sea. Judah lost that coast when Edom revolted from Jehoram (21:8-10), and two reigns of fighting later a teenager rebuilds the harbour. The country is coming back.

Fifty-two years in Jerusalem — the second longest reign in this book, after Manasseh's fifty-five. And the verdict on him has a shadow inside it. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.

According to all that Amaziah had done. The reader has just spent a chapter watching Amaziah, and knows what that measure is worth: right, yet not with a whole heart. The commendation is real, and it comes with a ceiling already printed on it.

He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper.

Read the two time clauses. In the days of Zechariah. As long as he sought the LORD. This is the second time in three reigns that the Chronicler has dated a king's godliness to the life of the man who taught him — Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest (24:2) — and both times the reader is being told in advance where the story is going to break.

A man who instructs a boy in the fear of God is one of God's better gifts and one of his most dangerous, because it is possible to be carried a very long way on somebody else's convictions and to mistake the ride for a walk. The test is not what a man believes while his teacher is alive. It is what he still believes at the funeral, and in the twenty years after.

verseByVerse.quote: He went out and made war against the Philistines and broke through the wall of Gath and the wall of Jabneh and the wall of Ashdod, and he built cities in the territory of Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines. God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabians who lived in Gurbaal and against the Meunites. The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah, and his fame spread even to the border of Egypt, for he became very strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good years are extraordinary, and the Chronicler will not let us admire them without telling us where they came from.

He went out and made war against the Philistines and broke through the wall of Gath and the wall of Jabneh and the wall of Ashdod, and he built cities in the territory of Ashdod.

Gath is Goliath's town. Judah's kings have been fighting that coast since David, and Uzziah does not merely raid it; he takes the walls down and puts his own towns up inside Philistine territory. Then east and south: the Arabians of Gurbaal, the Meunites, tribute from Ammon, and a name that carries as far as the Egyptian frontier.

And in the middle of the list, three words. God helped him.

That verb is going to bracket the whole rise. It appears here in verse 7 and again in verse 15, where his fame spreads because he was marvelously helped. And it happens to be this king's other name: the book of Kings calls him Azariah, which means the LORD has helped (2 Kgs 15:1-2). His own name was a sentence about where his strength came from, and he answered to it every day of his life.

The last clause of verse 8 is the one to keep an eye on: for he became very strong. Nothing is wrong with that sentence yet. In this book strength is a gift, and this king is being given it in armfuls. But the reader who has been paying attention since chapter 12 has learned to feel a slight chill whenever a king of Judah becomes strong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Marvelously Helped, till He Was Strong
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Towers at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate and the Angle; towers out in the wilderness and cisterns cut for the herds; farmers and vinedressers in the hills, for he loved the soil (vv. 9-10). A standing army mustered by named officials, 2,600 heads of families over 307,500 men (vv. 11-13), fully equipped down to the slingstones (v. 14). And in Jerusalem machines, invented by skillful men, to be on the towers and the corners, to shoot arrows and great stones. And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Helped is the word that holds these good years together — God helped him in verse 7, marvelously helped in verse 15 — and it is this king's other name. Kings calls him Azariah, which means the LORD has helped (2 Kgs 15:1-2). Everything in the inventory came in through that word.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is the line that makes him likeable. A king with an artillery programme and a standing army of three hundred thousand also dug cisterns in the desert and kept vinedressers in the hills, for he loved the soil. It is the only reason the Chronicler gives for anything Uzziah built.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate and at the Valley Gate and at the Angle, and fortified them. And he built towers in the wilderness and cut out many cisterns, for he had large herds, both in the Shephelah and in the plain, and he had farmers and vinedressers in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil. Moreover, Uzziah had an army of soldiers, fit for war, in divisions according to the numbers in the muster made by Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer, under the direction of Hananiah, one of the king's commanders. The whole number of the heads of fathers' houses of mighty men of valor was 2,600. Under their command was an army of 307,500, who could make war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy. And Uzziah prepared for all the army shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and stones for slinging. In Jerusalem he made machines, invented by skillful men, to be on the towers and the corners, to shoot arrows and great stones. And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is an inventory, and it is one of the most detailed portraits of a working kingdom anywhere in these two books.

Towers on the wall of Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate and the Angle — the very stretch Joash of Israel had knocked down in his father's reign (25:23), now rebuilt and fortified. Towers out in the open country, and cisterns cut in the rock for the herds. Farmers in the fertile lands, vinedressers in the hills.

And then a reason the Chronicler gives for none of the other building work: for he loved the soil.

It is the most human line in the chapter. Here is a man with a standing army and an artillery programme, and what the record says about his agricultural policy is that he liked farming. He wanted water in the wilderness and vines on the terraces because the land itself pleased him. That is a good thing in a king and it is a good thing in a man.

The army is mustered by name — Jeiel the secretary, Maaseiah the officer, Hananiah the commander — 2,600 heads of families over an army of 307,500. Set that against his father's muster of 300,000 for all Judah and Benjamin (25:5), which was the smallest since the kingdom split. The recovery is complete and then some. Every man of them is equipped: shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and stones for slinging.

In Jerusalem he made machines, invented by skillful men, to be on the towers and the corners, to shoot arrows and great stones.

Engines on the walls, throwing arrows and rocks. The Hebrew turns on a single root and reads something like devices devised by devisers — the writer is enjoying it. Judah has an arms industry, and a king who commissioned the research.

Then the last clause of the section, and everything after it is downhill. And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong.

Till. Not because he was strong, and not once he was strong. Until. The helping and the strength are set on either side of that one small word, and it is the hinge of a fifty-two year reign. He was carried all the way up by a help he did not manufacture, and the moment he could feel the strength in his own hands he stopped noticing whose it was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — It Is Not for You, Uzziah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction, and went into the temple to burn incense (v. 16). Azariah the chief priest follows him in with eighty priests, men of valor (v. 17), and stands him down: It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron ... Go out of the sanctuary ... it will bring you no honor from the LORD God (v. 18). He is angry, censer in hand, and the leprosy breaks out on his forehead in front of them (v. 19); they rush him out and he hurries to go (v. 20). And King Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death ... for he was excluded from the house of the LORD (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The word in verse 16 is ma'al, the sacrilege word — the same charge laid against Saul (1 Chr 10:13) and against the generation that lost the temple (36:14). And the law he broke is not obscure: Exodus 30:9 forbids unauthorized incense on that altar in so many words. The boundary is not a ceremony about rank. It is the difference between a holy God and a creature, and it is guarded for the creature's sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Eighty priests are called men of valor, which is the word this book uses for soldiers, and not one of them was carrying anything. They walked into the sanctuary after the most powerful man in the country, at the height of his reign, with nothing but a sentence, and they said it to his face.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense. But Azariah the priest went in after him, with eighty priests of the LORD who were men of valor, and they withstood King Uzziah and said to him, "It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have done wrong, and it will bring you no honor from the LORD God." Then Uzziah was angry. Now he had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead in the presence of the priests in the house of the LORD, by the altar of incense. And Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked at him, and behold, he was leprous in his forehead! And they rushed him out quickly, and he himself hurried to go out, because the LORD had struck him. And King Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death, and being a leper lived in a separate house, for he was excluded from the house of the LORD. And Jotham his son was over the king's household, governing the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense.

Four times now this book has watched a king reach the moment when nothing could touch him. Rehoboam abandoned the law when his rule was established (12:1). Jehoram murdered his brothers once he was established (21:4). Amaziah executed his father's assassins as soon as the royal power was firmly his (25:3). Now Uzziah, strong at last, walks into the sanctuary with a censer.

The word for what he does is ma'al, the sacrilege word — the charge laid against Saul when he consulted a medium (1 Chr 10:13) and against the generation that lost the temple (36:14). And the law is not obscure or technical. Exodus 30 sets that altar in front of the veil, gives the incense to Aaron's line morning and evening, and says in so many words: You shall not offer unauthorized incense on it (30:9).

Understand what the boundary is for. It is not a rule about rank, and God is not being precious about who holds the shovel. The incense altar stood at the closest point a human being could come to the presence of God, and the whole apparatus of priesthood existed to say that a sinner does not approach the Holy One on his own account and on his own terms. Uzziah is not being punished for a procedural error. He is claiming that fifty-two successful years have made him fit to walk in unmediated.

And then the bravest scene in the chapter. But Azariah the priest went in after him, with eighty priests of the LORD who were men of valor.

Men of valor is the phrase this book keeps for soldiers, and not one of these eighty was carrying a weapon. They followed the most powerful man in the country into the holy place at the height of his power, with nothing in their hands, and told him to his face: It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have done wrong, and it will bring you no honor from the LORD God.

No honour from the LORD God. They put their finger on the thing he actually came in for. He did not want the incense; he wanted the standing. And they tell him, in the one room where it matters, that this is the way to lose it.

Then Uzziah was angry. Now he had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead in the presence of the priests in the house of the LORD, by the altar of incense.

On his forehead. That is not a random square inch of skin. The high priest wore a plate of pure gold on his forehead, fastened to the turban with a blue cord, engraved like a signet with the words Holy to the LORD, so that the people's gifts might be accepted (Exod 28:36-38). Uzziah came into that room wanting a priest's place. He walked out with a mark of uncleanness on the exact spot where the priest carries the word holy.

Then a detail that says everything about how fast the room changed. They rushed him out quickly, and he himself hurried to go out, because the LORD had struck him. Both parties hurry. The man who forced his way in cannot now get out of the building fast enough.

And King Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death, and being a leper lived in a separate house, for he was excluded from the house of the LORD.

There is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking toward, and it is an exact reversal. He wanted more access to God than God had given him. He got none at all. For years afterwards, while his son ran the country, the king of Judah lived in a house on his own and watched the festivals from a distance, and every Passover of the rest of his life was a reminder of the morning he pushed past a priest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–23 — In the Year That King Uzziah Died
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, from first to last, Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz wrote (v. 22). He is buried with his fathers in the burial field that belonged to the kings, for they said, He is a leper (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler names Isaiah as his source, which means the two accounts are looking at the same reign. And Isaiah's own book opens its great vision with the date: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up (Isa 6:1). One man reached for the altar of incense and was carried out; the other fell on his face and had a coal brought to him from that altar (Isa 6:6).
verseByVerse.examples: Count the graves. Jehoram was kept out of the royal tombs (21:20). Joash was kept out (24:25). Amaziah was laid with his fathers (25:28). Uzziah is buried in the field beside the tombs, and the reason is given in six words: for they said, He is a leper. Fifty-two years, and the last sentence about him is a diagnosis.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, from first to last, Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz wrote. And Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the burial field that belonged to the kings, for they said, "He is a leper." And Jotham his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, from first to last, Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz wrote.

The Chronicler names his source, and the name stops the reader. Isaiah wrote the life of this king. Which means the man who watched Uzziah carried leprous out of the temple is the same man who wrote the sixth chapter of the book that bears his name, and dated it: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple.

Set the two scenes in the one building. A king with a high heart walks up to the altar of incense to take a place that was not his, and is carried out marked. A prophet comes into the same house, sees who is actually on the throne, and goes down flat: Woe is me! For I am lost. One man claimed the holy place; the other confessed he had no business in it. And the second man was the one who was cleansed — by a live coal that a seraph carried to him from the altar (Isa 6:6), the very altar the king had grabbed at.

That is the difference between pride and worship in one building and one lifetime. Holiness is not less dangerous to the humble man; Isaiah thought he was a dead man. It is that the humble man is met by a God who comes down the steps with fire in his hand and touches the mouth that confessed.

And Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the burial field that belonged to the kings, for they said, He is a leper.

Count the graves in six chapters. Jehoram was buried in the city of David but not in the tombs of the kings. Joash was buried in the city and kept out of the tombs. Amaziah was laid with his fathers. Uzziah gets the family field and not the family chamber, and the reason is recorded in six words that his own subjects said out loud over the coffin: He is a leper.

Fifty-two years, Philistine walls in rubble, cisterns in the desert, engines on the towers, a name known to the border of Egypt — and the last sentence of the record is a diagnosis. There is only one man who ever walked past the veil on his own account and was not struck, and he had no censer, because he was the offering. He goes in as our priest, and the astonishing invitation on the other side of his going is not stay out but let us then with confidence draw near (Heb 4:16) — near, by a door that was opened from the inside, for people who would never have survived forcing it.

26.theology:
The chapter turns on one word in verse 15: he was marvelously helped, till he was strong. Help and strength are the two halves of the reign, and the danger is entirely on the second side. This book has now watched four kings reach the point where nothing could touch them (12:1; 21:4; 25:3; 26:16), and in every case the sentence turns there.

What Uzziah does is called ma'al, sacrilege — the word used of Saul and of the generation that lost the temple. Exodus 30:9 forbids unauthorized incense on that altar by name. The boundary exists because a sinner does not approach the Holy One on his own account and on his own terms; the priesthood is not a privilege withheld but a mercy provided, and the man who steps over it is not being fined for a technicality.

Verse 21 is the exact reversal of verse 16. He wanted more access than God had granted and he ended with none — excluded from the house of the LORD. And Isaiah, who wrote this king's life (v. 22), came into that same house and went down on his face, and was cleansed with a coal from that same altar (Isa 6:1, 6).
26.examples:
He rebuilt the harbour his great-grandfather had lost, and the towers on the very stretch of wall that had been knocked down in his father's reign.

The one reason the record gives for his cisterns and vineyards is that he loved the soil.

He commissioned engineers to build machines for the towers, and Judah had an arms industry and a name as far as Egypt.

Eighty priests, called men of valour, followed an enraged king into the sanctuary carrying nothing at all, and told him to his face that he had no business there.

The leprosy came out on his forehead, which is where the high priest wore the gold plate engraved Holy to the LORD.

They rushed him out, and he himself hurried to go.

His own people said six words over his coffin, and the six words were the reason he was buried in the field and not the chamber.

27.title: He Became Mighty Because He Ordered His Ways
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerushah the daughter of Zadok.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD according to all that his father Uzziah had done, except he did not enter the temple of the LORD. But the people still followed corrupt practices.<sup>3</sup>He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD and did much building on the wall of Ophel.<sup>4</sup>Moreover, he built cities in the hill country of Judah, and forts and towers on the wooded hills.<sup>5</sup>He fought with the king of the Ammonites and prevailed against them. And the Ammonites gave him that year 100 talents of silver, and 10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley. The Ammonites paid him the same amount in the second and the third years.<sup>6</sup>So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.<sup>7</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars and his ways, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.<sup>8</sup>He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>And Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
27.overview: Nine verses, the shortest chapter in the book, and the cleanest verdict in this stretch of it. Jotham reigns sixteen years and does right as his father Uzziah had done, except he did not enter the temple of the LORD — while the people go on in corrupt practices (vv. 1-2). He rebuilds the upper gate of the temple, works on the wall of Ophel, and plants cities and forts through the hill country (vv. 3-4). He defeats Ammon, which pays a hundred talents of silver and twenty thousand cors of grain, three years running (v. 5). The reason is given in one sentence: So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God (v. 6). The records are cited, the regnal formula is printed a second time with nothing added, and he is buried in the city of David — and Ahaz reigns in his place (vv. 7-9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Except He Did Not Enter the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jotham is twenty-five, and reigns sixteen years (v. 1). The verdict is his father's with one clause added: he did right according to all that his father Uzziah had done, except he did not enter the temple of the LORD — and then, in the same verse, But the people still followed corrupt practices (v. 2). He builds the upper gate of the house of the LORD and works on the wall of Ophel (v. 3), and puts cities in the hill country and forts and towers on the wooded ridges (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The exception in verse 2 is the whole man. He took everything his father did in the good years and left out the one act that ruined him. Learning from a father's success is common; watching the thing that destroyed him and declining to repeat it, when you now hold the same power and the same censer is within reach, is rare.
verseByVerse.examples: The same verse that commends the king condemns the country. A throne can set the direction of a nation and cannot set its heart. Sixteen years of honest government did not make Judah godly, and the Chronicler says so in the same breath as the commendation rather than saving it for a footnote.

verseByVerse.quote: Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerushah the daughter of Zadok. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD according to all that his father Uzziah had done, except he did not enter the temple of the LORD. But the people still followed corrupt practices. He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD and did much building on the wall of Ophel. Moreover, he built cities in the hill country of Judah, and forts and towers on the wooded hills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD according to all that his father Uzziah had done, except he did not enter the temple of the LORD.

That exception is the man. Everything in it depends on what he had watched.

Jotham had run the country for years while his father lived in a separate house, unclean, shut out of the building he had forced his way into. He was the son who took over the administration in the middle of a scandal, and he grew up knowing exactly which morning it was that changed his family's life and exactly which door his father had walked through.

So he copied the good years. The building, the fighting, the ordering of a working kingdom, all of it lifted straight from Uzziah's better decades. And when he came to the one act that finished his father, he stopped. The censer was within reach, the guards would not have stopped him, and there was no one alive who could have prevented a king of Judah walking into that room. He did not go in.

Most of us learn quickly from what our families did well. Learning from what destroyed them is a different and much harder discipline, because the thing that destroyed them usually looked, at the time, like the natural next step for a man who had earned it.

Then the second half of the same verse, and it stops the chapter from being sentimental. But the people still followed corrupt practices.

A good king for sixteen years, and the country did not follow him. He built, he judged, he kept out of the sanctuary he had no right to enter, and his subjects went on with what they had always done. The Chronicler puts the commendation and the failure in the same sentence rather than hiding one of them in a footnote, because both are true and neither cancels the other.

Anybody who has ever led anything needs that verse. A parent, a pastor, an employer, a king — you can set a direction, and you cannot set a heart. Jotham was not a failure because Judah stayed corrupt, and Judah was not excused because Jotham was good. If anything the opposite: a people who had a straight man in front of them for sixteen years had run out of excuses.

What he built repays a glance as well. He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD — the gate the whole nation had marched a seven-year-old down through, four reigns back, to put him on the throne (23:20). Somebody has to keep the hinges working on the places where God once did something. That is a great deal of what faithful men do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Because He Ordered His Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He beats the Ammonites, and they pay 100 talents of silver, and 10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley, and the same again in the second year and the third (v. 5). Then the explanation, and it is the only one given: So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God (v. 6). The records are cited (v. 7), the regnal formula is printed a second time with nothing added to it (v. 8), and he is buried in the city of David — and Ahaz his son reigned in his place (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 puts the cause and the effect in one sentence and refuses to separate them. He became mighty because he ordered his ways. Not because he was gifted, well advised or fortunate in his enemies; the strength came out of the ordering, and the ordering was done before the LORD his God, which is to say in the one place where nobody else could see it.
verseByVerse.examples: A hundred talents of silver came into Judah's treasury three years running. His grandfather Amaziah wrote off a hundred talents at a prophet's word and was told the LORD could give him much more than that (25:9). The Chronicler does not join the two figures up. He simply prints them both and leaves the sum on the page.

verseByVerse.quote: He fought with the king of the Ammonites and prevailed against them. And the Ammonites gave him that year 100 talents of silver, and 10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley. The Ammonites paid him the same amount in the second and the third years. So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God. Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars and his ways, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He fought with the king of the Ammonites and prevailed against them. And the Ammonites gave him that year 100 talents of silver, and 10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley. The Ammonites paid him the same amount in the second and the third years.

Look at the numbers, because the Chronicler expects his reader to have been paying attention. A hundred talents of silver, three years running.

Two reigns ago, Jotham's grandfather Amaziah hired a hundred thousand northern mercenaries for a hundred talents of silver, and a man of God told him to send them home. Amaziah asked the only sensible question — what about the hundred talents I have already paid? — and was told: The LORD is able to give you much more than this (25:9). He obeyed, and wrote the money off.

Now Ammon pays a hundred talents into Judah's treasury, and does it again the next year, and again the year after that. Nobody in the text draws the line between the two sums. The figures are simply printed, a generation apart, and left for whoever is counting.

And there is grain with the silver: ten thousand cors of wheat and ten thousand of barley, each cor something over two hundred litres. Judah is being paid in bread. A man whose father loved the soil is receiving tribute in the form of harvests.

Then verse 6, which is the whole reign in one sentence. So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.

Not because he was clever or well advised or lucky in his enemies. He ordered his ways. The verb is the one this book has used from the beginning for the thing Rehoboam never did — he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD (12:14) — and for the good found in Jehoshaphat, that he had set his heart to seek God (19:3). It is the language of arrangement: a life put in order deliberately, on purpose, in a particular direction.

And it was done before the LORD his God, which is to say where nobody could check it. That is where an ordered life is actually built. Not in the public decisions, which everyone watches, but in the private ones, which no council minutes record: what he did first in the morning, what he refused when it was offered quietly, which room in the temple he would not enter when the door was open and no one would have said a word.

Nine verses. No prophet arrives, because none was needed. No enemy comes to the gate that he cannot handle. There is no crisis, no vision, no plague, no rebuke, no dramatic rescue of the kind that fills chapter 20 — and this book, which has spent twenty-six chapters on catastrophes and deliverances, gives one of its cleanest verdicts to a man whose story will not fill a page. Most faithful lives are chapter 27 and not chapter 20, and God is not disappointed by that. He wrote it down.

The formula is printed a second time in verse 8, exactly as it was for Jehoram — twenty-five years old, sixteen years in Jerusalem. When the Chronicler did that for Jehoram he used the repetition to land a sentence: and he departed with no one's regret (21:20). Here the second printing adds nothing at all, and then: And Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. No exclusion, no burial field, no six-word verdict muttered over the coffin. After four reigns of graded graves, one plain one.

And then the last clause of the chapter, which the reader of this book learns to read with dread. And Ahaz his son reigned in his place. The steadiest king in five generations hands the throne to the worst. Jotham ordered his ways before the LORD and could not order his son's, any more than he could order his people's, and the God who is honoured by a quiet, well-arranged life does not promise that it will be copied by the people we love most. He promises something better and slower: that the ordering itself was seen, in the place where it was done, by the One it was done before.

27.theology:
Verse 6 states a cause and refuses to look for another. Might came out of ordering, and the ordering was done before the LORD his God — in private, where no council minute records it. The verb is the book's own: Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD (12:14), and Jehoshaphat was commended because he had (19:3).

Verse 2 keeps two truths in one sentence. A king can be genuinely faithful and his nation still corrupt. Leadership sets a direction and cannot set a heart, and a people who had a straight man in front of them for sixteen years are less excusable, not more.

And the chapter's brevity is part of its teaching. No prophet is sent because none is needed; no crisis arrives; nothing here would preach as drama. A book full of plagues, sieges and deliverances gives one of its clearest commendations to a reign that will not fill a page.
27.examples:
He had watched his father carried leprous out of the sanctuary, and when he held the same power and the censer was within reach, he did not go in.

He rebuilt the upper gate — the gate the nation had brought a seven-year-old king down through, four reigns earlier.

A hundred talents of silver came in from Ammon three years running; his grandfather had written off a hundred talents on a prophet's word.

Judah was paid in wheat and barley, twenty thousand cors of it, in the reign after a king who loved the soil.

Sixteen years of honest government, and his subjects carried on exactly as before.

The best king in five generations fathered the worst one.

28.title: He Was Unfaithful to the LORD
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done,<sup>2</sup>but he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel. He even made metal images for the Baals,<sup>3</sup>and he made offerings in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and burned his sons as an offering, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree.<sup>5</sup>Therefore the LORD his God gave him into the hand of the king of Syria, who defeated him and took captive a great number of his people and brought them to Damascus. He was also given into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with great force.<sup>6</sup>For Pekah the son of Remaliah killed 120,000 from Judah in one day, all of them men of valor, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>7</sup>And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the king's son and Azrikam the commander of the palace and Elkanah the next in authority to the king.<sup>8</sup>The men of Israel took captive 200,000 of their relatives, women, sons, and daughters. They also took much spoil from them and brought the spoil to Samaria.<sup>9</sup>But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded, and he went out to meet the army that came to Samaria and said to them, "Behold, because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, he gave them into your hand, but you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven.<sup>10</sup>And now you intend to subjugate the people of Judah and Jerusalem, male and female, as your slaves. Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God?<sup>11</sup>Now hear me, and send back the captives from your relatives whom you have taken, for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you."<sup>12</sup>Certain chiefs also of the men of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against those who were coming from the war<sup>13</sup>and said to them, "You shall not bring the captives in here, for you propose to bring upon us guilt against the LORD in addition to our present sins and guilt. For our guilt is already great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel."<sup>14</sup>So the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and all the assembly.<sup>15</sup>And the men who have been mentioned by name rose and took the captives, and with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them. They clothed them, gave them sandals, provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk at Jericho, the city of palm trees. Then they returned to Samaria.<sup>16</sup>At that time King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria for help.<sup>17</sup>For the Edomites had again invaded and defeated Judah and carried away captives.<sup>18</sup>And the Philistines had made raids on the cities in the Shephelah and the Negeb of Judah, and had taken Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco with its villages, Timnah with its villages, and Gimzo with its villages. And they settled there.<sup>19</sup>For the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel, for he had made Judah act sinfully and had been very unfaithful to the LORD.<sup>20</sup>So Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came against him and afflicted him instead of strengthening him.<sup>21</sup>For Ahaz took a portion from the house of the LORD and the house of the king and of the princes, and gave tribute to the king of Assyria, but it did not help him.<sup>22</sup>In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD—this same King Ahaz.<sup>23</sup>For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him and said, "Because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me." But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.<sup>24</sup>And Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and he shut up the doors of the house of the LORD, and he made himself altars in every corner of Jerusalem.<sup>25</sup>In every city of Judah he made high places to make offerings to other gods, provoking to anger the LORD, the God of his fathers.<sup>26</sup>Now the rest of his acts and all his ways, from first to last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.<sup>27</sup>And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, in Jerusalem, for they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
28.overview: Ahaz is measured against David rather than against his own good father, and fails on every count: cast idols for the Baals, sacrifice on every hill, and his own sons burned in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (vv. 1-4). Syria and Israel come down together; 120,000 of Judah fall in a day, the heir and the two chief officers are killed, and 200,000 women and children are marched to Samaria (vv. 5-8). There the prophet Oded stops the army in the road — God gave Judah into your hand, but you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven — and four named chiefs of Ephraim clothe the prisoners, feed them, anoint them and carry the weak to Jericho (vv. 9-15). Ahaz buys Assyrian help and is afflicted by it; Edom and Philistia take what is left; and in the time of his distress he became yet more faithless (vv. 16-22). He sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, cuts up the temple vessels and shuts the doors (vv. 23-25). He is buried in the city but not in the tombs of the kings — and Hezekiah his son reigns in his place (vv. 26-27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Metal Images, and the Valley of Hinnom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz reigns sixteen years and does not do right as his father David had done (v. 1). He casts metal images for the Baals (v. 2), and he made offerings in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and burned his sons as an offering (v. 3), and sacrifices on every hill and under every green tree (v. 4). Therefore the LORD his God gave him into the hand of the king of Syria, and into the hand of Israel (v. 5); Pekah kills 120,000 of Judah in a day because they had forsaken the LORD (v. 6); an Ephraimite kills the king's son, the commander of the palace and the second man in the kingdom (v. 7); and 200,000 women and children are marched to Samaria (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 measures him against David, ten generations back, and not against Jotham, who was a good man and had been dead about five minutes. The standard for a son of David is never the man immediately in front of him. It is the covenant the family was given.
verseByVerse.examples: The valley in verse 3 is ge-hinnom, and the name outlived the king. By the time of the Gospels the word had become the word for hell itself. Judah's rubbish tip and its child-burning ground gave its name to the place of final judgment, and it was a king of David's line who lit the fires.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done, but he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel. He even made metal images for the Baals, and he made offerings in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and burned his sons as an offering, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done.

His father was Jotham, and Jotham was one of the best men in this book. The Chronicler walks straight past him and measures Ahaz against David, ten generations back. That is how the standard works for a son of David: not against the man immediately in front of him, but against the covenant the family was given in the first place.

What follows is a descent taken in four steps, and each one goes further than the last.

He even made metal images for the Baals. Not tolerated shrines on a hillside — a foundry. Somebody in Jerusalem was casting idols to order, with a workshop, a furnace and a royal commission.

And he made offerings in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and burned his sons as an offering, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.

Sons, plural. A king of Judah carried his own children down into a ravine on the south side of the city and put them in a fire, and the Chronicler tells us exactly why it is unbearable: this is the practice for which God evicted the previous occupants of the land. Israel was put into Canaan because Canaan did this. Now the son of David does it within sight of the temple.

The name of that ravine did not die with him. Ge-hinnom is the valley of the son of Hinnom, and by the time of the Gospels the word had passed into the language as the name for hell itself. Judah's burning-ground gave its name to final judgment.

And there is a quiet horror waiting three verses later. When the northern army breaks through, one of the men they kill is Maaseiah the king's son (v. 7) — a son Ahaz had not burned. He gave some of his children to the fire to buy safety, and the ones he kept were killed anyway, by an enemy God sent because of what he had done.

Idols never take what you offer and leave the rest alone. They take the payment and then come back for the thing the payment was meant to protect.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the LORD his God gave him into the hand of the king of Syria, who defeated him and took captive a great number of his people and brought them to Damascus. He was also given into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with great force. For Pekah the son of Remaliah killed 120,000 from Judah in one day, all of them men of valor, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the king's son and Azrikam the commander of the palace and Elkanah the next in authority to the king. The men of Israel took captive 200,000 of their relatives, women, sons, and daughters. They also took much spoil from them and brought the spoil to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore the LORD his God gave him into the hand of the king of Syria.

The LORD his God. The Chronicler will not drop the possessive even here, with the foundry running and the valley smoking. The God being sinned against is still the God of this man in particular, which is what makes it treachery rather than mere ignorance.

The war comes from two directions at once. Syria takes a great number of prisoners to Damascus, and then Israel from the north struck him with great force. This is a moment the reader of the prophets will recognise: Isaiah dates his seventh chapter to exactly this crisis, with Rezin of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah coming up against Jerusalem together (Isa 7:1), and says that the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook like trees in a wind.

For Pekah the son of Remaliah killed 120,000 from Judah in one day, all of them men of valor, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.

A hundred and twenty thousand in a day, and the narrator gives the cause in the same sentence as the number. Not a failure of tactics. They had forsaken the LORD. This book has used that verb of Rehoboam, of Asa's generation, of Joash after Jehoiada, and it will use it of the last generation before the exile.

Verse 7 names three of the dead, and the three names together are a decapitated government: the king's son, the commander of the palace, and Elkanah the next in authority to the king. The heir, the head of the household administration, and the second man in the kingdom, all killed by one Ephraimite in one battle.

Then verse 8, which is where the arithmetic stops being military. The men of Israel took captive 200,000 of their relatives, women, sons, and daughters.

Their relatives. Two hundred thousand mothers and children walked north to Samaria in a column, and the word the Chronicler uses for what they were to their captors is family. The kingdom had been split for two hundred years and the blood had not changed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The victorious northern army comes home to find a prophet waiting at the gate. Behold, because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, he gave them into your hand, but you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven, says Oded — and then the question: Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God? (vv. 9-10). Send the captives back (v. 11). Four chiefs of Ephraim are named and stand in the road (v. 12): You shall not bring the captives in here (v. 13). So the army puts down the prisoners and the spoil (v. 14), and the four men clothe the naked, give them sandals, feed them, anoint them, carry the weak on donkeys and take them home to Jericho (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Oded's argument holds two things together. God did hand Judah over; the northern army was the instrument. And the instrument is guilty for what it did with the freedom of that hour, because you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven. It is the principle Isaiah states of Assyria: the rod of God's anger is judged for the pride with which it swung (Isa 10:5-7). Being used by God is not the same as being approved by him.
verseByVerse.examples: While Samaritans are putting sandals on Judah's barefoot prisoners and lifting the weak onto donkeys, Judah's own king is burning his children in a ravine outside Jerusalem. The Chronicler prints those two facts a dozen verses apart and does not comment.

verseByVerse.quote: But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded, and he went out to meet the army that came to Samaria and said to them, "Behold, because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, he gave them into your hand, but you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven. And now you intend to subjugate the people of Judah and Jerusalem, male and female, as your slaves. Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God? Now hear me, and send back the captives from your relatives whom you have taken, for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you." Certain chiefs also of the men of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against those who were coming from the war and said to them, "You shall not bring the captives in here, for you propose to bring upon us guilt against the LORD in addition to our present sins and guilt. For our guilt is already great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel." So the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and all the assembly. And the men who have been mentioned by name rose and took the captives, and with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them. They clothed them, gave them sandals, provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk at Jericho, the city of palm trees. Then they returned to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What happens next is found in no other book of the Bible, and it is the moral centre of this chapter.

But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded, and he went out to meet the army that came to Samaria.

A prophet in Samaria. Not in Jerusalem, where the king is burning children, but in the capital of the northern kingdom, standing in the road in front of an army that has just won the largest victory in its history, with two hundred thousand prisoners behind it.

His argument is careful, and it holds two things at once. Because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, he gave them into your hand — that much is true, and he grants it. But you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven.

God used them. God is also going to hold them responsible for how they behaved while he was using them. Isaiah says the same thing of Assyria a few years later: the rod of God's anger is still judged for the pride with which it swung, because he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think (Isa 10:5-7). Being an instrument in God's hand is not a certificate of good conduct, and the man who tells himself that his cruelty is somehow God's business has misread the entire arrangement.

Then the question that lands on every victor in every age. Have you not sins of your own against the LORD your God?

And here comes the surprise of the chapter. Certain chiefs also of the men of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against those who were coming from the war.

Four northerners, named with their fathers' names, in a book that gives the northern kingdom almost nothing. They block the road into the city and say: not here. For our guilt is already great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel. They do not argue that the prisoners deserve better. They argue that Israel cannot afford another sin, which is an honest and self-aware thing for a nation to say about itself.

So the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and all the assembly. An army that had marched home with the plunder of a kingdom put it all down in the street because four men and a prophet told them to. There is no threat in the text and no miracle. Somebody spoke and they obeyed.

Then verse 15, and it should be read slowly, because it is one of the loveliest sentences in the Old Testament. They clothed all who were naked among them. They clothed them, gave them sandals, provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk at Jericho, the city of palm trees.

Clothes, shoes, a meal, oil on the skin, and the ones who could not walk lifted onto animals and carried the whole way down to Jericho. It is done out of the spoil — the very goods they had taken off these people are used to dress them again.

Any reader of the Gospels will feel where this is going. A man stripped and left half dead on the road that runs down from Jerusalem to Jericho; the respectable people who pass by; and then a Samaritan who pours on oil, sets him on his own animal and takes him where he will be cared for (Luke 10:30-34). The Lord who told that story knew this chapter, and whether or not he had it in mind, the shape is the same and the road is the same road.

Hold the two halves of this chapter together. In the south, the anointed king of the house of David is putting his sons in a fire. In the north, four men nobody has ever heard of are putting sandals on the feet of prisoners of war. Grace is not where the credentials are. It never has been.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahaz sends to Assyria for help (v. 16) while Edom raids from the south (v. 17) and the Philistines take six named towns of the Shephelah and settle in them (v. 18), for the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel (v. 19). Then the help arrives and turns out to be the next disaster: Tiglath-pileser came against him and afflicted him instead of strengthening him (v. 20), and the tribute stripped out of the temple, the palace and the princes did not help him (v. 21). And the narrator breaks in: In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD — this same King Ahaz (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 turns the book's hinge verb round. Since 7:14 the promise has run: if my people ... humble themselves. Here God does the humbling, to a nation, from the outside — and nothing comes of it. Being brought low is not the same as being humbled, and a man can be flattened by God and get up angrier than he lay down.
verseByVerse.examples: Distress is where the kings of this book normally turn. Rehoboam humbled himself when Shishak was at the gate (12:6); Manasseh will do it in a Babylonian prison (33:12). Ahaz gets the same treatment and goes the other way, and the historian, who almost never raises his voice, adds four words of his own: this same King Ahaz.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria for help. For the Edomites had again invaded and defeated Judah and carried away captives. And the Philistines had made raids on the cities in the Shephelah and the Negeb of Judah, and had taken Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco with its villages, Timnah with its villages, and Gimzo with its villages. And they settled there. For the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel, for he had made Judah act sinfully and had been very unfaithful to the LORD. So Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came against him and afflicted him instead of strengthening him. For Ahaz took a portion from the house of the LORD and the house of the king and of the princes, and gave tribute to the king of Assyria, but it did not help him. In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD—this same King Ahaz.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria for help.

There is the decision his whole reign turns on, and Isaiah was standing in front of him when he made it. The prophet had offered him a sign, any sign, deep as Sheol or high as heaven, and Ahaz had answered with the most pious sentence in the chapter: I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test (Isa 7:12). Then he sent for Assyria. Refusing God's help is rarely announced as unbelief. It is usually dressed as modesty, and it always has another plan already drafted.

Meanwhile the map is coming apart. Edom raids from the south and takes captives. The Philistines take six towns of the Shephelah and the Negeb — Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco, Timnah, Gimzo — and they settled there. Not a raid: an occupation. Judah is losing the land it has held since Joshua, town by named town.

For the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel.

Humbled is the word this book was built on. The promise at the dedication of the temple was if my people who are called by my name humble themselves (7:14), and it has been answered again and again — Rehoboam with Shishak at the gate, and Manasseh still to come. Here the verb is used the other way round. God humbles them. It is done to a nation from the outside, and it produces nothing at all.

Being brought low is not the same thing as being humbled. A man can be flattened by God and get up angrier than he went down, and that is precisely what happens next.

So Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came against him and afflicted him instead of strengthening him.

The help he bought arrived and turned on him. He had stripped the house of the LORD, the palace and the private wealth of his own princes to pay the invoice, but it did not help him. Two chapters ago God helped Uzziah for nothing. Ahaz paid a fortune for help and got an army of occupation.

At which point the historian, who hardly ever raises his voice, raises it.

In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the LORD — this same King Ahaz.

Distress is where the kings of this book turn round. It is the hinge of Rehoboam's story and it will be the hinge of Manasseh's. Ahaz is handed the same season and walks the other way, and the writer cannot let it pass without pointing at him: this same King Ahaz. Trouble does not soften anybody by itself. It only ever makes a man more of what he already was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him, reasoning out loud that the gods who helped Syria might help him — but they were the ruin of him and of all Israel (v. 23). He cuts the temple vessels in pieces, and he shut up the doors of the house of the LORD, and builds altars on every corner of Jerusalem (v. 24) and high places in every city of Judah (v. 25). The records are cited (v. 26), and he is buried in the city, in Jerusalem, for they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 24 is where the descent ends: not in idolatry alongside the temple but in the temple closed. The vessels are scrap, the doors are barred, the lamps are out, and there is nowhere in Judah left to bring a sacrifice. Everything the book has said about seeking and forsaking arrives at a locked door.
verseByVerse.examples: The next sentence of the story is the first verse of the next reign: In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them (29:3). The first month. Not after the coronation settled, not once the succession was secure. First.

verseByVerse.quote: For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him and said, "Because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me."
