But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel. And Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and he shut up the doors of the house of the LORD, and he made himself altars in every corner of Jerusalem. In every city of Judah he made high places to make offerings to other gods, provoking to anger the LORD, the God of his fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him and said, Because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.

His grandfather Amaziah did this in silence, carrying home the gods of Edom after beating Edom (25:14). Ahaz explains himself, and hearing the reasoning out loud makes it worse. He has watched Syria win and concluded that Syria's gods are the ones with the power — when the narrator has just told us in verse 5 exactly who handed him over, and it was not Rimmon.

He is worshipping the weapon that was used on him and ignoring the hand that swung it. But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.

Then the last acts, and they are demolition. And Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and he shut up the doors of the house of the LORD.

The vessels were the ones Solomon made and Joash's chest paid to replace and Uzziah's priests handled every morning. They are cut up for the metal. And then the doors are barred. Not desecrated, not shared with another god, not filled with a rival altar — shut. The lamps go out. The morning and evening offerings stop. For the first time since Solomon prayed in that courtyard, there is nowhere in Judah to bring a sacrifice.

He replaces it with saturation: altars in every corner of Jerusalem, high places in every city of Judah. A man who shuts one door has to open a hundred others, because the appetite the door was there to satisfy does not go away when the door is locked. Nobody in Judah worshipped less under Ahaz. They simply worshipped everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of his acts and all his ways, from first to last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, in Jerusalem, for they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, in Jerusalem, for they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel.

Count the graves one more time. Jehoram was buried in the city of David but not in the tombs. Joash was buried in the city of David and kept out of the tombs. Amaziah was laid with his fathers. Uzziah went into the burial field beside the chamber. Jotham went in without a word of qualification. And Ahaz is buried in the city, in Jerusalem — the Chronicler will not even write the city of David over him. He is put somewhere inside the walls, and the record notes that they did not carry him where the kings go.

That is the bottom of the book. The temple is dark and locked, the vessels are scrap, the borders are gone, the towns are occupied, a hundred and twenty thousand men are dead, two hundred thousand were marched away and only came home because four strangers had a conscience, and the king who did it is in a grave nobody wanted to name.

And then the last six words of the chapter. And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.

A son of Ahaz. One of the boys who was not taken down into the valley. Whatever else that sentence means, it means the promise of 21:7 is still burning, and it has come through a foundry, a fire, two invasions and a locked temple, and it is now in the hands of a young man who will get up in the first month of his first year and open the doors.

There is one more thing to say about this reign, and it comes from outside this book. The king who refused a sign was given one anyway. Standing in front of Ahaz in the middle of the Syrian and Ephraimite war, with Judah's heart shaking like trees in a wind, Isaiah said: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel (Isa 7:14). A father in Jerusalem was putting his own sons into the fire to buy help from gods who were not there. And into that reign, over that man's head, God promised a Son of his own — not taken from him but given, and given for people exactly like Ahaz. God with us, spoken over the worst king in the book.

28.theology:
Oded's speech is the chapter's clearest theology. God handed Judah over, and the army he used is guilty for what it did while being used. Isaiah says the same of Assyria: the rod of God's anger is judged for the pride with which it swung (Isa 10:5-7). No one is licensed by being an instrument.

Verse 19 inverts the promise the whole book rests on. Since 7:14 the word has been if my people ... humble themselves. Here God humbles Judah from the outside, and nothing follows. Being brought low is not repentance; trouble makes a man more of what he already is, which is why the narrator interrupts himself in verse 22.

And the descent ends not in rival worship but in no worship: the vessels cut up, the doors shut, the lamps out, and nowhere in Judah to bring a sacrifice. Then the first sentence of the next reign opens them again in the first month of the first year (29:3).
28.examples:
A foundry in Jerusalem was casting idols to royal order.

He put some of his sons in the fire to buy safety, and an Ephraimite killed one of the sons he had kept.

Two hundred thousand mothers and children walked north in a column, and the text calls them the captors' relatives.

Four northerners nobody has heard of blocked the road into Samaria and would not let the prisoners through the gate.

They dressed the naked out of the plunder taken off them, put sandals on their feet, anointed them, and carried the ones who could not walk to Jericho on donkeys.

He stripped the temple, the palace and his own princes to pay Assyria, and Assyria afflicted him instead of helping him.

He shut the doors of the house of the LORD and opened altars on every corner in Jerusalem.

29.title: He Opened the Doors of the House of the LORD
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abijah the daughter of Zechariah.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done.<sup>3</sup>In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them.<sup>4</sup>He brought in the priests and the Levites and assembled them in the square on the east<sup>5</sup>and said to them, "Hear me, Levites! Now consecrate yourselves, and consecrate the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers, and carry out the filth from the Holy Place.<sup>6</sup>For our fathers have been unfaithful and have done what was evil in the sight of the LORD our God. They have forsaken him and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD and turned their backs.<sup>7</sup>They also shut the doors of the vestibule and put out the lamps and have not burned incense or offered burnt offerings in the Holy Place to the God of Israel.<sup>8</sup>Therefore the wrath of the LORD came on Judah and Jerusalem, and he has made them an object of horror, of astonishment, and of hissing, as you see with your own eyes.<sup>9</sup>For behold, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this.<sup>10</sup>Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us.<sup>11</sup>My sons, do not now be negligent, for the LORD has chosen you to stand in his presence, to minister to him and to be his ministers and make offerings to him."<sup>12</sup>Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites; and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehallelel; and of the Gershonites, Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah;<sup>13</sup>and of the sons of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeuel; and of the sons of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah;<sup>14</sup>and of the sons of Heman, Jehuel and Shimei; and of the sons of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel.<sup>15</sup>They gathered their brothers and consecrated themselves and went in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD, to cleanse the house of the LORD.<sup>16</sup>The priests went into the inner part of the house of the LORD to cleanse it, and they brought out all the uncleanness that they found in the temple of the LORD into the court of the house of the LORD. And the Levites took it and carried it out to the brook Kidron.<sup>17</sup>They began to consecrate on the first day of the first month, and on the eighth day of the month they came to the vestibule of the LORD. Then for eight days they consecrated the house of the LORD, and on the sixteenth day of the first month they finished.<sup>18</sup>Then they went in to Hezekiah the king and said, "We have cleansed all the house of the LORD, the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the table for the showbread and all its utensils.<sup>19</sup>All the utensils that King Ahaz discarded in his reign when he was faithless, we have made ready and consecrated, and behold, they are before the altar of the LORD."<sup>20</sup>Then Hezekiah the king rose early and gathered the officials of the city and went up to the house of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>And they brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats for a sin offering for the kingdom and for the sanctuary and for Judah. And he commanded the priests, the sons of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>So they slaughtered the bulls, and the priests received the blood and threw it against the altar. And they slaughtered the rams, and their blood was thrown against the altar. And they slaughtered the lambs, and their blood was thrown against the altar.<sup>23</sup>Then the goats for the sin offering were brought to the king and the assembly, and they laid their hands on them,<sup>24</sup>and the priests slaughtered them and made a sin offering with their blood on the altar, to make atonement for all Israel. For the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.<sup>25</sup>And he stationed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, according to the commandment of David and of Gad the king's seer and of Nathan the prophet, for the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets.<sup>26</sup>The Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets.<sup>27</sup>Then Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offering be offered on the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also, and the trumpets, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel.<sup>28</sup>The whole assembly worshiped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded. All this continued until the burnt offering was finished.<sup>29</sup>When the offering was finished, the king and all who were present with him bowed themselves and worshiped.<sup>30</sup>And Hezekiah the king and the officials commanded the Levites to sing praises to the LORD with the words of David and of Asaph the seer. And they sang praises with gladness, and they bowed down and worshiped.<sup>31</sup>Then Hezekiah said, "You have now consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come near; bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." And the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings.<sup>32</sup>The number of the burnt offerings that the assembly brought was 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs; all these were for a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>33</sup>And the consecrated offerings were 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep.<sup>34</sup>But the priests were too few and could not flay all the burnt offerings, so until other priests had consecrated themselves, their brothers the Levites helped them, until the work was finished— for the Levites were more upright in heart than the priests in consecrating themselves.<sup>35</sup>Besides the great number of burnt offerings, there was the fat of the peace offerings, and there were the drink offerings for the burnt offerings. Thus the service of the house of the LORD was restored.<sup>36</sup>And Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had provided for the people, for the thing came about suddenly.
29.overview:
Hezekiah does right according to all that David his father had done — the sentence his father was denied by one word (28:1) — and in the first year and the first month he opens the doors of the temple and repairs them (vv. 1-3). He gathers the priests and Levites and confesses the last generation's sin as our sin, itemises what stopped, names what it cost, and says it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD (vv. 4-11).

Fourteen Levites in seven pairs from seven families arise; the priests clear the inner house, the Levites carry the filth to the Kidron, and in sixteen days the work is done and Ahaz's discarded vessels are back before the altar (vv. 12-19). The king rises early; a sin offering is made for the kingdom, the sanctuary and Judah, with the assembly's hands on the goats and atonement made for all Israel (vv. 20-24). The music is restored by a commandment traced back to the LORD, and the song begins when the offering begins and ends when it ends (vv. 25-31). The people give more than the priests can handle, the Levites step in, and the service of the house is restored — for the thing came about suddenly (vv. 32-36).
29.theology:
Verse 6 is a model of inherited confession. Hezekiah is twenty-five and personally guiltless of everything he describes, and he says our fathers. Owning a family's or a church's sin as one's own, out loud, is the hardest and most fruitful sentence a reformer ever speaks.

Verses 27-28 tie praise to atonement on one clock: the song begins when the burnt offering begins and runs until it is finished. Singing in Scripture is not a mood the congregation generates; it is the sound made while a sacrifice is being offered, and it lives or dies with that altar. Verse 31 then gives the order plainly — offering, blood, song, and only then come near. Access follows atonement and never leads it.

Verse 24 stretches the atonement past the border. Hezekiah commands the sin offering to be made for all Israel — for the kingdom that had just killed 120,000 of his people and taken 200,000 captive. The next chapter posts the invitations.

And verse 36 gives the credit away. They rejoiced because God had provided, and the speed of it was the evidence: the thing came about suddenly. What looked like a young king's project had been prepared behind a locked door.
29.examples:
A new king's first month is for making the throne safe. Jehoram used his on his brothers, Amaziah on his father's assassins; Hezekiah used his on a set of hinges.

He said our fathers, standing in the guilt with the men he was about to ask for sixteen days of filthy work, when his own father was the chief offender.

The last king to give the Levites a job was told no by inaction — the Levites did not act quickly (24:5). This time: Then the Levites arose.

Men whose hereditary work was harps and cymbals spent a fortnight carrying rubbish down to the Kidron.

They found the vessels Ahaz had thrown out, cleaned them, and set them in front of the altar so the king would see them as he came in.

The king and every man in the courtyard put a hand on the head of a goat.

He paid for a sin offering for the northern kingdom, which had killed a hundred and twenty thousand of his people within living memory.

There were more offerings than there were consecrated priests to handle them, and the juniors had got ready first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — In the First Month, He Opened the Doors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah is twenty-five, and he does right according to all that David his father had done (vv. 1-2) — the sentence his father failed by one word (28:1). Then: In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them (v. 3). He assembles priests and Levites in the eastern square (v. 4) and speaks: consecrate yourselves and the house, and carry out the filth from the Holy Place (v. 5). For our fathers have been unfaithful — they forsook him, turned their faces away, turned their backs (v. 6), shut the doors, put out the lamps, stopped the incense and the offerings (v. 7). Hence the wrath, the horror and the hissing as you see with your own eyes (v. 8), and the dead and the captives (v. 9). Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD (v. 10). My sons, do not now be negligent, for the LORD has chosen you (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 is the model of an honest confession by a man who inherited the mess. He says our fathers, though the chief offender was his own father and he himself is twenty-five. He names the sin without softening it, states what it cost in casualties his hearers can count, and then moves — in the same speech — to what he intends to do about it.
verseByVerse.examples: A new king's first month is normally spent making the throne safe. Jehoram used his to kill his six brothers (21:4); Amaziah waited until the power was firmly his and then executed his father's assassins (25:3). Hezekiah spent his getting the doors of a locked building open, in the first month, in the first year.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abijah the daughter of Zechariah. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done. In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abijah the daughter of Zechariah.

Those two numbers have been printed in this book before, together, four chapters back. Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem (25:1). Same age at the crowning, same span on the throne — and one of them carried home the gods of the people he had just defeated, and the other opened the doors of the house of God in his first month. The figures on a man's file tell you nothing about him.

And his mother's name is kept: Abijah the daughter of Zechariah. She was married to Ahaz. She lived in the palace during the years when children of that household were carried down into the Hinnom valley, and this son of hers was not one of them. The record gives us her name and not a word of her story, which is how it usually goes with the people God uses most.

And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done.

Read that against the sentence twenty-seven verses earlier, at the head of the last chapter: And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done (28:1). The same measure, laid on a father and his son, with one word changed. Ahaz is the only king in this book to be given that sentence in the negative, and his son is handed it back whole.

Then the first thing he does.

In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them.

The first year and the first month, and verse 17 will tell us it was the first day of that month. A new king's opening weeks are for making the throne safe, and this book has shown us how that is normally done. Jehoram used his to put his six brothers to the sword (21:4). Amaziah waited until the royal power was firmly his and then executed his father's assassins (25:3). Athaliah used hers on the nursery.

Hezekiah, aged twenty-five, with a father dead in disgrace, an Assyrian occupation on the books, six towns of the Shephelah in Philistine hands and a country full of corner-altars, went to a locked building and got the doors open.

Not knocked down; opened, and then repaired. His father had shut them and let them rot. The first public act of the reign was carpentry, and it announced everything that followed. Whatever else this king was going to be short of, access to God was not going to be one of the shortages.

verseByVerse.quote: He brought in the priests and the Levites and assembled them in the square on the east and said to them, "Hear me, Levites! Now consecrate yourselves, and consecrate the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers, and carry out the filth from the Holy Place. For our fathers have been unfaithful and have done what was evil in the sight of the LORD our God. They have forsaken him and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD and turned their backs. They also shut the doors of the vestibule and put out the lamps and have not burned incense or offered burnt offerings in the Holy Place to the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He assembles the priests and Levites in the square on the east — outside the building, because the building is not yet fit to stand in — and gives the speech that starts the reformation.

Hear me, Levites! Now consecrate yourselves, and consecrate the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers, and carry out the filth from the Holy Place.

The order is exact and it does not vary anywhere in Scripture: consecrate yourselves first, then the house. Men who have not dealt with themselves cannot clean anything holy. And the word translated filth is a brutal one — the term for menstrual defilement, the strongest word for uncleanness the language had. That is what was lying in the Holy Place of the temple of God after sixteen years of Ahaz.

Then the diagnosis, and the first word of it decides what kind of man is speaking.

For our fathers have been unfaithful and have done what was evil in the sight of the LORD our God.

Our fathers. He is twenty-five years old. He personally shut nothing, melted nothing, burned no child in the Hinnom valley, and the man who did all of it was his own father and died two minutes ago. He could have said your fathers and been factually correct. He could have said my father Ahaz and been popular. He says our, and stands inside the guilt with the men he is addressing.

That is what honest confession sounds like when you have inherited a mess you did not make. Not the disowning of it, which is easy and cheap, and not a private grievance about the people who made it, which is easier still. He owns the family's sin as his own, out loud, in front of the men he is about to ask to do sixteen days of filthy work.

The three verbs of verse 6 are a picture of one movement: they forsook him, turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD, and turned their backs. That is how it goes. First the heart leaves, then the eyes, and last the body, and each step looks like nothing much on the day it is taken.

Verse 7 lists what stopped, and it reads as an inventory of absence: the doors shut, the lamps put out, no incense burned, no burnt offerings made. Four things, and each one was a daily thing. The temple did not blow up. It went quiet.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the wrath of the LORD came on Judah and Jerusalem, and he has made them an object of horror, of astonishment, and of hissing, as you see with your own eyes. For behold, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this. Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us. My sons, do not now be negligent, for the LORD has chosen you to stand in his presence, to minister to him and to be his ministers and make offerings to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore the wrath of the LORD came on Judah and Jerusalem, and he has made them an object of horror, of astonishment, and of hissing, as you see with your own eyes.

As you see with your own eyes. He does not ask them to accept a doctrine. He asks them to look out of the window. There are Philistine garrisons in towns that were Judah's a year ago; there is an Assyrian tribute schedule; there are households in that square with no father in them.

For behold, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this.

For this. He draws the line himself, from the locked doors to the graves, and he does it in public. Everyone standing there had buried somebody in the last few years; a hundred and twenty thousand fell in a single day under Ahaz, and two hundred thousand went north in a column. The young king tells them what that was, and he does not blame Pekah for it.

Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us.

It is in my heart. Nobody made him do this. There is no prophet in this chapter, no defeat in progress, no crisis forcing his hand — Assyria will not come for another fourteen years. He is not managing a situation. He wants this, and he says so in the first person, and the whole reformation of chapters 29 to 31 comes out of one man's settled desire.

My sons, do not now be negligent, for the LORD has chosen you to stand in his presence, to minister to him and to be his ministers and make offerings to him.

My sons, from a man of twenty-five to the priesthood of Judah. It is a father's word, not a commander's, and what he gives them is not a threat but their own job description. Do not be slack, because of who chose you and what he chose you for: to stand in his presence.

That is the only motive he offers, and it is the right one. He does not tell them the nation needs them, or that the times are desperate, or that history is watching. He tells them the LORD picked them out to stand in front of him, and that a man who has been given that has no business being casual about it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — Out to the Brook Kidron
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the Levites arose — fourteen men, named in seven pairs, from Kohath, Merari, Gershon, Elizaphan, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (vv. 12-14). They gather their brothers, consecrate themselves, and go in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD (v. 15). The priests work inside the house and carry the uncleanness out to the court; the Levites take it from there to the brook Kidron (v. 16). Seven days to reach the vestibule, eight more inside, finished on the sixteenth of the month (v. 17). They report to the king, item by item (v. 18), ending: All the utensils that King Ahaz discarded in his reign when he was faithless, we have made ready and consecrated, and behold, they are before the altar of the LORD (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 gives the chain of authority in six words: they went in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD. The king's order is obeyed because of what stands behind it. A command that rests on Scripture can move fourteen men and their families to spend sixteen days carrying filth down a hill.
verseByVerse.examples: The last king to gather the priests and Levites and give them a job was Joash, and the record of that day reads: But the Levites did not act quickly (24:5). Here the sentence is Then the Levites arose. Same office, same building, different generation, and the difference was a man in the square who spoke to them as sons and told them God had chosen them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites; and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehallelel; and of the Gershonites, Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah; and of the sons of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeuel; and of the sons of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah; and of the sons of Heman, Jehuel and Shimei; and of the sons of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel. They gathered their brothers and consecrated themselves and went in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD, to cleanse the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Levites arose.

Two words, and they answer a sentence from five chapters back. The last king to gather the priests and Levites and give them a job to do was Joash, who told them to go and collect the repair fund and to be quick about it — and the record of that morning is: But the Levites did not act quickly (24:5). Same office, same building, a hundred years later, and this time they get up.

And then fourteen names, which is the sort of list a modern reader skims and the Chronicler never wastes. Count them: they come in seven pairs, out of seven families. Two from Kohath, two from Merari, two from Gershon — the three ancient clans of Levi. Two from Elizaphan. And then two each from Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, which are the three guilds of singers David himself set apart for the service (1 Chr 25:1).

The whole house of Levi is represented, and the musicians are in the cleaning party. Men whose hereditary work was harps and cymbals spent the next fortnight carrying rubbish out of a building. Nobody stood on his speciality.

They gathered their brothers and consecrated themselves and went in as the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD, to cleanse the house of the LORD.

As the king had commanded, by the words of the LORD. There is the chain, and it runs the right way round. They are not obeying Hezekiah because he is charming or because he is the king; the clause behind his authority is the word of God, and it is because his order rests there that fourteen men and their families are willing to spend sixteen days doing the worst job in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests went into the inner part of the house of the LORD to cleanse it, and they brought out all the uncleanness that they found in the temple of the LORD into the court of the house of the LORD. And the Levites took it and carried it out to the brook Kidron. They began to consecrate on the first day of the first month, and on the eighth day of the month they came to the vestibule of the LORD. Then for eight days they consecrated the house of the LORD, and on the sixteenth day of the first month they finished. Then they went in to Hezekiah the king and said, "We have cleansed all the house of the LORD, the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the table for the showbread and all its utensils. All the utensils that King Ahaz discarded in his reign when he was faithless, we have made ready and consecrated, and behold, they are before the altar of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests went into the inner part of the house of the LORD to cleanse it, and they brought out all the uncleanness that they found in the temple of the LORD into the court of the house of the LORD. And the Levites took it and carried it out to the brook Kidron.

A relay in two zones. Only priests may go into the inner house, so priests do that part and bring what they find as far as the court; from the court the Levites take over and carry it down the hill. Even in an emergency, even with the place in this state, the boundary Uzziah died crossing is kept. Reform does not mean the rules stop applying; it means somebody has finally started keeping them.

And they carry it to the Kidron, which is the right address. That is where Asa burned his own grandmother's Asherah image (15:16), and where the people will throw Jerusalem's altars in the next chapter (30:14). The valley on the east side of the city was Judah's tip for dead gods.

The calendar in verse 17 repays a slow walk. They start on the first day of the first month. It takes seven days simply to work through the courts and arrive at the vestibule — the porch, the outermost part of the house itself. Then eight more days inside, and they finish on the sixteenth.

Sixteen days. There is no drama in any of it. No fire falls, no prophet speaks, nothing happens that anyone would put in a song, and a modern account of a revival would leave the whole fortnight out. But the singing in the second half of this chapter is standing on those sixteen days, and it could not have happened without them.

Then the report, and it is itemised, because a general assurance would not do. The altar of burnt offering and all its utensils. The table for the showbread and all its utensils. And then the sentence that must have been worth the whole fortnight to say out loud:

All the utensils that King Ahaz discarded in his reign when he was faithless, we have made ready and consecrated, and behold, they are before the altar of the LORD.

They found them. Whatever Ahaz had thrown out rather than cut up had been lying somewhere for years, and the Levites went and got it back, cleaned it, consecrated it, and set it out in front of the altar so that the king could see it as he came in. A son standing in a courtyard looking at the vessels his father threw away, back in their places, ready for use.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — When the Burnt Offering Began, the Song Began
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah rose early and brought the officials up to the house (v. 20). Seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs and seven goats, a sin offering for the kingdom and for the sanctuary and for Judah (v. 21); the blood is thrown against the altar (v. 22); the king and the assembly lay their hands on the goats (v. 23) and the priests make atonement for all Israel (v. 24). The Levites are stationed with the instruments of David by a commandment traced to David, Gad and Nathan and behind them to the LORD (vv. 25-26). And when the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also, and it ran until the offering was finished (vv. 27-28). The king and everyone with him bow (v. 29); the Levites sing with the words of David and of Asaph the seer (v. 30); and Hezekiah says, You have now consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come near (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 27-28 set the singing and the sacrifice to the same clock. The song starts when the offering starts and stops when it is finished. Praise here is not a warm-up or an afterthought; it is the sound a people make while atonement is being carried out in front of them, and it has no existence apart from that.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 23 has the king of Judah and the whole assembly with their hands on the heads of four goats. Nobody stood at a distance and let the professionals handle it. Every man in that courtyard put his hand on an animal that was about to die and said, in the only language the ceremony had, that his own guilt was going onto it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah the king rose early and gathered the officials of the city and went up to the house of the LORD. And they brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats for a sin offering for the kingdom and for the sanctuary and for Judah. And he commanded the priests, the sons of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the LORD. So they slaughtered the bulls, and the priests received the blood and threw it against the altar. And they slaughtered the rams, and their blood was thrown against the altar. And they slaughtered the lambs, and their blood was thrown against the altar. Then the goats for the sin offering were brought to the king and the assembly, and they laid their hands on them, and the priests slaughtered them and made a sin offering with their blood on the altar, to make atonement for all Israel. For the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Hezekiah the king rose early and gathered the officials of the city and went up to the house of the LORD.

Rose early. Sixteen days of waiting while other men worked, and on the morning the house was ready he was up before he needed to be. There is no ceremony in the detail and that is why it is there.

What happens next is not a celebration. It is a sin offering, and it comes first.

Seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, seven goats — the number of completeness applied four times over — for a sin offering for the kingdom and for the sanctuary and for Judah. Three spheres: the state, the building and the people. Everything the last generation touched needed cleansing, and the government was named first.

Verse 22 then reports the killing three times over, and will not abbreviate it. So they slaughtered the bulls, and the priests received the blood and threw it against the altar. And they slaughtered the rams, and their blood was thrown against the altar. And they slaughtered the lambs, and their blood was thrown against the altar. Three clauses, one for each kind of animal, because it happened three times and each time a creature died and its blood went against the stone. A sacrificial system is not an efficient thing and was never meant to be. It is designed to be slow, physical and repetitive, so that nobody in the courtyard could mistake forgiveness for a formality.

Then verse 23, which is the theological heart of the ceremony. Then the goats for the sin offering were brought to the king and the assembly, and they laid their hands on them.

Both king and assembly, hands on the heads of the animals. Nobody watched from a distance while the professionals handled the difficulty. In the only language the ceremony possessed, every man in that court said: what is being done to this creature is what should be done to me, and I am putting my guilt where it can be carried away.

And then, in verse 24, a phrase that goes further than anyone would expect from a king of Judah in this particular decade. The priests made a sin offering with the blood on the altar to make atonement for all Israel. For the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.

All Israel. The northern kingdom had killed a hundred and twenty thousand Judeans in one day and marched two hundred thousand women and children up the road within living memory. Hezekiah pays for their sin offering. He is not their king, they have not asked, most of them will never hear of it, and Assyria will end their kingdom within a few years. He commands atonement for them anyway, and the next chapter will show him writing letters north to invite them to dinner.

verseByVerse.quote: And he stationed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, according to the commandment of David and of Gad the king's seer and of Nathan the prophet, for the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets. The Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. Then Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offering be offered on the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also, and the trumpets, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel. The whole assembly worshiped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded. All this continued until the burnt offering was finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he stationed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, according to the commandment of David and of Gad the king's seer and of Nathan the prophet, for the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets.

The music is not a matter of taste, and the Chronicler goes out of his way to say so. He traces it through three names — David, Gad the seer, Nathan the prophet — and then behind all three: the commandment was from the LORD through his prophets. Israel sang because God said to.

Verse 26 then shows us the band. The Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. Two groups, two authorities. The strings and cymbals are David's, set apart by him for this service; the trumpets are older, two of hammered silver, made at God's command and given to the sons of Aaron as a perpetual statute — and the statute says exactly when to sound them: you shall blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings (Num 10:2, 8, 10). Moses and David in one orchestra, and neither part of it invented by Hezekiah.

Then the moment the chapter has been building toward, and it turns on a single word of timing.

Then Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offering be offered on the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began also, and the trumpets, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel.

The offering began, and the song began with it. Not before, while the crowd was gathering, and not after, once the unpleasant part was over. The knife and the first note went together. And verse 28 closes the bracket at the other end: All this continued until the burnt offering was finished.

The singing and the sacrifice are on the same clock. That is not a stage direction; it is a statement about what praise is. The song is the noise a rescued people make while the price of their rescue is being paid in front of them. It has no life of its own, no existence apart from the altar it is timed to, and it stops when the offering stops.

Which is why the church has never stopped singing. Our offering was made once and is finished, and finished is the word the sacrifice itself used. The song that began when he was lifted up runs on the same clock as that offering, and since the offering is never repeated and never expires, neither does the music. The whole assembly worshipped, says verse 28, and the singers sang and the trumpeters sounded — and the reason it did not have to stop for breath was standing on the altar in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the offering was finished, the king and all who were present with him bowed themselves and worshiped. And Hezekiah the king and the officials commanded the Levites to sing praises to the LORD with the words of David and of Asaph the seer. And they sang praises with gladness, and they bowed down and worshiped. Then Hezekiah said, "You have now consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come near; bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." And the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the offering was finished, the king and all who were present with him bowed themselves and worshiped.

The music stops and the whole company goes down on its face. The loud part was not the point of the loud part.

And Hezekiah the king and the officials commanded the Levites to sing praises to the LORD with the words of David and of Asaph the seer.

With the words of David and of Asaph. They sang the Psalms. The hymnbook was already written and had been for two and a half centuries, and it had gone on existing all through Ahaz's reign in a building nobody could get into. Then somebody opened the doors and the words were still there.

Hold on to that in a dark decade. The songs of the church survive the people who stop singing them. They wait.

And they sang with gladness, and they bowed down and worshiped. Gladness and prostration in the same sentence, and no sense that the two are in tension. A people can be flat on the floor and delighted at the same time; in fact that is roughly the definition.

Then Hezekiah said, You have now consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come near; bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the LORD.

Come near. That is the invitation the whole day has been working toward, and notice the order it comes in: the sin offering was made, the blood was thrown, the song was sung, and now — now — come near. Access follows atonement; it never leads it. And what comes in response is not a levy but a flood, and all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings. Nobody had to be assessed. They had been shut out of that courtyard for sixteen years and they arrived carrying what they had.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–36 — The Thing Came About Suddenly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The assembly brings 70 bulls, 100 rams and 200 lambs for burnt offering (v. 32), and 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep as consecrated offerings (v. 33). But the priests were too few, so the Levites help them until the work is done — for the Levites were more upright in heart than the priests in consecrating themselves (v. 34). With the fat of the peace offerings and the drink offerings, the service of the house of the LORD was restored (v. 35). And Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had provided for the people, for the thing came about suddenly (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 36 hands the whole chapter back. Hezekiah opened the doors, wrote the speech, called the assembly and paid for the bulls, and the sentence that closes the account says God provided and it happened fast. The man who did the most in the chapter is not the subject of its last verb.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 34 is an awkward line that the Chronicler prints anyway: the priests were outnumbered and outpaced by the Levites, who were quicker to consecrate themselves than their seniors were. And that shortage is not left hanging — 30:3 gives it as the reason Passover had to be moved to the second month.

verseByVerse.quote: The number of the burnt offerings that the assembly brought was 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs; all these were for a burnt offering to the LORD. And the consecrated offerings were 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep. But the priests were too few and could not flay all the burnt offerings, so until other priests had consecrated themselves, their brothers the Levites helped them, until the work was finished— for the Levites were more upright in heart than the priests in consecrating themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The numbers tell you what the mood was. Seventy bulls, a hundred rams, two hundred lambs for burnt offering; six hundred bulls and three thousand sheep as consecrated offerings. A country that had been paying tribute to Assyria out of a stripped treasury brought that into Jerusalem in a few days.

And then a problem, and it is the best kind a reformer can have.

But the priests were too few and could not flay all the burnt offerings, so until other priests had consecrated themselves, their brothers the Levites helped them, until the work was finished.

The generosity outran the staffing. There were more animals on the ground than there were consecrated men to deal with them, and the Levites went outside their normal duties and took up the knives until enough priests had got themselves ready.

Then the Chronicler adds a line he did not have to add, and it is uncomfortable.

For the Levites were more upright in heart than the priests in consecrating themselves.

The senior order was the slower order. The men with the higher office and the closer access were the ones dragging their feet about getting ready, and their juniors were quicker off the mark. It is stated flatly, with no attempt to protect anyone's dignity, in a book written by somebody who plainly loves the temple and its ministry.

Rank is not readiness. A man can hold the office, know the liturgy, have the right family and the right training, and be the last person in the building to deal with himself. The position does not do it for him, and everybody around him can tell.

And that shortage does not go away when the chapter ends. It is the reason, named in so many words at 30:3, that the Passover had to be moved to the second month: the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number. The revival had to work around its own clergy for another four weeks.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides the great number of burnt offerings, there was the fat of the peace offerings, and there were the drink offerings for the burnt offerings. Thus the service of the house of the LORD was restored. And Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had provided for the people, for the thing came about suddenly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Besides the great number of burnt offerings, there was the fat of the peace offerings, and there were the drink offerings for the burnt offerings. Thus the service of the house of the LORD was restored.

Restored. The doors were open, the vessels were on the tables, the lamps were lit, the incense was burning, the offerings were going up morning and evening, and the choir was in its place singing David's words. Everything in the inventory of absence in verse 7 has been answered item for item.

Then the last verse of the chapter, which takes it all out of Hezekiah's hands.

And Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had provided for the people, for the thing came about suddenly.

Two clauses, and neither is what a court chronicler would have written. The first gives the credit away: they rejoiced because God had provided. Hezekiah opened the doors, wrote the speech, called the assembly, paid for the bulls and stood there from dawn — and the sentence that closes the account does not have him as its subject. He is in the crowd, rejoicing at what somebody else did.

The second clause is stranger and better. For the thing came about suddenly. Suddenly. After sixteen years of a locked temple and a foundry casting Baals and children burning in the Hinnom valley, it took under a month. The doors on day one, the house clean by the sixteenth, the altar smoking and the choir singing before the month was out.

They had every reason to expect it to be slow. Reformations of that size are supposed to take a generation, and the men doing this one had no funds, an occupying power on the border and a priesthood that could not organise itself. It went fast because God had prepared it, and the speed was the evidence: what looked like Hezekiah's project turned out to be something God had been arranging while nobody could see it, waiting on the far side of a locked door for a young man to come with a key.

That is how it usually is. The long dark stretch is not God waiting for us to become worth helping, and the sudden turn, when it comes, is not the reward for the sixteen days of cleaning. It is the uncovering of what he had ready all along.

30.title: The LORD Heard Hezekiah and Healed the People
30.text: <sup>1</sup>Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the house of the LORD at Jerusalem to keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>2</sup>For the king and his princes and all the assembly in Jerusalem had taken counsel to keep the Passover in the second month—<sup>3</sup>for they could not keep it at that time because the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number, nor had the people assembled in Jerusalem—<sup>4</sup>and the plan seemed right to the king and all the assembly.<sup>5</sup>So they decreed to make a proclamation throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, that the people should come and keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel, at Jerusalem, for they had not kept it as often as prescribed.<sup>6</sup>So couriers went throughout all Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his princes, as the king had commanded, saying, "O people of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may turn again to the remnant of you who have escaped from the hand of the kings of Assyria.<sup>7</sup>Do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who were faithless to the LORD God of their fathers, so that he made them a desolation, as you see.<sup>8</sup>Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD and come to his sanctuary, which he has consecrated forever, and serve the LORD your God, that his fierce anger may turn away from you.<sup>9</sup>For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and your children will find compassion with their captors and return to this land. For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him."<sup>10</sup>So the couriers went from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, and as far as Zebulun, but they laughed them to scorn and mocked them.<sup>11</sup>However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.<sup>12</sup>The hand of God was also on Judah to give them one heart to do what the king and the princes commanded by the word of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And many people came together in Jerusalem to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month, a very great assembly.<sup>14</sup>They set to work and removed the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for burning incense they took away and threw into the brook Kidron.<sup>15</sup>And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month. And the priests and the Levites were ashamed, so that they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings into the house of the LORD.<sup>16</sup>They took their accustomed posts according to the Law of Moses the man of God. The priests threw the blood that they received from the hand of the Levites.<sup>17</sup>For there were many in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves. Therefore the Levites had to slaughter the Passover lamb for everyone who was not clean, to consecrate it to the LORD.<sup>18</sup>For a majority of the people, many of them from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover otherwise than as prescribed. For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, "May the good LORD pardon everyone<sup>19</sup>who sets his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even though not according to the sanctuary's rules of cleanness."<sup>20</sup>And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.<sup>21</sup>And the people of Israel who were present at Jerusalem kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with great gladness, and the Levites and the priests praised the LORD day by day, singing with all their might to the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who showed good skill in the service of the LORD. So they ate the food of the festival for seven days, sacrificing peace offerings and giving thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>23</sup>Then the whole assembly agreed together to keep the feast for another seven days. So they kept it for another seven days with gladness.<sup>24</sup>For Hezekiah king of Judah gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for offerings, and the princes gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. And the priests consecrated themselves in great numbers.<sup>25</sup>The whole assembly of Judah, and the priests and the Levites, and the whole assembly that came out of Israel, and the sojourners who came out of the land of Israel, and the sojourners who lived in Judah, rejoiced.<sup>26</sup>So there was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem.<sup>27</sup>Then the priests and the Levites arose and blessed the people, and their voice was heard, and their prayer came to his holy habitation in heaven.
30.overview:
Hezekiah writes to all Israel and Judah, and posts letters north to Ephraim and Manasseh, calling them to Jerusalem for a Passover kept in the second month — because the priests were not consecrated in sufficient number and the people had not gathered, and the plan seemed right to the king and all the assembly (vv. 1-5). The letter itself is the promise of 7:14 in an envelope: return, and he will turn again to you, for the LORD your God is gracious and merciful (vv. 6-9). Most of the north laughs the couriers out of the market square; some men of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and walk south, and the hand of God gives Judah one heart (vv. 10-12).

The assembly's first act is to throw Ahaz's street altars into the Kidron, and the shame of the laity's readiness finally moves the clergy to consecrate themselves (vv. 13-16). Most of the crowd is unclean and eats otherwise than as prescribed, so the king prays for pardon for everyone who sets his heart to seek God — and the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people (vv. 17-20). Seven days of singing with all their might, the king going round encouraging the musicians, then another seven by common agreement, paid for by the king and outpaid by his princes (vv. 21-24). Five groups rejoice, sojourners among them; there had been nothing like it since Solomon; and the blessing of the priests reaches God's dwelling place in heaven (vv. 25-27).
30.theology:
Verses 18-20 are the chapter's centre and the book's promise landing. The people are in the wrong and the narrator says so — they ate otherwise than as prescribed. Hezekiah asks not for permission but for pardon, and the ground he offers is the direction of a man's heart: everyone who sets his heart to seek God, which joins this book's two great verbs in one clause (11:16; 12:14; 19:3). God's answer uses 7:14's own words — he heard, and he healed. The standard was not lowered; the people were forgiven.

The letter of verses 6-9 shows what a summons to repentance sounds like when the one issuing it has no leverage. Hezekiah cannot compel a foreign kingdom. He describes God — gracious and merciful, in the words God used of himself to Moses — and asks them to come. Most of them mock, and nothing in the invitation is altered on that account.

And verse 27 answers 6:21. Solomon asked God to listen from heaven, his dwelling place; here the priests' blessing over a mixed and irregular crowd arrives there. The house did what it was prayed into being to do.
30.examples:
He wrote to the kingdom that had killed 120,000 of his people, and he had already paid for their sin offering before he sent the invitation.

Rather than keep the calendar exactly and hold no Passover at all, the council moved it a month, and the record says the plan seemed right to them.

A man walked into a market square, read out the king's letter, was jeered at, and went on to the next town, all the way to Zebulun.

Men from Asher and Zebulun made the longest journey in the country from towns where the messenger had just been laughed at.

Tens of thousands of pilgrims spent their first day in Jerusalem pulling down street altars and carrying them to the Kidron.

The priests were shamed into consecrating themselves by the readiness of foreigners who had walked for a fortnight.

The king went round the musicians in the middle of the largest gathering in living memory and told the ones with real skill that they were doing it well.

His princes gave three thousand more sheep than he did, and the record prints both figures.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah writes to all Israel and Judah, and letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, calling them to Jerusalem for the Passover (v. 1). The king, his princes and the assembly had taken counsel to keep it in the second month (v. 2), because the priests were not consecrated in sufficient number and the people had not gathered (v. 3), and the plan seemed right to the king and all the assembly (v. 4). A proclamation goes out throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan ... for they had not kept it as often as prescribed (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The law allowed a second-month Passover for a man made unclean by a corpse or away on a long journey (Num 9:10-11). Hezekiah takes a provision written for an individual and applies it to a nation, and verse 4 does not hide that this was a judgment: the plan seemed right. The alternative was to keep the letter of the calendar and hold no Passover at all.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 gives the two reasons, and they are the two problems left standing at the end of the last chapter: not enough consecrated priests, and the people not yet gathered. A reformation that is one month old has to work around its own unreadiness, and this one did.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the house of the LORD at Jerusalem to keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel. For the king and his princes and all the assembly in Jerusalem had taken counsel to keep the Passover in the second month— for they could not keep it at that time because the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number, nor had the people assembled in Jerusalem— and the plan seemed right to the king and all the assembly. So they decreed to make a proclamation throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, that the people should come and keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel, at Jerusalem, for they had not kept it as often as prescribed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the house of the LORD at Jerusalem to keep the Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel.

Take in who is being invited. Ephraim and Manasseh are the northern kingdom, and within living memory the northern kingdom killed a hundred and twenty thousand men of Judah in a single day and marched two hundred thousand women and children up the road to Samaria (28:6, 8). Hezekiah's own generation buried those men. He writes to the people who did it and asks them to dinner.

He had already paid for their sin offering in the previous chapter, when he commanded atonement for all Israel (29:24). Now he sends the invitations. Note the order: he made provision for them before he asked anything of them.

Then the calendar problem, and the way it is handled tells you a great deal about the man.

Passover falls on the fourteenth day of the first month. The cleansing of the temple had run from the first of that month to the sixteenth (29:17), straight through the date. And verse 3 gives the two reasons they could not keep it: the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number, nor had the people assembled in Jerusalem — which is precisely the problem the last chapter ended with (29:34).

So they move it a month. The law of Moses does allow a second-month Passover, but it was written for an individual: a man made unclean by a dead body, or away on a long journey, may keep it in the second month (Num 9:10-11). Hezekiah takes a provision made for one man in awkward circumstances and applies it to a whole nation in awkward circumstances, and the text does not pretend this was obvious. And the plan seemed right to the king and all the assembly.

That is a judgment call, made in council, and it is the right one. The alternative was to keep the calendar exactly and hold no Passover at all — to be scrupulous about the date and let a nation go another year without the meal that told it who it was. Some rules exist to protect a thing, and a man who keeps the rule while losing the thing has understood neither.

The proclamation goes out from Beersheba to Dan. The old phrase runs the other way round — from Dan to Beersheba, north to south — and the Chronicler flips it, here and when David counts the people (1 Chr 21:2). He measures outward from Judah's end, and the whole length of the land is meant. And then a quiet admission from a man with no interest in flattering his own people: for they had not kept it as often as prescribed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The couriers carry a letter: O people of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may turn again to the remnant of you who have escaped from the hand of the kings of Assyria (v. 6). Do not be like your fathers and brothers, who were faithless so that he made them a desolation, as you see (v. 7); do not be stiff-necked, but yield yourselves to the LORD and come to his sanctuary (v. 8); for the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him (v. 9). The couriers are laughed at from city to city (v. 10). However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem (v. 11), and in Judah the hand of God gave the people one heart (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The letter is the promise of 7:14 put in an envelope and posted. Return, and he will turn again to you; the word runs three times in four verses. And the ground offered is not Judah's hospitality or Hezekiah's goodwill but God's own character, quoted back from Exodus: gracious and merciful.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of the north laughed. The Chronicler does not soften it — they laughed them to scorn and mocked them — and he does not report that Hezekiah rewrote the letter, shortened the journey or lowered the terms. He sent it, they mocked it, and some men from three tribes walked two hundred miles anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: So couriers went throughout all Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his princes, as the king had commanded, saying, "O people of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may turn again to the remnant of you who have escaped from the hand of the kings of Assyria. Do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who were faithless to the LORD God of their fathers, so that he made them a desolation, as you see. Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD and come to his sanctuary, which he has consecrated forever, and serve the LORD your God, that his fierce anger may turn away from you. For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and your children will find compassion with their captors and return to this land. For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter itself is one of the most remarkable documents in the Old Testament. A king of Judah, writing to a foreign kingdom that has recently made war on him, asking them to come home to God.

O people of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may turn again to the remnant of you who have escaped from the hand of the kings of Assyria.

He calls the third patriarch Israel and not Jacob, because Israel is the name these people still carry and he means them to hear that it is their God he is talking about, not Judah's local arrangement.

And the shape of the sentence is the shape of the gospel. Return, that he may turn again. The same verb both ways. Nothing in it suggests that God has to be talked round; the turning of God toward them is presented as the settled response to their turning toward him.

The word remnant tells us where in history we are standing. Assyria has already begun the deportations. Whole districts of the north are gone. The people reading this letter are survivors, and Hezekiah says so to their faces without cruelty and without pretending it happened by accident.

Do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who were faithless to the LORD God of their fathers, so that he made them a desolation, as you see.

Your brothers, not just your fathers. Some of the men who caused this are still alive. As you see — the same appeal Hezekiah made to his own priests (29:8): look out of the window, the evidence is standing in your own countryside.

Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD.

The picture behind stiff-necked is an ox that will not turn when the rein is pulled. And the phrase behind yield yourselves is, literally, give the hand — the gesture of a man submitting, pledging, putting his hand in someone else's. Stop bracing your neck; put out your hand.

Then the last verse of the letter, and it does not argue. It describes God.

For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him.

Those are the words God used of himself to Moses on the mountain, when he passed by and said what he was like. Hezekiah takes God's own self-description and posts it to a hostile audience two hundred miles away, and offers it as the whole reason for making the journey.

He has also just made them a promise that must have been almost unbearable to read: your brothers and your children will find compassion with their captors and return to this land. These are families with sons in Assyria. He is telling them that the road back for the people they have lost runs through their own repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: So the couriers went from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, and as far as Zebulun, but they laughed them to scorn and mocked them. However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. The hand of God was also on Judah to give them one heart to do what the king and the princes commanded by the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the couriers went from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, and as far as Zebulun, but they laughed them to scorn and mocked them.

City by city. Picture the job. A man on foot with a letter in his hand walks into a market square, reads out an invitation from the king of Judah to come and worship at Jerusalem, and is jeered at. Then he walks to the next town and does it again. And the next. All the way up to Zebulun in the far north.

The Chronicler does not tidy this away, and preachers should not either. The best invitation in the book, from a king who had already paid for their sin offering, carrying the kindest description of God in the Old Testament, was received in most of the north as a joke.

And nothing is changed in response. Hezekiah does not recall the couriers, soften the terms, move the venue nearer or drop the bit about being stiff-necked. The invitation goes out as written, the response is what it is, and the king lets it be what it is.

However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.

However. One word, and the whole chapter turns on it.

Three tribes are named, and two of them — Asher and Zebulun — are as far north as Israel goes. Those men had the longest walk and the loudest neighbours. They set out from towns where the messenger had just been laughed out of the square, which means every one of them was known to be going and known to be a fool for going.

And the verb used of them is the verb this whole book is built on. They humbled themselves — the word of 7:14, the word Rehoboam found under Shishak and Manasseh will find in a Babylonian prison. It is used here of a handful of northerners with no temple, no priesthood, no Davidic king and no record of obedience, who read a letter and did what it said.

The hand of God was also on Judah to give them one heart to do what the king and the princes commanded by the word of the LORD.

Even the good response is credited elsewhere. Judah came together, and the Chronicler will not let that be read as competent leadership or national mood. The hand of God gave them one heart. Unity in worship is a thing that is given, and where it appears somebody should thank God for it rather than the committee.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — May the Good LORD Pardon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A very great assembly gathers (v. 13) and its first act is demolition: the altars in Jerusalem are pulled down and thrown into the Kidron (v. 14). The lamb is killed on the fourteenth day, and the priests and the Levites were ashamed, so that they consecrated themselves (v. 15); the priests throw the blood handed to them by the Levites (v. 16), who have had to kill the lambs for everyone unclean (v. 17). A majority of the people, many from the northern tribes, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover otherwise than as prescribed — so Hezekiah prays: May the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God ... even though not according to the sanctuary's rules of cleanness (vv. 18-19). And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 puts this book's two great verbs in one clause: a man who sets his heart to seek God. It is what Rehoboam never did (12:14) and what ordinary northerners had done under Rehoboam (11:16). And verse 20 answers with 7:14's own two verbs — the LORD heard and healed.
verseByVerse.examples: Read verse 18 without flinching: they ate otherwise than as prescribed. The narrator calls the irregularity what it is; nobody pretends the rules did not apply or that these people had met them. What happened is not that the standard was lowered. A king prayed, and God pardoned.

verseByVerse.quote: And many people came together in Jerusalem to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month, a very great assembly. They set to work and removed the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for burning incense they took away and threw into the brook Kidron. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month. And the priests and the Levites were ashamed, so that they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings into the house of the LORD. They took their accustomed posts according to the Law of Moses the man of God. The priests threw the blood that they received from the hand of the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And many people came together in Jerusalem to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month, a very great assembly.

A very great assembly. That is the phrase used of the crowd at Solomon's dedication of the temple (7:8), and the Chronicler will come back to Solomon explicitly before the chapter is out.

And the first thing this enormous, joyful crowd does is not sing.

They set to work and removed the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for burning incense they took away and threw into the brook Kidron.

Ahaz had built altars in every corner of Jerusalem (28:24), and they were still there. The temple had been scrubbed a month earlier, but the streets had not. So before the lamb is killed, tens of thousands of pilgrims go through the city pulling down the furniture of the last reign and carrying it to the same valley the temple's filth went to.

Worship and demolition in the same week, in that order. It is no use holding a feast in honour of God in a city that still has the alternatives standing on every corner in case the feast does not work out.

Then a sentence about the clergy that must have stung to write. And the priests and the Levites were ashamed, so that they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings into the house of the LORD.

They were ashamed. What shamed them was the sight of ordinary people, including foreigners from the north who had walked for two weeks, arriving ready when the men whose whole existence was this building were not. In the previous chapter the Levites had outpaced the priests (29:34); here the congregation outpaces them both, and it is the congregation's zeal that finally gets the professionals to deal with themselves.

There is no rebuke recorded and no royal order. Shame did it. That is not always a bad instrument, and a man in ministry who has never felt it watching someone else's devotion is probably not paying attention.

Verse 16 notes that they took their accustomed posts according to the Law of Moses the man of God — everyone in his own place, by the book — and then adds a small irregularity: the priests threw the blood that they received from the hand of the Levites. Normally the head of each household killed his own lamb. Verse 17 explains why they could not.

verseByVerse.quote: For there were many in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves. Therefore the Levites had to slaughter the Passover lamb for everyone who was not clean, to consecrate it to the LORD. For a majority of the people, many of them from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover otherwise than as prescribed. For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, "May the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even though not according to the sanctuary's rules of cleanness." And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there were many in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves. Therefore the Levites had to slaughter the Passover lamb for everyone who was not clean, to consecrate it to the LORD.

Here is the problem the whole chapter has been walking toward. A great crowd has come, much of it from the north, and a majority of them are not in a fit state to be there. They have not cleansed themselves. Some of them almost certainly did not know how; they had grown up in a kingdom that had not kept this feast properly for two hundred years.

So the Levites step in and kill the lambs on their behalf, which is not how Passover works. And then verse 18 says the thing plainly, and the Chronicler does not look away from it:

For a majority of the people, many of them from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover otherwise than as prescribed.

Otherwise than as prescribed. That is the narrator's own verdict. This was irregular, it was against the written rule, and the people doing it were in the wrong. Nobody in the text pretends the rules had been suspended or that these men had met them.

And into that room comes a prayer.

May the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even though not according to the sanctuary's rules of cleanness.

Pardon, he asks. Not permission, not an exemption, not a ruling that it was fine after all. He asks God to forgive people who are doing this wrongly, and the ground he offers is the set of their hearts: everyone who sets his heart to seek God.

That clause carries both of this book's great verbs at once. Setting the heart is what Rehoboam never did — he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD (12:14) — and what the ordinary people who left the north in his day did do (11:16). Seeking is the thread that runs from Asa to Jehoshaphat to Uzziah. Hezekiah asks God to look at the direction a man is facing.

And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.

Heard, and healed. Those are the two verbs of the promise this whole book was built on: then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land (7:14). The sentence God spoke over that courtyard when Solomon dedicated it comes back, word for word, over a crowd of half-instructed foreigners eating the wrong way.

Take this carefully, because it can be misused in both directions. It is not a licence to be careless with what God has commanded; the text calls the irregularity irregular, and the reformation running through these three chapters is entirely about getting things done as Moses and David laid them down. But neither is God's house a place where the badly prepared are turned away at the door while a king watches.

Anyone who has ever come to the Lord's Table feeling unfit should sit with verse 20 for a while. The people it was written about were unfit, and they knew it, and they came anyway because they wanted God more than they wanted to be safe from criticism. A man prayed for them, and God pardoned and healed them.

There is a greater intercessor than Hezekiah, and he does not stand beside the table asking God to overlook the state of the people at it. He is the Lamb on it.
