His prayer for the unready and the half-taught and the ceremonially hopeless is not a request that the standard be waived, because he has met the standard himself and is offering it on their behalf. The LORD heard Hezekiah. He always hears his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven days of unleavened bread with great gladness, the Levites and priests praising day by day, singing with all their might (v. 21), while Hezekiah goes round speaking encouragingly to the Levites who showed good skill (v. 22). Then the whole assembly agreed together to keep the feast for another seven days (v. 23), paid for by the king's 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep and the princes' 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep — and the priests consecrate themselves in great numbers (v. 24). Five groups rejoice, sojourners among them (v. 25). So there was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon ... there had been nothing like this (v. 26). The priests and Levites bless the people, and their voice was heard, and their prayer came to his holy habitation in heaven (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 27 closes a circuit opened at the dedication. Solomon had asked God to listen from heaven your dwelling place (6:21), and here the blessing of the priests reaches exactly that address. The building has done what it was prayed into being to do.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 24 repays a second reading for the arithmetic. The king gave a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep. The princes gave a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep. His officials outgave him, publicly, and the record says so without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel who were present at Jerusalem kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with great gladness, and the Levites and the priests praised the LORD day by day, singing with all their might to the LORD. And Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who showed good skill in the service of the LORD. So they ate the food of the festival for seven days, sacrificing peace offerings and giving thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers. Then the whole assembly agreed together to keep the feast for another seven days. So they kept it for another seven days with gladness. For Hezekiah king of Judah gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for offerings, and the princes gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. And the priests consecrated themselves in great numbers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people of Israel who were present at Jerusalem kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with great gladness, and the Levites and the priests praised the LORD day by day, singing with all their might to the LORD.

Singing with all their might. Not tastefully, not professionally — with everything they had, every day for a week, from men who a fortnight earlier had been too embarrassed to consecrate themselves.

And Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who showed good skill in the service of the LORD.

The Hebrew is warmer than the English: he spoke to their heart. In the middle of the largest gathering Jerusalem had seen in two and a half centuries, with a nation to govern and an Assyrian empire on his northern border, the king went round the musicians and told them they were doing it well.

It is a small thing and it is not a small thing. He did not merely thank them for turning up; the text says he commended the ones who showed good skill. Somebody had practised, and the king noticed, and said so. Anyone who leads anything should read that verse and then go and find three people.

Then the whole assembly agreed together to keep the feast for another seven days. So they kept it for another seven days with gladness.

Nobody ordered this. The assembly agreed together. A crowd that had been mocked on the way there, that had arrived unclean and been prayed over, decided at the end of a week that they were not finished, and stayed. Solomon's dedication ran seven days and seven days (7:8-9), and this is the first time since then that anybody has wanted a fortnight.

Somebody had to pay for it, and the accounts are printed. For Hezekiah king of Judah gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for offerings, and the princes gave the assembly 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep.

Do the arithmetic and something quietly good appears. The princes gave three thousand more sheep than the king did. His own officials outgave him, publicly, and the Chronicler writes down both figures without a word of explanation. A leader who has taught his people to give will one day be outgiven by them, and the healthiest possible response is the one Hezekiah shows here, which is none at all.

And the last clause of verse 24 closes a wound: And the priests consecrated themselves in great numbers. The shortage that pushed Passover back a month, the thing that made the Levites do the priests' work in chapter 29, is over. It took a fortnight of other people's worship to fix it.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly of Judah, and the priests and the Levites, and the whole assembly that came out of Israel, and the sojourners who came out of the land of Israel, and the sojourners who lived in Judah, rejoiced. So there was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem. Then the priests and the Levites arose and blessed the people, and their voice was heard, and their prayer came to his holy habitation in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 25 reads like a guest list, and should be read as one, because of who is on it.

The whole assembly of Judah, and the priests and the Levites, and the whole assembly that came out of Israel, and the sojourners who came out of the land of Israel, and the sojourners who lived in Judah, rejoiced.

Five groups. Judah. The clergy. The northerners who made the journey. And then twice over, the sojourners — resident foreigners, from the north and from Judah, who had attached themselves to Israel's God and were kept at that table by a provision as old as the first Passover in Egypt (Exod 12:48).

The meal that commemorated a nation's rescue out of Egypt is being eaten by Judeans, by Ephraimites who had been at war with them, and by foreigners. That is what the God of Israel does with a table when he is allowed to set it.

So there was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem.

The Chronicler measures it against Solomon, and he is careful about what he is measuring. It is the joy in Jerusalem that has had no equal for two and a half centuries. When he comes to Josiah's Passover he will use a different benchmark and a longer reach — no Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet (35:18) — and the two statements are not competing. One is about the scale of the gladness; the other is about the keeping of the feast.

Between those two Passovers lies the reign of Manasseh, and the Chronicler knows it as he writes this. The great joy of chapter 30 did not inoculate Judah against anything. It was still worth having.

Then the priests and the Levites arose and blessed the people, and their voice was heard, and their prayer came to his holy habitation in heaven.

That last clause closes a circuit that was opened two hundred and fifty years earlier in the same courtyard. When Solomon dedicated this building he asked one thing over and over: listen from heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive (6:21). He had no guarantee. He was a man standing on a platform in a new building asking God to treat it as an address.

And here, after the division, the Baals, the murdered brothers, the locked doors and the burning children, a priest lifts his hands over a mixed and irregular crowd, and the record says the sound went to the place Solomon named. The house did what it was prayed into existence to do.

The temple is gone now, and the arrangement it stood for was never the final one. But the traffic it carried has not stopped. A greater Son of David has gone into the holy habitation itself, not with the blood of a thousand bulls but with his own, and the prayers of people who come to him unclean and half-taught and late in the month still arrive — heard, pardoned, and healed, at the address Solomon could only ask about.

31.title: He Did What Was Good and Right and Faithful
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when all this was finished, all Israel who were present went out to the cities of Judah and broke in pieces the pillars and cut down the Asherim and broke down the high places and the altars throughout all Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all. Then all the people of Israel returned to their cities, every man to his possession.<sup>2</sup>And Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, division by division, each according to his service, the priests and the Levites, for burnt offerings and peace offerings, to minister in the gates of the camp of the LORD and to give thanks and praise.<sup>3</sup>The contribution of the king from his own possessions was for the burnt offerings: the burnt offerings of morning and evening, and the burnt offerings for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the appointed feasts, as it is written in the Law of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>And he commanded the people who lived in Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and the Levites, that they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>As soon as the command was spread abroad, the people of Israel gave in abundance the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and of all the produce of the field. And they brought in abundantly the tithe of everything.<sup>6</sup>And the people of Israel and Judah who lived in the cities of Judah also brought in the tithe of cattle and sheep, and the tithe of the dedicated things that had been dedicated to the LORD their God, and laid them in heaps.<sup>7</sup>In the third month they began to pile up the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month.<sup>8</sup>When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel.<sup>9</sup>And Hezekiah questioned the priests and the Levites about the heaps.<sup>10</sup>Azariah the chief priest, who was of the house of Zadok, answered him, "Since they began to bring the contributions into the house of the LORD, we have eaten and had enough and have plenty left, for the LORD has blessed his people, so that we have this large amount left."<sup>11</sup>Then Hezekiah commanded them to prepare chambers in the house of the LORD, and they prepared them.<sup>12</sup>And they faithfully brought in the contributions, the tithes, and the dedicated things. The chief officer in charge of them was Conaniah the Levite, with Shimei his brother as second,<sup>13</sup>while Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were overseers assisting Conaniah and Shimei his brother, by the appointment of Hezekiah the king and Azariah the chief officer of the house of God.<sup>14</sup>And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, keeper of the east gate, was over the freewill offerings to God, to apportion the contribution reserved for the LORD and the most holy offerings.<sup>15</sup>Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah were faithfully assisting him in the cities of the priests, to distribute the portions to their brothers, old and young alike, by divisions,<sup>16</sup>except those enrolled by genealogy, males from three years old and upward—all who entered the house of the LORD as the duty of each day required—for their service according to their offices, by their divisions.<sup>17</sup>The enrollment of the priests was according to their fathers' houses; that of the Levites from twenty years old and upward was according to their offices, by their divisions.<sup>18</sup>They were enrolled with all their little children, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, the whole assembly, for they were faithful in keeping themselves holy.<sup>19</sup>And for the sons of Aaron, the priests, who were in the fields of common land belonging to their cities, there were men in the several cities who were designated by name to distribute portions to every male among the priests and to everyone among the Levites who was enrolled.<sup>20</sup>Thus Hezekiah did throughout all Judah, and he did what was good and right and faithful before the LORD his God.<sup>21</sup>And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered.
31.overview: The pilgrims go home from the Passover and take down the shrines on the way — pillars, Asherim, high places and altars through Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all (v. 1). Hezekiah restores the priestly and Levitical courses (v. 2), funds the whole sacrificial calendar out of his own estate (v. 3), and then commands the city to give the clergy their portion that they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD (v. 4). The response is immediate and lasts five months: firstfruits and tithes piled in heaps from the third month to the seventh, so that the king and princes come and bless both the LORD and his people (vv. 5-8). Hezekiah questions the priests about the heaps, and Azariah answers that they have eaten and had enough and have plenty left, for the LORD has blessed his people (vv. 9-10). Storerooms are then built, nineteen men are named to receive and distribute, and the rolls take in the Levites' wives and children down to three-year-olds in the country towns (vv. 11-19). The summary: he did what was good and right and faithful, and every work he undertook, seeking his God, he did with all his heart (vv. 20-21).
31.theology:
Verse 1 records the first complete clearance of the high places in the book. Asa and Jehoshaphat both pulled some down and the text still had to say they stood (15:17; 20:33). What finally did it was not a stronger decree but the congregation itself, on the way home from a fortnight of worship, taking axes to shrines nobody had ordered them to touch.

Verses 3-4 set the order of leadership: the king funds the offerings out of his own property before he asks anyone else for a shekel, and the stated purpose of the clergy's portion is that they may give themselves to the law of God. Provision exists for the sake of teaching.

And the word this chapter keeps using of men handling other people's goods is faithful — four times in twenty verses (vv. 12, 15, 18, 20). Where the subject is money and food given to God, Scripture asks for reliability rather than brilliance, and it puts the king and the storekeepers under the same adjective.

Verse 21 gives Hezekiah the whole heart that Amaziah was denied (25:2) — and 32:25 will report that same heart lifted up. The commandment is not a target a good king can reach and hold; it waited for a better Son of David.
31.examples:
The men who tore down the shrines were the congregation, walking home from the feast, and some of them kept going into territory their king did not govern.

The king paid for the whole sacrificial calendar out of his own estate before he asked the city for anything.

The heaps grew for five months, from the grain harvest to the fruit harvest, with people bringing the first of each crop as it came off the ground.

He walked in and asked the priests about the heaps, and the chief priest answered that they had eaten and had enough.

The storerooms were built after the giving, because nobody had expected this much.

Nineteen men are named, and their entire work in this chapter is receiving sacks and handing out portions.

A Levite's three-year-old daughter in an outlying town was on the roll, and men were designated by name to see that her portion reached her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Every Man to His Possession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now when all this was finished, the pilgrims go home by way of every shrine in the country: pillars broken, Asherim cut down, high places and altars pulled down through Judah and Benjamin and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all. Then all the people of Israel returned to their cities, every man to his possession (v. 1). Hezekiah restores the divisions of priests and Levites for offerings and for thanks and praise (v. 2), funds the daily, Sabbath and festival burnt offerings from his own possessions (v. 3), and then commands Jerusalem to give the priests and Levites their portion, that they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The high places have stood through every reform in this book. Asa pulled some down and the record still says they remained (14:3; 15:17); Jehoshaphat pulled more down and the record still says they remained (17:6; 20:33). Here, at last: until they had destroyed them all. It took the joy of chapter 30 to do what four royal decrees could not.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 comes before verse 4, and the order is the point. The king funds the whole sacrificial calendar out of his own estate first, and asks the city to support the ministry second. And the reason he gives for the stipend is not that the clergy deserve a living but that a man who is scratching for food cannot give himself to the law of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all this was finished, all Israel who were present went out to the cities of Judah and broke in pieces the pillars and cut down the Asherim and broke down the high places and the altars throughout all Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all. Then all the people of Israel returned to their cities, every man to his possession. And Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, division by division, each according to his service, the priests and the Levites, for burnt offerings and peace offerings, to minister in the gates of the camp of the LORD and to give thanks and praise. The contribution of the king from his own possessions was for the burnt offerings: the burnt offerings of morning and evening, and the burnt offerings for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the appointed feasts, as it is written in the Law of the LORD. And he commanded the people who lived in Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and the Levites, that they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when all this was finished, all Israel who were present went out to the cities of Judah and broke in pieces the pillars and cut down the Asherim and broke down the high places and the altars throughout all Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had destroyed them all.

Notice who is doing it. Not the king's officers, not a demolition squad with a warrant — all Israel who were present, meaning the men who had just spent a fortnight at the Passover. They went home from a feast and dismantled the shrines in their own villages on the way, and some of them kept going into Ephraim and Manasseh, which were not Hezekiah's to govern.

And this is the sentence four generations of reform had never managed to write: until they had destroyed them all. Asa pulled high places down, and the record still says they were not taken out of Israel (14:3; 15:17). Jehoshaphat pulled more down, and the record still says the people sacrificed on them (17:6; 20:33). Royal decrees kept failing at exactly this point, because a shrine on a hill outside a village is protected by the village.

What finally took them down was not a stronger law. It was a fortnight of joy in Jerusalem. Men who had eaten the Passover, been prayed over, sung for two weeks and gone home glad had no further use for the alternatives, and they took axes to them without being told.

Then, in six words that most readers step over: every man to his possession. They went back to the farm. The feast ended, and thousands of ordinary people returned to work, carrying what had happened to them into an ordinary year.

Which is where the rest of the chapter comes in, and it is the least glamorous material in these three chapters. The doors were open and the singing had happened. Somebody now had to make sure there would be a lamb on the altar next Tuesday morning, and a Levite fed in a country town in eighteen months' time.

Hezekiah restores the divisions, priests and Levites by course, for offerings and for thanks and praise — and the text calls the temple the camp of the LORD, wilderness language for a stone building four centuries old. Israel's God is still travelling with his people.

And then two verses in an order that matters.

The contribution of the king from his own possessions was for the burnt offerings: the burnt offerings of morning and evening, and the burnt offerings for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the appointed feasts, as it is written in the Law of the LORD. And he commanded the people who lived in Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and the Levites.

He pays first, out of his own estate, for the entire sacrificial calendar. Then he asks the city to fund the ministry. No one in Jerusalem was asked to give to something the king had not already put his own money into.

And the reason given for the clergy's portion belongs in front of any church that budgets: that they might give themselves to the Law of the LORD. Not because the priests had earned it or were owed a standard of living, but because a man scratching for food cannot give himself to the Scriptures, and a people who will not feed their teachers have decided, whether they mean to or not, to be taught by men with no time to study.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — They Laid Them in Heaps
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As soon as the command was spread abroad, the firstfruits come in — grain, wine, oil, honey, everything the fields produced — and the tithe of everything, in abundance (v. 5). The country towns bring the tithe of cattle and sheep and the dedicated things, and laid them in heaps (v. 6). In the third month they began to pile up the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month (v. 7). Hezekiah and the princes come and look at them and blessed the LORD and his people Israel (v. 8). The king questions the priests about the heaps (v. 9), and Azariah the chief priest answers: we have eaten and had enough and have plenty left, for the LORD has blessed his people (v. 10). So the king orders chambers prepared in the house of the LORD, and they prepare them (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Azariah's sentence puts the credit in the right place twice over. The priests have more than they can eat, and the reason he gives is not that the priesthood is well managed or that the appeal was well run. The LORD has blessed his people. The surplus in the clergy's store is evidence of what God did in the farmers' fields.
verseByVerse.examples: The heaps took five months to build. They started in the third month, when the grain comes in, and finished in the seventh, when the fruit and the oil are gathered. That is not one spectacular collection; it is a whole agricultural year, harvest by harvest, with people bringing the first of each crop as it came off the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the command was spread abroad, the people of Israel gave in abundance the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and of all the produce of the field. And they brought in abundantly the tithe of everything. And the people of Israel and Judah who lived in the cities of Judah also brought in the tithe of cattle and sheep, and the tithe of the dedicated things that had been dedicated to the LORD their God, and laid them in heaps. In the third month they began to pile up the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month. When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as the command was spread abroad, the people of Israel gave in abundance the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and of all the produce of the field. And they brought in abundantly the tithe of everything.

As soon as. There is no interval between the command and the response, and no campaign — the word went out and things started arriving. Honey is on the list, which is a small surprise, because honey was never burned on the altar. It could still be given. Whatever a man's ground produced, he brought the first of it.

And laid them in heaps.

Then the detail that makes the scene: In the third month they began to pile up the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month.

Five months. The third month is when the grain comes in; the seventh is when the fruit and the oil are gathered. So this is not one great collection on one great day. It is a whole agricultural year, crop by crop, with a farmer bringing the first of the barley in May and the first of the olives in October, and the piles in the temple courts getting steadily larger all summer while everyone walked past them.

That is what sustained giving looks like. The Passover was a fortnight; this took half a year, and the second is the harder and the better test.

When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel.

Both. He blessed God for it, which is right, and then he blessed the people who had carried it in, which is a thing leaders forget. The generosity was genuinely theirs and he said so out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hezekiah questioned the priests and the Levites about the heaps. Azariah the chief priest, who was of the house of Zadok, answered him, "Since they began to bring the contributions into the house of the LORD, we have eaten and had enough and have plenty left, for the LORD has blessed his people, so that we have this large amount left." Then Hezekiah commanded them to prepare chambers in the house of the LORD, and they prepared them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Hezekiah questioned the priests and the Levites about the heaps.

He asked. The king walked into the temple courts, looked at a great deal of other people's grain sitting in piles, and put questions to the men responsible for it. That is not suspicion; it is care. Money and food given to God's work belong to the givers and to God, and somebody in authority should always be asking about the heaps.

Azariah the chief priest, who was of the house of Zadok, answered him, Since they began to bring the contributions into the house of the LORD, we have eaten and had enough and have plenty left, for the LORD has blessed his people, so that we have this large amount left.

Read that answer slowly, because there are two things in it and both are lovely.

The first is contentment. We have eaten and had enough. The chief priest of Judah reports that the clergy are fed. He does not describe a need, angle for more, or explain what the priesthood could achieve with additional resource. There was enough, and he said so.

The second is where he puts the credit. He does not say the appeal worked, or that the people were generous, or that the reform has been well managed. The LORD has blessed his people. The surplus in the priests' storeroom is offered as evidence of what God had been doing all summer in other men's fields.

Then Hezekiah commanded them to prepare chambers in the house of the LORD, and they prepared them.

The storerooms are built after the giving, not before it. Nobody in this chapter constructed a facility and then went looking for something to put in it. The people gave, the heaps grew for five months in the open, and only when it became obvious that this was going to continue did the king order somewhere to keep it.

This is now the third time in three chapters that Hezekiah's problem has been abundance. There were too many offerings for the priests to flay (29:34); the feast was extended by popular demand and paid for twice over (30:23-24); and now there is more grain than there is roof to keep it under. Revivals have their own logistics, and they are the pleasant kind.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the chambers ready, the stores are put under management. And they faithfully brought in the contributions, the tithes, and the dedicated things under Conaniah the Levite and Shimei his brother (v. 12), with ten named overseers under them, appointed by the king and the chief officer of the house of God (v. 13). Kore the keeper of the east gate is put over the freewill offerings (v. 14), with six men faithfully assisting him in the cities of the priests, to distribute the portions to their brothers, old and young alike (v. 15). The rolls take in males from three years old, and the Levites' little children, their wives, their sons, and their daughters (vv. 16-18), and men are designated by name in the country towns to hand out portions there (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: One word runs through this chapter about stores and lists and nothing else: faithful. They faithfully brought in (v. 12); they were faithfully assisting (v. 15); they were faithful in keeping themselves holy (v. 18); and the king did what was good and right and faithful (v. 20). Where the subject is other people's food and money, that is the virtue Scripture asks for and keeps naming.
verseByVerse.examples: Nineteen men are named here by name, and their whole job is warehousing and distribution. Two in charge, ten overseers, a gatekeeper over the freewill gifts, six more out in the priests' towns. Not one of them preaches or sings in this chapter. They count sacks and hand out portions, and the Chronicler wrote down all nineteen names.

verseByVerse.quote: And they faithfully brought in the contributions, the tithes, and the dedicated things. The chief officer in charge of them was Conaniah the Levite, with Shimei his brother as second, while Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were overseers assisting Conaniah and Shimei his brother, by the appointment of Hezekiah the king and Azariah the chief officer of the house of God. And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, keeper of the east gate, was over the freewill offerings to God, to apportion the contribution reserved for the LORD and the most holy offerings. Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah were faithfully assisting him in the cities of the priests, to distribute the portions to their brothers, old and young alike, by divisions, except those enrolled by genealogy, males from three years old and upward—all who entered the house of the LORD as the duty of each day required—for their service according to their offices, by their divisions. The enrollment of the priests was according to their fathers' houses; that of the Levites from twenty years old and upward was according to their offices, by their divisions. They were enrolled with all their little children, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, the whole assembly, for they were faithful in keeping themselves holy. And for the sons of Aaron, the priests, who were in the fields of common land belonging to their cities, there were men in the several cities who were designated by name to distribute portions to every male among the priests and to everyone among the Levites who was enrolled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is a list of names and duties, and a modern reader's eye slides off it. Slow down, because the Chronicler is doing something deliberate.

And they faithfully brought in the contributions, the tithes, and the dedicated things. Conaniah the Levite in charge, Shimei his brother as second. Then ten more named men as overseers — Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath and Benaiah — appointed jointly by the king and the chief officer of the house of God. Then Kore the keeper of the east gate over the freewill offerings, with six more men assisting him out in the priests' towns.

Nineteen men, named, with their fathers' names where it matters and their exact responsibilities set down. Not one of them preaches in this chapter or sings a note. They receive sacks, record them, store them and hand them out, and the record of God's dealings with Judah has their names in it permanently.

And one word keeps coming back. They faithfully brought in (v. 12). Six men were faithfully assisting (v. 15). The families on the roll were faithful in keeping themselves holy (v. 18). And the king, in the summary, did what was good and right and faithful (v. 20). Four times in twenty verses, and the subject throughout is other people's food and money.

That is not an accident. Where the goods belong to somebody else and are given to God, the virtue the Bible asks for is not brilliance or vision. It is faithfulness — the plain quality of a man who writes down what came in and hands out what was meant to go out, whether or not anybody checks.

Then look at who is fed. The portions go to their brothers, old and young alike, by divisions. The enrolment takes in males from three years old and upward. The Levites are enrolled with all their little children, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, the whole assembly.

Three years old. Somewhere in a country town in Judah there was a Levite's daughter who could barely talk, and the national distribution system had her on a list and a portion set aside for her. And verse 19 makes sure the distance does not defeat it: in the outlying priests' towns there were men designated by name to hand out the portions, so that nobody a long way from Jerusalem simply got forgotten.

A revival is measured by more than its singing. This one can be measured by whether a three-year-old in a village three days' walk away had food on the table that winter, and the answer is that nineteen men had been given her name.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thus Hezekiah did throughout all Judah, and he did what was good and right and faithful before the LORD his God (v. 20). And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Three chapters of reformation are summed up in two verses, and the summary is about the heart and not the results. He sought God; he did it with all his heart; and he prospered — which is Uzziah's own formula (26:5) laid on a better man.
verseByVerse.examples: With all his heart. Amaziah did what was right yet not with a whole heart (25:2), and this book has been measuring kings on that scale since Asa. Hezekiah is given the sentence whole. And the very next chapter will record that his heart was lifted up and he did not make return (32:25). Both verdicts are true, and the second does not cancel the first.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Hezekiah did throughout all Judah, and he did what was good and right and faithful before the LORD his God. And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus Hezekiah did throughout all Judah, and he did what was good and right and faithful before the LORD his God.

Three words for one reign. Good — it did people actual good. Right — it matched what God had commanded, which Hezekiah kept checking against the law of Moses and the order of David at every stage. Faithful — the same word the storekeepers were given four verses earlier. The king is commended in the same language as the men counting sacks.

And every work that he undertook in the service of the house of God and in accordance with the law and the commandments, seeking his God, he did with all his heart, and prospered.

Every work that he undertook. Not the highlights. The doors and the hinges, the sixteen days of carrying filth to the Kidron, the letters that were laughed at, the second-month Passover, the courses, the storerooms, the lists of three-year-olds. All of it, and all of it done seeking his God.

And then the phrase this book has been withholding for fifteen chapters. With all his heart.

Amaziah did what was right yet not with a whole heart (25:2). Joash did right while his mentor lived. Uzziah sought God while his teacher lived. Asa's heart was called wholly true and he still jailed a prophet. Here at last is a king of whom it is said without qualification: with all his heart, and prospered.

And it is not the end of his story. The very next chapter will say that his heart was lifted up and he did not make return according to the benefit done to him (32:25). Both sentences are in the same book about the same man, and the second does not delete the first. Even the best of them could not hold it.

Which is why the phrase matters more than the man. Loving God with all the heart is not a high standard that a determined king can just about reach; it is the first commandment, and the whole record of Judah is the record of people who could not keep it for a lifetime. Then a Son of David came who did every work he undertook seeking his God, with all his heart, from the carpenter's shop to the cross, and never once needed the qualifying clause. He kept the commandment whole, and what he did with that obedience was hand it over — to the half-hearted, the lately-converted and the badly-prepared, so that people who have never managed a single wholehearted day are counted as having done what he did.

32.title: He Will Not Come into This City
32.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah and encamped against the fortified cities, thinking to win them for himself.<sup>2</sup>And when Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and intended to fight against Jerusalem,<sup>3</sup>he planned with his officers and his mighty men to stop the water of the springs that were outside the city; and they helped him.<sup>4</sup>A great many people were gathered, and they stopped all the springs and the brook that flowed through the land, saying, "Why should the kings of Assyria come and find much water?"<sup>5</sup>He set to work resolutely and built up all the wall that was broken down and raised towers upon it, and outside it he built another wall, and he strengthened the Millo in the city of David. He also made weapons and shields in abundance.<sup>6</sup>And he set combat commanders over the people and gathered them together to him in the square at the gate of the city and spoke encouragingly to them, saying,<sup>7</sup>"Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria and all the horde that is with him, for there are more with us than with him.<sup>8</sup>With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles." And the people took confidence from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.<sup>9</sup>After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was besieging Lachish with all his forces, sent his servants to Jerusalem to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria, 'On what are you trusting, that you endure the siege in Jerusalem?<sup>11</sup>Is not Hezekiah misleading you, that he may give you over to die by famine and by thirst, when he tells you, "The LORD our God will deliver us from the hand of the king of Assyria"?<sup>12</sup>Has not this same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, "Before one altar you shall worship, and on it you shall burn your sacrifices"?<sup>13</sup>Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of other lands? Were the gods of the nations of those lands at all able to deliver their lands out of my hand?<sup>14</sup>Who among all the gods of those nations that my fathers devoted to destruction was able to deliver his people from my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you from my hand?<sup>15</sup>Now, therefore, do not let Hezekiah deceive you or mislead you in this fashion, and do not believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to deliver his people from my hand or from the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God deliver you out of my hand!'"<sup>16</sup>And his servants said still more against the LORD God and against his servant Hezekiah.<sup>17</sup>And he wrote letters to cast contempt on the LORD, the God of Israel, and to speak against him, saying, "Like the gods of the nations of the lands who have not delivered their people from my hands, so the God of Hezekiah will not deliver his people from my hand."<sup>18</sup>And they shouted it with a loud voice in the language of Judah to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten and terrify them, in order that they might take the city.<sup>19</sup>And they spoke of the God of Jerusalem as they spoke of the gods of the peoples of the earth, which are the work of men's hands.<sup>20</sup>Then Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this and cried to heaven.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD sent an angel, who cut off all the mighty warriors and commanders and officers in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he came into the house of his god, some of his own sons struck him down there with the sword.<sup>22</sup>So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hand of all his enemies, and he provided for them on every side.<sup>23</sup>And many brought gifts to the LORD to Jerusalem and precious things to Hezekiah king of Judah, so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations from that time onward.<sup>24</sup>In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death, and he prayed to the LORD, and he answered him and gave him a sign.<sup>25</sup>But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came upon him and Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>26</sup>But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.<sup>27</sup>And Hezekiah had very great riches and honor, and he made for himself treasuries for silver, for gold, for precious stones, for spices, for shields, and for all kinds of costly vessels;<sup>28</sup>storehouses also for the yield of grain, wine, and oil; and stalls for all kinds of cattle, and sheepfolds.<sup>29</sup>He likewise provided cities for himself, and flocks and herds in abundance, for God had given him very great possessions.<sup>30</sup>This same Hezekiah closed the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and directed them down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.<sup>31</sup>And so in the matter of the envoys of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the sign that had been done in the land, God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart.<sup>32</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his good deeds, behold, they are written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.<sup>33</sup>And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honor at his death. And Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
32.overview:
Assyria invades — and the clause the Chronicler puts in front of it is after these things and these acts of faithfulness (v. 1). Hezekiah stops the springs, rebuilds the wall, adds a second wall, arms the country (vv. 2-5), and tells the people that with Sennacherib is an arm of flesh but with them is the LORD their God — and they lean on his words (vv. 6-8). Sennacherib answers with a campaign in four channels: envoys, speeches, letters, and a shouted broadcast in Hebrew at the men on the wall, arguing that Hezekiah's own reforms have offended their God and that no god anywhere has stopped Assyria (vv. 9-19).

King and prophet cry to heaven; one angel empties the camp; Sennacherib goes home and is killed by his sons in his own god's temple; and Hezekiah is exalted in the sight of the nations (vv. 20-23). Then he falls ill, is healed with a sign, and did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud — until he humbles himself, and the wrath is deferred in the days of Hezekiah (vv. 24-26). Riches, storehouses, the Gihon tunnel; the Babylonian envoys, and God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart; and a burial in the upper part of the royal tombs with a nation's honours (vv. 27-33).
32.theology:
Verse 1 suspends the book's own rule in its opening clause. The invasion came after the acts of faithfulness. Chronicles, of all books, is the one that most insists sin brings trouble — and it is Chronicles that says plainly here that trouble is not always a verdict.

Verses 3-8 hold faith and work together without strain. He blocks every spring for miles and builds a second wall, and preaches that the battle belongs to God. Faith settles who the outcome belongs to; it does not settle whether to pick up a shovel.

Verse 19 names the enemy's actual error. Sennacherib's evidence was real and his reasoning was sound; he had simply filed the living God among things that are the work of men's hands. Arguments built on the wrong category cannot be rescued by being well made.

And verse 31 says God withdrew on purpose, to know all that was in his heart — Moses' own idiom for the wilderness (Deut 8:2). The test informs the man, not God. It was run on the best king in the book, and it found something.
32.examples:
Between the promise and the invasion he blocked every spring for miles, rebuilt a wall, added a second one outside it, and set an armoury working.

Almost every line of his speech at the gate was a sentence God had already said to somebody else in a worse position.

The Assyrians shouted in Hebrew at the men on the wall, over the government's head, because the soldiers would understand it and their officers could not stop them hearing it.

The cleverest thing the enemy said was that pulling down the high places had offended God.

The most consequential prayer in Judah's history is recorded in four words, and the next sentence is the angel.

The king who catalogued gods that could not save was killed in his own god's temple by his own sons.

Pride did not get into Hezekiah through a failure. It came in through an answered prayer.

His tunnel is still there, and a person can walk through it today with the water round their knees.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — With Us Is the LORD Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib invades and encamps against the fortified cities (v. 1). Hezekiah plans with his officers to stop the springs outside Jerusalem — Why should the kings of Assyria come and find much water? (vv. 2-4) — rebuilds the broken wall, raises towers, throws up a second wall outside it, strengthens the Millo and makes weapons and shields in abundance (v. 5). Then he gathers the people in the square at the gate and speaks to them: Be strong and courageous ... for there are more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 is the most important clause in the chapter for anyone in trouble. The invasion came after these things and these acts of faithfulness — after the doors, the Passover, the heaps and the whole-hearted seeking of 31:21. This book normally reads a nation's fortunes off its obedience, and here it flags its own pattern as suspended in the opening line. What is happening to Hezekiah is not a verdict on Hezekiah.
verseByVerse.examples: Between the promise that God will fight for them and the arrival of the Assyrians, this king blocked every spring for miles, rebuilt a wall, added a second one, and set an armoury working. Faith and engineering in the same fortnight, and the Chronicler admires both without the slightest sense that they are in competition.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah and encamped against the fortified cities, thinking to win them for himself. And when Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and intended to fight against Jerusalem, he planned with his officers and his mighty men to stop the water of the springs that were outside the city; and they helped him. A great many people were gathered, and they stopped all the springs and the brook that flowed through the land, saying, "Why should the kings of Assyria come and find much water?" He set to work resolutely and built up all the wall that was broken down and raised towers upon it, and outside it he built another wall, and he strengthened the Millo in the city of David. He also made weapons and shields in abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah.

Stop at that first clause, because it is doing something this book almost never does. Chronicles reads a nation's fortunes off its obedience with an unusual directness: Abijah relied on the LORD and won, Asa leaned on Syria and got wars, Ahaz forsook God and lost six towns. Here the historian writes the words these acts of faithfulness, and the very next thing in the sentence is the largest army on earth coming over the border.

He does it deliberately. The doors had been opened, the temple cleansed, the Passover kept, the shrines pulled down, the heaps piled up, and the king had done every work seeking his God with all his heart. And then Assyria came.

Anyone who has been taught that obedience buys safety needs this verse standing where they can see it. What was happening to Hezekiah was not a verdict on Hezekiah. There are chapters in a faithful life that follow faithfulness and are still terrible, and this book, which of all books in Scripture most insists that sin brings trouble, is the one that says so.

Now watch what a man of faith does with a fortnight's warning.

He planned with his officers and his mighty men to stop the water of the springs that were outside the city ... Why should the kings of Assyria come and find much water?

He holds a staff meeting and denies the enemy his water supply. Then he rebuilds every broken section of the wall, raises towers on it, throws up a second wall outside the first, strengthens the old fortification in the city of David, and turns out weapons and shields in quantity.

The phrase in verse 5 translated he set to work resolutely is, underneath, the verb for strengthening oneself — the same word used of Jehoiada taking courage in the seventh year (23:1) and Amaziah taking courage before Edom (25:11). It is a word for a man bracing himself and getting on with it.

There is no tension in the text between this and the sermon he is about to preach. He believes God will fight for Jerusalem, and he blocks the springs. Faith is not the decision to leave the shovel in the shed. It is the decision about who the outcome belongs to, and that decision leaves a man free to work like a professional at everything in front of him.

There is one thing the Chronicler leaves out, and it belongs here for honesty's sake. The book of Kings records that before all this Hezekiah sent to Sennacherib at Lachish and said I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold — stripping the gold from the temple doors he himself had opened (2 Kgs 18:14-16). It bought nothing. The army came anyway. The Chronicler does not print it, and the speech in verse 8 is more remarkable for it: this is a man who had already tried buying his way out and found there was nothing on the other side of the payment.

verseByVerse.quote: And he set combat commanders over the people and gathered them together to him in the square at the gate of the city and spoke encouragingly to them, saying, "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria and all the horde that is with him, for there are more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles." And the people took confidence from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he set combat commanders over the people and gathered them together to him in the square at the gate of the city and spoke encouragingly to them.

Spoke encouragingly is the same expression used two chapters ago, when he went round thanking the temple musicians for their skill (30:22). Underneath it is a Hebrew phrase meaning that he spoke to their heart. He did it to the choir in a good week and to the militia in a bad one.

And the speech itself is almost entirely made of other people's words.

Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria and all the horde that is with him.

That is what Moses said to Israel on the edge of Canaan, and what he said to Joshua, and what David said to Solomon when he handed him the plans for the temple. Hezekiah is not improvising courage. He is reaching for sentences that God had already said to men in worse positions than his, and handing them on.

For there are more with us than with him.

Which is what Elisha said to a terrified servant on a hillside at Dothan with an army round the town: those who are with us are more than those who are with them (2 Kgs 6:16). The arithmetic is not a figure of speech in either place. The king is telling a crowd that can see the smoke of a burning countryside that they are, at this moment, the larger force.

With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God, to help us and to fight our battles.

An arm of flesh. Not a weak arm — Assyria was the most efficient killing machine the world had yet produced, and Hezekiah had watched it eat the northern kingdom. He does not tell his people that Sennacherib is overrated. He tells them what Sennacherib is made of.

Hanani said the same thing to Asa in this book, and Asa put him in the stocks for it: you leaned on the king of Syria and not on the LORD your God, and the eyes of the LORD run to and fro through the whole earth looking for the heart that is wholly his (16:7-9). Hezekiah has learned what Asa refused to learn, and he preaches it at the gate.

And the people took confidence from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.

The verb underneath took confidence is the verb for leaning your weight on something. A frightened city put its weight on a speech, and the speech held, because almost every line in it had come from God in the first place. That is the whole business of preaching in one verse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — On What Are You Trusting?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the siege of Lachish, Sennacherib sends envoys with a message for the people as much as the king (v. 9): On what are you trusting, that you endure the siege in Jerusalem? (v. 10). Hezekiah is misleading you into death by famine and thirst (v. 11); and has he not taken away his high places and his altars and cut worship down to one altar (v. 12)? Then the catalogue: no god of any nation has ever delivered anyone from Assyria's hand, how much less will your God deliver you (vv. 13-15). His servants say more against the LORD (v. 16); he writes letters to cast contempt on the LORD (v. 17); and they shout it in Hebrew at the men on the wall to frighten and terrify them (v. 18) — speaking of the God of Jerusalem as of gods that are the work of men's hands (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 12 is the cleverest sentence an enemy speaks in this book. Sennacherib takes the single most obedient act of Hezekiah's reign — pulling down the high places and centralising worship at the one altar God appointed — and presents it to the men on the wall as the reason their God will not help them. Obedience recast as offence, and said in their own language.
verseByVerse.examples: The campaign runs on four channels in eleven verses: envoys, a speech, further speech, written letters, and a shouted broadcast in Judah's own tongue aimed over the government's head at the men standing on the wall. It is not a demand for surrender. It is an operation designed to make a frightened population stop trusting its own king and its own God.

verseByVerse.quote: After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was besieging Lachish with all his forces, sent his servants to Jerusalem to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem, saying, "Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria, 'On what are you trusting, that you endure the siege in Jerusalem? Is not Hezekiah misleading you, that he may give you over to die by famine and by thirst, when he tells you, "The LORD our God will deliver us from the hand of the king of Assyria"? Has not this same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, "Before one altar you shall worship, and on it you shall burn your sacrifices"? Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of other lands? Were the gods of the nations of those lands at all able to deliver their lands out of my hand? Who among all the gods of those nations that my fathers devoted to destruction was able to deliver his people from my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you from my hand? Now, therefore, do not let Hezekiah deceive you or mislead you in this fashion, and do not believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to deliver his people from my hand or from the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God deliver you out of my hand!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reply comes from a king who is in the middle of taking another Judean city, and it is aimed past Hezekiah at the people on the wall.

On what are you trusting, that you endure the siege in Jerusalem?

It is the right question, asked by the wrong man for the wrong reason. Everything in this chapter turns on it, and Sennacherib knows enough to go straight there. He does not begin with his catapults. He begins by asking a hungry city what exactly it is leaning on.

Then he goes after the king personally. Is not Hezekiah misleading you, that he may give you over to die by famine and by thirst? Your king is going to get you killed, and he is doing it with a religious promise. Drive a wedge between a frightened people and the man telling them to trust God, and the wall will open by itself.

Then the sentence that shows real intelligence, and real malice.

Has not this same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, Before one altar you shall worship, and on it you shall burn your sacrifices?

He is telling them that their king has offended their own God by reducing his shrines. To a pagan mind this is common sense: more altars, more worship, more divine goodwill. And to a Judean farmer whose village high place was pulled down last year by his own neighbours, it would have landed hard.

It takes the single most obedient act of the reign — the clearance of chapter 31, the thing no king since Solomon had managed — and presents it as the reason God will not turn up. That is how the enemy of souls generally works. Not by recommending sin, which is too obvious, but by standing next to a man who has just obeyed God at cost and whispering that this is exactly why things are going badly.

Then the catalogue, and it is genuinely impressive. Who among all the gods of those nations that my fathers devoted to destruction was able to deliver his people from my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you from my hand?

He has the receipts. Nation after nation, god after god, none of them able to stop an Assyrian army, and he can name them. His argument from experience is sound, his evidence is real, and his conclusion is catastrophically wrong, because he has made one mistake: he has put the God of Israel on the same list.

verseByVerse.quote: And his servants said still more against the LORD God and against his servant Hezekiah. And he wrote letters to cast contempt on the LORD, the God of Israel, and to speak against him, saying, "Like the gods of the nations of the lands who have not delivered their people from my hands, so the God of Hezekiah will not deliver his people from my hand." And they shouted it with a loud voice in the language of Judah to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten and terrify them, in order that they might take the city. And they spoke of the God of Jerusalem as they spoke of the gods of the peoples of the earth, which are the work of men's hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The campaign does not stop with one speech. Verse 16 says his servants said still more against the LORD God and against his servant Hezekiah. Verse 17 says he wrote letters to cast contempt on the LORD, the God of Israel. Verse 18 says they shouted it with a loud voice in the language of Judah to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten and terrify them, in order that they might take the city.

Count the channels. Envoys sent in person. A prepared speech. Further speech beyond it. Written documents. And a shouted broadcast in Hebrew, aimed deliberately over the government's head at ordinary soldiers standing on the parapet, because they would understand it and their officers could not stop them hearing it.

And the stated purpose is in the verse: to frighten and terrify them, in order that they might take the city. Fear was the weapon. The siege engines were the backup.

Then the Chronicler tells us what the whole operation actually amounted to, and he does it in one sentence of theology.

And they spoke of the God of Jerusalem as they spoke of the gods of the peoples of the earth, which are the work of men's hands.

There is the mistake, named. It is not that Sennacherib overestimated his army; his army was everything he said it was. It is that he filed the living God under a heading — local deity, carved, portable, comparable — and then reasoned faultlessly from the wrong category.

Men do this still, and usually with better manners. God gets treated as one item in a range: a set of values, a cultural inheritance, a comfort mechanism, something people find helpful. Every argument built on that filing is as tight as Sennacherib's and as doomed, because the God of Jerusalem is not the work of anybody's hands, and being wrong about what something is cannot be repaired by being clever about it afterwards.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this and cried to heaven (v. 20). The LORD sends one angel, who cuts off the warriors and officers in the Assyrian camp; Sennacherib goes home with shame of face, and his own sons kill him in the house of his god (v. 21). The LORD saves the city and provided for them on every side (v. 22), and gifts pour in until Hezekiah is exalted in the sight of all nations (v. 23). Then he falls sick, prays, and is answered with a sign (v. 24) — but Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud, and wrath came (v. 25). But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart ... so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 21 is the answer to verses 13-15 delivered in the terms Sennacherib chose. He had listed the gods who could not save their peoples out of his hand. He was killed in the temple of his own god, by his own sons, in the one place his god should have been able to protect him.
verseByVerse.examples: Two men prayed, and the Chronicler does not tell us a word of what they said. The prayer that emptied the largest army in the world is summarised in four words — and cried to heaven — and the next thing in the text is the angel.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this and cried to heaven. And the LORD sent an angel, who cut off all the mighty warriors and commanders and officers in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he came into the house of his god, some of his own sons struck him down there with the sword. So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hand of all his enemies, and he provided for them on every side. And many brought gifts to the LORD to Jerusalem and precious things to Hezekiah king of Judah, so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations from that time onward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this and cried to heaven.

Two men. The king and the prophet, together, on their faces. It is the only place in these two books where those two offices are shown praying as a pair, and the Chronicler puts them in one clause with a single verb between them.

And he does not tell us a word of what they said. Kings and Isaiah both record the prayer at length; here it is four words — and cried to heaven — and then the next sentence is the angel. The most consequential prayer in Judah's history is summarised the way a man summarises something he assumes his readers already know how to do.

And the LORD sent an angel, who cut off all the mighty warriors and commanders and officers in the camp of the king of Assyria.

One angel. No battle, no sortie from the gate, no clever use of the tunnel, and none of the second wall required. The book of Kings supplies the number — a hundred and eighty-five thousand in a night — and the Chronicler does not bother with it. He notes which ranks died: the warriors, the commanders, the officers. The apparatus that had eaten the northern kingdom was taken apart in the dark by one messenger.

So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he came into the house of his god, some of his own sons struck him down there with the sword.

Read that beside his own speech. He had asked which of the gods of the nations had ever been able to deliver his people out of his hand. He died in his own god's temple, at the hands of his own children, in the one building on earth where his god ought to have been able to reach him. The answer to his question was given in the terms he chose.

So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem ... and he provided for them on every side. And many brought gifts to the LORD to Jerusalem and precious things to Hezekiah king of Judah, so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations from that time onward.

Exalted in the sight of all nations. Hold that word for one verse, because the next thing the Chronicler wants to tell us is what happened inside the man who had just been exalted.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death, and he prayed to the LORD, and he answered him and gave him a sign. But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came upon him and Judah and Jerusalem. But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death, and he prayed to the LORD, and he answered him and gave him a sign.

One verse for a story that fills a chapter elsewhere: the illness, the turned face, the weeping, the fifteen years added, the shadow going backwards on the steps. The Chronicler gives the whole of it in twenty-eight words, because he is not writing about the healing. He is writing about what the healing did to the man.

But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud.

The sin is named, and the name is ingratitude. Not idolatry, not cruelty, not a broken commandment anyone could point to in a court — he received an enormous kindness and did not make return for it. That is exactly what was said of Joash, who did not remember the kindness Jehoiada had shown him (24:22), and it is the fourth time in eight chapters that a heart has been lifted up: Amaziah's after Edom (25:19), Uzziah's when he was strong (26:16), and now Hezekiah's after he had been raised from his deathbed.

There is something almost unbearable about the placement. This is the man who wrote the letters north, who prayed for the unclean at the Passover, who did every work seeking his God with all his heart. Pride did not get in through his failures. It came in through the answered prayer.

An unanswered prayer will make a man cry out. An answered one, badly handled, can make him think he is somebody, and there is no season more spiritually dangerous than the week after God does exactly what you asked.

But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.

He humbled himself. The verb is the one this whole book was built on at 7:14, and Hezekiah reaches for it in time, and the wrath is turned aside. That is the good news of the verse, and it is real: a proud man who catches himself and goes down is not too late.

And then the last five words, which are the coldest in the chapter. In the days of Hezekiah. Not cancelled. Deferred. The book of Kings lets us hear the tone of that: when Isaiah told him what was coming, Hezekiah said the word of the LORD was good, and thought, Why not, if there will be peace and security in my days? (2 Kgs 20:19).

A man can repent genuinely of his own pride and still be content that the bill falls after his own funeral. His son Manasseh is in the last verse of this chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–33 — God Left Him to Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Great riches and honour: treasuries for silver, gold, stones, spices, shields and costly vessels, storehouses for grain and wine and oil, stalls and sheepfolds and cities, for God had given him very great possessions (vv. 27-29). He closes the upper outlet of Gihon and brings the water down inside the city, and Hezekiah prospered in all his works (v. 30). Then the envoys of Babylon come to ask about the sign, and God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart (v. 31). Isaiah's vision is cited as the record (v. 32), and he is buried in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, with all Judah doing him honour — and Manasseh his son reigned in his place (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 31 says God stood back on purpose. The idiom is Moses' — forty years in the wilderness, testing you to know what was in your heart (Deut 8:2) — and it does not mean God needed the information. A test is run so that what is inside a man comes out where he and everyone else can see it, and this one was run on the best king in the book.
verseByVerse.examples: Count the burials once more. Jehoram departed with no one's regret and was kept out of the tombs (21:20); Joash was kept out (24:25); Uzziah went into the field beside them (26:23); Ahaz was buried in the city and not carried to the chamber at all (28:27). Hezekiah is laid in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, and a whole nation turns out to honour him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hezekiah had very great riches and honor, and he made for himself treasuries for silver, for gold, for precious stones, for spices, for shields, and for all kinds of costly vessels; storehouses also for the yield of grain, wine, and oil; and stalls for all kinds of cattle, and sheepfolds. He likewise provided cities for himself, and flocks and herds in abundance, for God had given him very great possessions. This same Hezekiah closed the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and directed them down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works. And so in the matter of the envoys of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the sign that had been done in the land, God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart. Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his good deeds, behold, they are written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honor at his death. And Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wealth is catalogued with obvious pleasure: treasuries for silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields and costly vessels; storehouses for grain, wine and oil; stalls for cattle and folds for sheep; whole cities. And the Chronicler puts the reason in the middle of it — for God had given him very great possessions.

This same Hezekiah closed the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and directed them down to the west side of the city of David.

That is the tunnel. The spring lay outside the wall; the city needed it inside. So his engineers cut a channel through solid rock under the hill — a third of a mile of it, with two teams working toward each other from both ends — and brought the water out inside the defences. It is still there. A person can walk through it today with the water round their knees, in the dark, under the city of David, and come out where Hezekiah's men came out.

Then verse 31, which is the strangest sentence in the chapter and the hardest to shake off.

And so in the matter of the envoys of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the sign that had been done in the land, God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart.

God left him to himself. Deliberately, and for a stated purpose.

Babylon was a rising power a long way east, and it had heard about the shadow on the steps. Its ambassadors arrived to ask about it, and a king who had recently been exalted in the sight of all nations showed them everything he had — which is the part Kings tells and Chronicles leaves out. And in that room, at that hour, God stood back.

The phrase to know all that was in his heart is Moses' phrase for the forty years in the wilderness: God led Israel that way testing you to know what was in your heart (Deut 8:2). It never means that God was short of information. A test does not inform the examiner; it brings out into daylight what was already inside the candidate, so that he and everybody else can finally see it.

Which means that the withdrawal itself was a mercy of a severe kind. Hezekiah did not know what was in his heart. He had been told at verse 25 and had repented at verse 26, and there was still enough of it left to walk a foreign delegation round his treasury. So God let go for an afternoon, and the man found out.

Whoever has been through a season when God seemed to have stepped back — when the sense of his nearness that carried you for years simply was not there — should sit with that verse rather than panic at it. It is not always desertion. Sometimes it is the only way a man ever learns what he has been leaning on.

And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the upper part of the tombs of the sons of David, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honor at his death.

Set that against the graves this book has been quietly grading. Jehoram departed with no one's regret, buried in the city and not in the tombs. Joash was killed in his bed and kept out of them. Uzziah went into the field beside them, because he was a leper. Ahaz was put somewhere inside the walls and the Chronicler would not even write the city of David over him. Hezekiah is carried to the upper part of the royal chamber, and a whole city turns out.

He was a great king and he was not the King. He opened the doors, and he stripped their gold when he was frightened; he prayed and heaven emptied an army, and he came off his sickbed proud; he humbled himself, and was content that the reckoning should fall after he was gone. God left him to himself for one afternoon and there was more than enough there to lose him.

There was another Son of David whom God did not leave to himself as a test, but forsook as a substitute — in the dark, on a hill outside this same city, crying out about it. He was tested in every way and nothing came out of that heart but obedience. And because he was left, no one who is his is ever left; the promise to them is the one Moses gave Joshua and Hezekiah preached at the gate, and it holds all the way to the grave and out the other side: He will not leave you or forsake you.

33.title: When He Was in Distress He Entreated
33.text: <sup>1</sup>Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>3</sup>For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down, and he erected altars to the Baals, and made Asheroth, and worshiped all the host of heaven and served them.<sup>4</sup>And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem shall my name be forever."<sup>5</sup>And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And he burned his sons as an offering in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, and used fortune-telling and omens and sorcery, and dealt with mediums and with necromancers. He did much evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger.<sup>7</sup>And the carved image of the idol that he had made he set in the house of God, of which God said to David and to Solomon his son, "In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever,<sup>8</sup>and I will no more remove the foot of Israel from the land that I appointed for your fathers, if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded them, all the law, the statutes, and the rules given through Moses."<sup>9</sup>Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel.<sup>10</sup>The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they paid no attention.<sup>11</sup>Therefore the LORD brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria, who captured Manasseh with hooks and bound him with chains of bronze and brought him to Babylon.<sup>12</sup>And when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.<sup>13</sup>He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.<sup>14</sup>Afterward he built an outer wall for the city of David west of Gihon, in the valley, and for the entrance into the Fish Gate, and carried it around Ophel, and raised it to a very great height.
