He also put commanders of the army in all the fortified cities in Judah.<sup>15</sup>And he took away the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, and all the altars that he had built on the mountain of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he threw them outside of the city.<sup>16</sup>He also restored the altar of the LORD and offered on it sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving, and he commanded Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God.<sup>18</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, behold, they are in the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.<sup>19</sup>And his prayer, and how God was moved by his entreaty, and all his sin and his faithlessness, and the sites on which he built high places and set up the Asherim and the images, before he humbled himself, behold, they are written in the Chronicles of the Seers.<sup>20</sup>So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his house, and Amon his son reigned in his place.<sup>21</sup>Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem.<sup>22</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as Manasseh his father had done. Amon sacrificed to all the images that Manasseh his father had made, and served them.<sup>23</sup>And he did not humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself, but this Amon incurred guilt more and more.<sup>24</sup>And his servants conspired against him and put him to death in his house.<sup>25</sup>But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon. And the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.
33.overview:
Twelve years old at his accession, fifty-five years on the throne — the longest reign in the book, and the worst. He rebuilds the high places Hezekiah had cleared, raises altars to the Baals and to the host of heaven in both courts of the temple, burns his sons in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, works his way through Deuteronomy 18's list of forbidden arts, and sets a carved image in the house of God — of which God had said he would put his name there forever, if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded (vv. 1-8). Judah is led to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed (v. 9).

God speaks and is ignored (v. 10), so Assyria takes the king away with hooks and bronze chains to Babylon (v. 11). And when he was in distress, he entreated the LORD and humbled himself greatly, and God was moved by his entreaty and brought him home — then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God (vv. 12-13). He builds, clears out every idol he had installed, restores the altar and offers thank offerings, though the people go on sacrificing at the high places (vv. 14-17). The archives keep his prayer and his sin together, dated before he humbled himself, and he is buried in his house (vv. 18-20). Amon takes his father's sins and not his father's repentance, is murdered in two years, and the people of the land crown Josiah (vv. 21-25).
33.theology:
This is 7:14 tested past the point where anyone would expect it to hold. The promise was for a people who humble themselves and pray and seek and turn; here is a man who put an idol in God's house and burned his own children, doing precisely that in an Assyrian prison — and God was moved by his entreaty. The Chronicler spends nine verses making sure we cannot minimise the sins first. The mercy is not calibrated against them.

Verses 7-8 quote God's promise with its condition attached at the moment the condition is being broken. That is this book's explanation of the exile: not Babylonian strength but a stated if only, broken inside the building where it was spoken.

And the chapter is scrupulous about what repentance does and does not do. It brought him home and restored his throne; it did not undo the country's habits (v. 17), it did not clear his record (vv. 18-19), and it did not get him into the royal tombs (v. 20). Forgiveness is immediate; consequences keep their own timetable.

Then verse 23 turns the mercy into a standard. Amon is condemned not by comparison with David but by comparison with Manasseh — because he had watched grace happen at his own dinner table and would not have it.
33.examples:
The king reigned twenty-nine years and was given fifteen more when he was ill; his son was twelve at his accession. The sums put that birth inside the added years.

The one complete clearance of the high places in the book, done by ordinary people walking home from a Passover, was rebuilt by the next king.

He went down the list in Deuteronomy 18 item by item — the list that named why the previous occupants of the land were evicted.

God kept sending seers to him for half a century, and they were written down at the time by somebody, while nobody was listening.

He was walked out of his own country on the end of a hook, and the city he was taken to was Babylon.

He came home and threw out of the city the idols he had spent his life installing, and offered thank offerings on the altar he had displaced.

His people went on sacrificing at the shrines — to the right God, in the wrong places.

Amon was about ten when his father came home changed, and what he chose to inherit was the first half of the reign.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — More Evil Than the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manasseh is twelve at his accession and reigns fifty-five years, the longest reign in the book (v. 1). He rebuilds the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down, raises altars to the Baals and the Asheroth, and worships the host of heaven (vv. 2-3). He builds altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, In Jerusalem shall my name be forever, and more of them in both courts (vv. 4-5). He burns his sons in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and takes up fortune-telling, omens, sorcery, mediums and necromancers (v. 6). He sets a carved image in the house of God, and the Chronicler quotes God's word to David and Solomon over it, condition and all (vv. 7-8). Manasseh led Judah ... to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 7 and 8 print God's promise and its condition immediately before verse 9 records the breach. I will put my name forever ... if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded them. This is where the Chronicler explains the exile: not as bad luck or Babylonian strength, but as a stated condition that was broken in the building where the promise was made.
verseByVerse.examples: The list in verse 6 is Deuteronomy 18:10-11 gone through item by item — burning a son, divination, omens, sorcery, mediums, the dead consulted. It is the passage that told Israel what the previous occupants of the land had done and why they were evicted, and a king of Judah worked his way down it.

verseByVerse.quote: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down, and he erected altars to the Baals, and made Asheroth, and worshiped all the host of heaven and served them. And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem shall my name be forever." And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.

Fifty-five years. No king in this book reigned longer — not David, not Solomon, not Asa, not Uzziah with his fifty-two — and the longest reign in Judah's history belongs to the worst man who ever held the throne. Whatever length of days means in Scripture, it is not a scoreboard.

And there is an arithmetic here to do slowly, because the numbers are all in the text.

Hezekiah reigned twenty-nine years. In the middle of that reign he was sick to the point of death, prayed, and was told: I will add fifteen years to your life (2 Kgs 20:6). Fifteen from twenty-nine puts the illness in his fourteenth year. Manasseh was twelve when he came to the throne, which puts his birth in his father's seventeenth year.

Manasseh was born in the added years.

The text does not comment and neither should we. It does not say the extension was a mistake, and it does not say the boy would have been better unborn; God had his own purposes in those fifteen years, and one of them will be visible in the last verse of this commentary. But the sum is there for anyone who cares to do it, and it should be left to sit the next time we are certain we know what to ask God for.

And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.

That clause is a frame, and the Chronicler will close it seven verses later. Manasseh begins by doing what the nations did — the peoples God drove out to make room for Israel — and verse 9 will say he ended by doing worse than the nations God destroyed. He started at their level and went past them, and the two verbs get heavier as he goes.

It is the same sentence that was written over his great-grandfather Ahaz (28:3), which tells you what has happened to the house of David. The one charge Israel was never supposed to face is that it had become indistinguishable from the people it replaced, and it has now been laid against two kings of Judah inside five chapters.

For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down.

That is the first thing recorded of him, and it is aimed straight at chapter 31. The one complete clearance of the high places in the whole book — the thing Asa could not finish and Jehoshaphat could not finish, done at last by ordinary people walking home from a Passover — was rebuilt by the next king. What a generation gives its strength to, the following generation can undo in an afternoon.

Then he escalates. Altars to the Baals, Asherah poles, and the worship of all the host of heaven, which is to say the sun, moon and stars: the whole visible sky recruited as gods.

And then he goes indoors.

And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, In Jerusalem shall my name be forever. And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD.

Read the shape of that sentence. The Chronicler cannot report the altars without quoting, in the same breath, the promise they were built inside. The building where God put his name forever now has star-altars in both its courtyards. Hezekiah's cleansing lasted one generation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he burned his sons as an offering in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, and used fortune-telling and omens and sorcery, and dealt with mediums and with necromancers. He did much evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger. And the carved image of the idol that he had made he set in the house of God, of which God said to David and to Solomon his son, "In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever, and I will no more remove the foot of Israel from the land that I appointed for your fathers, if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded them, all the law, the statutes, and the rules given through Moses." Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he burned his sons as an offering in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, and used fortune-telling and omens and sorcery, and dealt with mediums and with necromancers.

His sons. Plural, in the same ravine where his great-grandfather Ahaz burned his (28:3), and this is the man whose own father had been a byword for reform. Three generations: Ahaz burning children, Hezekiah opening the temple doors, Manasseh back in the valley with a fire.

The rest of the verse reads like a list, and it is one. Open Deuteronomy 18 and the items come in the same order: anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer (18:10-11). That passage exists to tell Israel what the previous occupants of Canaan had done and why they were thrown out of the land. Manasseh went down it item by item, like a man working through a menu.

And the carved image of the idol that he had made he set in the house of God.

Not a shrine on a hill. Not an altar in the courtyard. An image, in the house. And once more the Chronicler will not report it without the promise attached, and this time he gives the promise in full, including the part with a condition in it:

In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever, and I will no more remove the foot of Israel from the land that I appointed for your fathers, if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded them, all the law, the statutes, and the rules given through Moses.

If only. There is the hinge of the whole history, quoted at the exact moment it is being broken. God had said Israel's feet would never be moved off that land again — on a stated condition, spoken to David and to Solomon in the same courtyard where the idol is now standing. Everything that happens in the last three chapters of this book follows from those two words and what Judah did with them.

Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do more evil than the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel.

More evil than the Canaanites. That is the verdict, and it settles the question of whether the exile was fair. The nations were driven out of that land for exactly these practices, in front of Israel, as a demonstration. Judah watched the demonstration, was given the land, was given the law, was given the temple and the prophets and four hundred years of warnings, and went further than the people it replaced.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — Then Manasseh Knew That the LORD Was God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they paid no attention (v. 10). So the commanders of the Assyrian army take him with hooks, bind him in bronze chains and carry him to Babylon (v. 11). And when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers (v. 12). He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: This is 7:14 tested at its outer limit and holding. The promise was if my people ... humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn. Here is a man who filled the temple with idols and burned his own children, doing exactly that in a foreign prison — and God was moved by his entreaty. If the offer reaches him it has no upper limit at all.
verseByVerse.examples: Note the order in verse 13. God was moved, heard, and brought him home; and then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God. He had been told it for fifty-five years by prophets he ignored. He came to know it on the other side of being forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they paid no attention. Therefore the LORD brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria, who captured Manasseh with hooks and bound him with chains of bronze and brought him to Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they paid no attention.

God spoke first. Before the Assyrians, before the hooks, before anything happened to him at all, the LORD spoke — and verse 18 will tell us there were seers who came to him with messages, plural, over years.

Fifty-five years of a man setting up star-altars in God's courtyards and killing his own children, and God kept sending people to talk to him. That is what the patience of God looks like when it is stretched out across half a century; it does not look like approval, and at the time it does not look like much of anything.

Therefore the LORD brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria, who captured Manasseh with hooks and bound him with chains of bronze and brought him to Babylon.

Hooks and bronze chains. The Assyrians had a way of handling captured kings that was designed for the watching crowd rather than for security, and the reliefs they carved of it show ropes running to rings set in the prisoner's face. The man who had commanded Judah for half a century was walked out of his own country on the end of one.

And of all the destinations, Babylon. Not Nineveh, where a reader would expect an Assyrian army to take its prisoners, but the city that in a hundred years will burn this temple and carry off the last king of David's line. Manasseh went there first, alone, in chains, and — as the next two verses will say — came back.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers. He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.

Three things in one verse, and each of them matters.

When he was in distress. Not in a season of reflection, not after reading something, not because a preacher finally got through. He broke when everything else had been taken off him. That is a common enough road and there is no shame in it; God is not too proud to receive a man who comes because he has run out of alternatives.

The LORD his God. The possessive has come back. It has been absent from this chapter — verse 6 said he did much evil in the sight of the LORD, flatly — and now, in a prison, the historian writes his God again.

And humbled himself greatly. The verb is the one the whole book turns on, the word of 7:14, the thing Rehoboam did under Shishak and Hezekiah did after his pride and Amon will refuse to do in twelve verses' time. And here alone it carries an intensifier. Not humbled himself. Humbled himself greatly.

He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom.

God was moved by his entreaty. He entreated, and God let himself be entreated. The God whose temple courtyards had star-altars in them, whose house had an idol standing in it, in whose sight this man had burned his own children, was moved by the prayer of that man in chains.

If that sentence does not stop a reader, nothing in this book will. Every argument that someone is too far gone dies here. Not because Manasseh's sins were smaller than they looked — the Chronicler has spent nine verses making sure we cannot think that — but because the mercy of God is not calibrated against them at all.

Anybody who has prayed for years for someone whose life has gone past the point where decent people expect anything should keep verse 13 somewhere they can find it. The prophets who came to Manasseh over five decades and were ignored did not know this verse was coming. They died before it happened. The word they left in that man's memory was still in there when the chains went on.

Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.

Then. After the entreaty, after the hearing, after the journey home. He had been told it since he was a boy in Hezekiah's palace, and he learned it at last on the other side of being forgiven. A man does not usually come to know God by being convinced of an argument. He comes to know him by being let off.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He comes back and works: an outer wall for the city of David, raised to a very great height, and commanders in every fortified city (v. 14). He clears the foreign gods and the image and every altar he had built out of the house of the LORD and out of Jerusalem, and throws them outside the city (v. 15); he restores the altar of the LORD, offers peace and thank offerings on it, and commands Judah to serve the LORD (v. 16). Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God (v. 17). The records name his prayer, the seers who spoke to him, and also all his sin and his faithlessness ... before he humbled himself (vv. 18-19). He is buried in his house (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 18 and 19 file the prayer and the sin in the same archive, twice over. The Chronicler will not let Manasseh's repentance erase his record, and he will not let the record cancel the repentance. Both go down, and the dividing phrase is before he humbled himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 is the honest limit of a late reformation. He pulled the idols out, restored the altar and ordered the nation to serve the LORD, and his people went on sacrificing at the shrines — to the right God now, in the wrong places. Fifty-five years of habit are not undone by a few good ones, even sincere ones.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward he built an outer wall for the city of David west of Gihon, in the valley, and for the entrance into the Fish Gate, and carried it around Ophel, and raised it to a very great height. He also put commanders of the army in all the fortified cities in Judah. And he took away the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, and all the altars that he had built on the mountain of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he threw them outside of the city. He also restored the altar of the LORD and offered on it sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving, and he commanded Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is the test of whether the prison prayer was real, and the Chronicler gives it to us in the form of a work list.

He builds an outer wall for the city of David, west of Gihon, round to the Fish Gate and about the Ophel, and raised it to a very great height. He puts commanders in every fortified city. A restored man went back to his job and did it properly, which is usually where genuine repentance shows up first.

Then the reversal of his own life's work.

And he took away the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, and all the altars that he had built on the mountain of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he threw them outside of the city.

He carried out with his own authority every object he had spent decades installing. Some of those altars he had commissioned as a young man; the image in the house was his own. There is no record that he made speeches about it. He had them taken out and thrown over the wall.

He also restored the altar of the LORD and offered on it sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving, and he commanded Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.

Thank offerings, from Manasseh. Of all the sacrifices in the system, the one this man brought was the one for people with something to be grateful about.

And then the sentence that keeps the chapter honest.

Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God.

Nevertheless. He got the idols out of the temple and he could not get the country back. His people kept going up to the local shrines, and the historian is careful and fair about it: they were sacrificing to the right God now, in the wrong places. Half a restoration.

Such is the shape of a late repentance, and it should be said plainly rather than softened. Manasseh's turning was real, and God received it, and it did not undo fifty-five years. The habits he taught a nation outlived his change of mind. Forgiveness is instant; consequences keep their own timetable, and a man who comes to God at the end of a long wrong road will usually spend the rest of his life looking at damage he cannot repair.

Which is a reason to come now, and never a reason not to come.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, behold, they are in the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. And his prayer, and how God was moved by his entreaty, and all his sin and his faithlessness, and the sites on which he built high places and set up the Asherim and the images, before he humbled himself, behold, they are written in the Chronicles of the Seers. So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his house, and Amon his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The closing formula is longer than usual, and what it chooses to preserve is the point.

Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, behold, they are in the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.

His prayer is in the national archive. So are the words of the seers he ignored for decades — they were written down at the time, by somebody, while nobody was listening.

Then verse 19 does it again, and adds the other half.

And his prayer, and how God was moved by his entreaty, and all his sin and his faithlessness, and the sites on which he built high places and set up the Asherim and the images, before he humbled himself, behold, they are written in the Chronicles of the Seers.

The prayer and the sin, filed together. Not the prayer instead of the sin. The record even keeps the addresses — the sites on which he built high places — a list of map references of the places a forgiven man ruined.

And running through both verses is the phrase that cuts his life in two: before he humbled himself. That is now how everything about him is dated. There is a before and there is an after, and the hinge is not a battle or a coronation but a man in irons deciding to bend.

Keep that within reach when the past will not stay buried. God's forgiveness does not delete the file; it settles the account. Scripture never pretends a pardoned man has a clean history, and it does not need to, because a covered sin honestly recorded is exactly what makes the mercy legible. Take the record away and you have taken the gospel with it.

So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his house.

In his house. Not in the tombs of the kings — Kings tells us it was the garden (2 Kgs 21:18). Set that against Hezekiah in the upper part of the royal chamber with a nation mourning. Manasseh was forgiven, restored to his throne, and buried in his own back garden. Both of those are true at once, and neither cancels the other.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — He Did Not Humble Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amon reigns two years and does evil as Manasseh his father had done, sacrificing to the images his father had made (vv. 21-22). And he did not humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself, but this Amon incurred guilt more and more (v. 23). His servants kill him in his house (v. 24), and the people of the land execute the conspirators and make Josiah king (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 23 is the sentence the whole chapter exists to make possible. Amon is not condemned by comparison with Hezekiah or David but by comparison with Manasseh — with the worst man in the book, at the one point where the worst man in the book got it right. A father's repentance becomes the standard his son is measured against.
verseByVerse.examples: For the third time in this book the ordinary people step in and keep the line of David on the throne. They crowned Ahaziah after the raid (22:1) and Uzziah after an assassination (26:1), and now they deal with Amon's murderers and put an eight-year-old in his place.

verseByVerse.quote: Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as Manasseh his father had done. Amon sacrificed to all the images that Manasseh his father had made, and served them. And he did not humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself, but this Amon incurred guilt more and more. And his servants conspired against him and put him to death in his house. But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon. And the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as Manasseh his father had done.

Note carefully which part of his father he copied. Amon was ten years old or so when Manasseh came home from Babylon; he watched the old man pull the idols out of the temple and throw them over the wall, and heard him command Judah to serve the LORD. And what he chose to inherit was the first half of the reign.

Amon sacrificed to all the images that Manasseh his father had made, and served them.

The images his father made — and, presumably, that his father had thrown out of the city. He went and got them back. A son can reach past a parent's repentance to the sins the parent abandoned, and it happens more often than anyone likes to admit.

And he did not humble himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself, but this Amon incurred guilt more and more.

There is the sentence this whole chapter has been building the ground for. Amon is not condemned by a comparison with David or Hezekiah. He is condemned by a comparison with Manasseh — with the worst king in the history of Judah, at the single point where the worst king in the history of Judah got it right.

That is a terrible and merciful arrangement. It means that no one's family history is so dark that there is nothing in it to be measured by, and it means that the mercy shown to a man becomes evidence in the case against everyone who watched it and would not have it. Amon knew that God receives the humbled, because he had eaten dinner with the proof of it for ten years.

And his servants conspired against him and put him to death in his house.

His own household staff, in his own house, after two years. He is the third king in ten chapters to be killed by his own people — Joash was finished in his bed by servants avenging a murdered prophet (24:25), Amaziah was run down at Lachish by a conspiracy out of Jerusalem (25:27), and now Amon. A throne is not a safe place, and a king who has made himself hated has nowhere private left to sleep.

Then, for the third time in this book, the ordinary people stepped in: they had put Ahaziah on the throne when a raid emptied the palace (22:1) and Uzziah on it after an assassination (26:1), and now the people of the land execute the conspirators and crown an eight-year-old named Josiah. The line of David keeps being rescued by people whose names nobody writes down.

And it did need rescuing, because of where it was going. Turn to the first page of the New Testament and read down the list: Uzziah the father of Jotham, Jotham the father of Ahaz, Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah (Matt 1:9-10).

Manasseh is in the genealogy of Jesus Christ. The man with the star-altars in God's courtyards and his sons' ashes in the Hinnom valley stands in the line that runs to Bethlehem, named, without apology, in the opening paragraph of the Gospel. God did not merely forgive him and leave him at the edge of the story. He kept him in the family, and the descendant who came of that line went down into a distress deeper than any Babylonian prison, so that men like Manasseh — which is to say, men like us — could be heard when they finally entreat.

34.title: His Heart Was Tender
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and walked in the ways of David his father; and he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.<sup>3</sup>For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet a boy, he began to seek the God of David his father, and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherim, and the carved and the metal images.<sup>4</sup>And they chopped down the altars of the Baals in his presence, and he cut down the incense altars that stood above them. And he broke in pieces the Asherim and the carved and the metal images, and he made dust of them and scattered it over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.<sup>5</sup>He also burned the bones of the priests on their altars and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>And in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, and as far as Naphtali, in their ruins all around,<sup>7</sup>he broke down the altars and beat the Asherim and the images into powder and cut down all the incense altars throughout all the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had cleansed the land and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, and Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God.<sup>9</sup>They came to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that had been brought into the house of God, which the Levites, the keepers of the threshold, had collected from Manasseh and Ephraim and from all the remnant of Israel and from all Judah and Benjamin and from the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>And they gave it to the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD. And the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD gave it for repairing and restoring the house.<sup>11</sup>They gave it to the carpenters and the builders to buy quarried stone, and timber for binders and beams for the buildings that the kings of Judah had let go to ruin.<sup>12</sup>And the men did the work faithfully. Over them were set Jahath and Obadiah the Levites, of the sons of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to have oversight. The Levites, all who were skillful with instruments of music,<sup>13</sup>were over the burden-bearers and directed all who did work in every kind of service, and some of the Levites were scribes and officials and gatekeepers.<sup>14</sup>While they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses.<sup>15</sup>Then Hilkiah answered and said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan.<sup>16</sup>Shaphan brought the book to the king, and further reported to the king, "All that was committed to your servants they are doing.<sup>17</sup>They have emptied out the money that was found in the house of the LORD and have given it into the hand of the overseers and the workmen."<sup>18</sup>Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read from it before the king.<sup>19</sup>And when the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes.<sup>20</sup>And the king commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying,<sup>21</sup>"Go, inquire of the LORD for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD, to do according to all that is written in this book."<sup>22</sup>So Hilkiah and those whom the king had sent went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter) and spoke to her to that effect.<sup>23</sup>And she said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: 'Tell the man who sent you to me,<sup>24</sup>Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the curses that are written in the book that was read before the king of Judah.<sup>25</sup>Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands, therefore my wrath will be poured out on this place and will not be quenched.<sup>26</sup>But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Regarding the words that you have heard,<sup>27</sup>because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD.<sup>28</sup>Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place and its inhabitants.'" And they brought back word to the king.<sup>29</sup>Then the king sent and gathered together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>30</sup>And the king went up to the house of the LORD, with all the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the priests and the Levites, all the people both great and small. And he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD.<sup>31</sup>And the king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes, with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant that were written in this book.<sup>32</sup>Then he made all who were present in Jerusalem and in Benjamin join in it. And the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers.<sup>33</sup>And Josiah took away all the abominations from all the territory that belonged to the people of Israel and made all who were present in Israel serve the LORD their God. All his days they did not turn away from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.
34.overview:
Josiah comes to the throne at eight and does right; he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left — the ruler Deuteronomy 17 gave for kings (vv. 1-2). At sixteen he began to seek God; at twenty he began to purge, grinding the idols to dust and scattering it over the graves of their worshippers, burning the priests' bones on their own altars — the word spoken at Bethel three centuries earlier, naming him (vv. 3-5; 1 Kgs 13:2). He crosses into the ruins of the fallen northern kingdom and clears that too (vv. 6-7).

At twenty-six he sends officials to repair the temple; the money is collected from north and south, the musicians run the building site, the men work faithfully — and Hilkiah finds the Book of the Law, lost in the house of God (vv. 8-14). Shaphan reports the accounts first and the book second, and reads it aloud; the king tears his clothes and sends to inquire (vv. 15-21). Huldah answers in two halves: the disaster on Judah is settled and unquenchable, and because your heart was tender ... I also have heard you (vv. 22-28). So Josiah gathers the whole nation, reads them the covenant himself, binds himself to it at the royal pillar with all his heart and soul, brings the people in — and all his days they did not turn away (vv. 29-33).
34.theology:
Verse 14 is the quiet horror of the chapter. The covenant document was lost inside the building that existed to house it, and it surfaced during a building project because somebody was moving money. Nobody had missed it. Two generations had not abandoned the word of God so much as mislaid it — which is how it is usually lost.

Verse 19 shows what hearing it does. Josiah had already sought God for ten years, purged two kingdoms and cleansed the house, and the reading of Scripture tore him open. The book does not measure a man against his own past or his neighbours; it measures him against God, and there is no honest reading of it that leaves anyone comfortable.

Huldah's oracle then holds two settled things together. Judah's judgment will not be quenched; this one man is heard. The reformation that followed could not save the nation and was worth every year of it.

And what God commends in verse 27 is not one thing Josiah built. A tender heart, a humbled self, torn clothes, tears. The first of those is the one item on the list that a man cannot manufacture, and Ezekiel would name its source within a lifetime: a heart of stone removed and a heart of flesh given (Ezek 36:26).
34.examples:
He sought God for four years before he pulled anything down.

He stood and watched the altars come down, ground the images to powder, and emptied the powder over the graves of the men who had worshipped them.

He walked north through the burned-out villages of a kingdom that no longer existed and dismantled its altars, for people who were mostly dead or deported.

The choir were the foremen on the building site, over the labourers and directing every trade.

The Bible turned up in the temple because somebody was carrying a chest of money out of a room, and nobody had noticed it was missing.

Shaphan gave the king the building accounts first, and then mentioned that the priest had given him a book.

The high priest and four royal officials walked across Jerusalem to a house in the Second Quarter to ask a woman what God was saying.

Told that his own eyes would be spared, he called the entire nation together and read them the curses himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — While He Was Yet a Boy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Josiah is eight at his accession and reigns thirty-one years, walking in David's ways; he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left (vv. 1-2). Three dates follow: in his eighth year, while he was yet a boy, he began to seek the God of David; in his twelfth he began to purge Judah of the high places and the images (v. 3). The altars are chopped down in his presence, the images ground to dust and scattered over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them (v. 4), and the bones of their priests burned on their own altars (v. 5). Then he crosses the border into Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon and Naphtali, in their ruins all around (v. 6), breaking altars throughout all the land of Israel before returning to Jerusalem (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 5 is the fulfilment of a word three hundred years old. At the dedication of Jeroboam's altar a man of God cried out that a son would be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, who would burn human bones on it (1 Kgs 13:2). The prophecy named him before any of his ancestors on that list had been born, and he fulfilled it without any indication in this chapter that he knew he was doing it.
verseByVerse.examples: The order in verse 3 is the whole man. He sought God at sixteen and started pulling things down at twenty. Four years of private seeking came before one public act of reform, and every axe-stroke in verses 4 to 7 stands on that.

verseByVerse.quote: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and walked in the ways of David his father; and he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left. For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet a boy, he began to seek the God of David his father, and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherim, and the carved and the metal images.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and walked in the ways of David his father; and he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

That last phrase is a quotation, and knowing where it comes from changes the chapter. Open Deuteronomy 17, the passage that lays down what a king of Israel may and may not be. It ends: that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left (17:20).

So the Chronicler measures Josiah with the ruler God gave for kings, and he passes. Hold on to that, because the two verses immediately before it in Deuteronomy say something this chapter is about to make unbearable: every king was to write himself a personal copy of the law, keep it with him, and read in it all the days of his life (17:18-19).

Now read verse 3, which gives three dates and puts them in an order that is the making of this man.

For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet a boy, he began to seek the God of David his father, and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places.

Do the arithmetic. He came to the throne at eight. The eighth year of his reign makes him sixteen; the twelfth makes him twenty. At sixteen he began to seek God. At twenty he began to pull things down.

Four years between the two, and the order is not accidental. This is a boy raised in the household of Amon, grandson of Manasseh, whose father was murdered by the palace staff when he was seven. Nobody taught him to seek God; the last two men on that throne had spent their lives teaching Judah the opposite. And at sixteen, with the country still full of his grandfather's shrines, he started looking for the God of David.

Then he waited four years before he touched anything.

Everything that follows — the axes, the dust on the graves, the sweep through the northern ruins, the covenant read aloud to a nation — stands on those four private years. Reform that starts before the seeking does is only ever demolition, and there is a great deal of it about. What made Josiah different from a young man with strong opinions about other people's religion is that he had spent four years wanting God before he lifted a hammer.

verseByVerse.quote: And they chopped down the altars of the Baals in his presence, and he cut down the incense altars that stood above them. And he broke in pieces the Asherim and the carved and the metal images, and he made dust of them and scattered it over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. He also burned the bones of the priests on their altars and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem. And in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, and as far as Naphtali, in their ruins all around, he broke down the altars and beat the Asherim and the images into powder and cut down all the incense altars throughout all the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they chopped down the altars of the Baals in his presence, and he cut down the incense altars that stood above them.

In his presence. He did not sign an order and read about it later; he stood in the wreckage while it happened, and the verbs move from they to he in the middle of the sentence. A twenty-year-old king with an axe in his hand.

Then something more deliberate than destruction. And he broke in pieces the Asherim and the carved and the metal images, and he made dust of them and scattered it over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.

He ground the idols to powder and then went and emptied the powder over the graves of the men who had worshipped them. It is a statement, and everyone who watched understood it: this is what your gods came to, and this is where it has left you. The idol and the idolater in the same handful of dust.

He also burned the bones of the priests on their altars.

And here a very old sentence comes due. Three hundred years earlier, at the dedication of Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, an unnamed man of God had cried out against the stones: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you (1 Kgs 13:2).

Josiah by name. Spoken before Rehoboam's grandson was born, before Athaliah, before Ahaz, before Manasseh — and there is nothing in this chapter to suggest the king knew the prophecy existed. He was simply doing the next right thing in front of him, and a word three centuries old came true on his hands.

Then the geography opens out and something quietly extraordinary happens. And in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, and as far as Naphtali, in their ruins all around.

Those are northern towns, and Josiah has no authority there. He has no authority there because there is no longer anybody who has: the northern kingdom fell to Assyria a lifetime ago and the phrase the Chronicler uses is in their ruins all around. A king of Judah walked north through burned-out villages and dismantled the altars of a country that no longer existed, for the sake of people who were mostly dead or deported.

It was not policy; there was no political gain in it. He did it because the ground belonged to God and the altars were an offence on it, and somebody was finally in the neighbourhood who cared.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Kings of Judah Had Let It Go to Ruin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In his eighteenth year, when he had cleansed the land and the house, Josiah sends three officials to repair the temple (v. 8). The money has been collected by the Levites at the thresholds from Manasseh and Ephraim and the remnant of Israel as well as Judah (v. 9), and it goes to workmen buying quarried stone and timber for the buildings that the kings of Judah had let go to ruin (vv. 10-11). And the men did the work faithfully, under Levites — including the musicians, who are set over the burden-bearers (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Found. The law of God had been physically lost inside the building whose entire purpose was to house it, and it surfaced during a building project, while somebody was carrying money out of a room. Nobody had missed it. That is what two generations of Manasseh and Amon had done to Judah, and it is a more frightening sentence than any of the idols in chapter 33.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 puts the choir in charge of the scaffolding. The Levites skillful with instruments of music are set over the labourers and direct every kind of work on the site. It happened before, when Hezekiah's singers spent a fortnight carrying filth to the Kidron (29:12-16). Nobody in these chapters stands on his speciality.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had cleansed the land and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, and Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God. They came to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that had been brought into the house of God, which the Levites, the keepers of the threshold, had collected from Manasseh and Ephraim and from all the remnant of Israel and from all Judah and Benjamin and from the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And they gave it to the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD. And the workmen who were working in the house of the LORD gave it for repairing and restoring the house. They gave it to the carpenters and the builders to buy quarried stone, and timber for binders and beams for the buildings that the kings of Judah had let go to ruin. And the men did the work faithfully. Over them were set Jahath and Obadiah the Levites, of the sons of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to have oversight. The Levites, all who were skillful with instruments of music, were over the burden-bearers and directed all who did work in every kind of service, and some of the Levites were scribes and officials and gatekeepers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had cleansed the land and the house, he sent Shaphan ... and Maaseiah ... and Joah ... to repair the house of the LORD his God.

Note the order once more: cleansed first, then repaired. Six years of clearing out came before a single stone was cut. There is no point restoring the fabric of a building that is still being used for the wrong thing.

The funding is described with care, and one detail in it is easy to miss. The money had been collected by the Levites on the doors from Manasseh and Ephraim and from all the remnant of Israel and from all Judah and Benjamin. Northerners were putting money in the box. Whatever was left of the ten tribes after the Assyrian deportations was helping to pay for the repair of the temple in Jerusalem.

And what it paid for is described bluntly: quarried stone and timber for beams, for the buildings that the kings of Judah had let go to ruin.

The kings of Judah. Not the Assyrians, not the Babylonians, not time and weather. The house of David let the house of God fall down. It is a hard line to write about one's own dynasty and the Chronicler writes it.

And the men did the work faithfully.

That word again — the word that ran four times through the storerooms of Hezekiah's reign (31:12-20). Where the job is stone and timber and other people's money, faithfully is the adjective Scripture keeps reaching for.

Then a detail that ought to make anyone smile. The Levites, all who were skillful with instruments of music, were over the burden-bearers and directed all who did work in every kind of service.

And verse 13 finishes the staffing list: some of the Levites were scribes and officials and gatekeepers. The clerks who kept the accounts, the men who ran the administration and the men on the doors all came out of the same tribe. A body of people set apart for the service of God turned out to contain, between them, every skill a national restoration needed.

The musicians were running the site. The men whose training was harps and cymbals were the foremen over the labourers, organising deliveries and directing every trade on the job. It happened once before in this book, when Hezekiah's singers spent a fortnight carrying rubbish down to the Kidron (29:12-16). Twice now, when the house of God has needed hard, unglamorous work, the first men to put their instruments down and pick something else up have been the choir.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of moving the cash, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses (v. 14). He hands it to Shaphan the secretary (v. 15), who goes to the king and reports the building accounts first (vv. 16-17), and then adds: Hilkiah the priest has given me a book. And he reads from it before the king (v. 18). And when the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes (v. 19). He sends five men — the high priest, the secretary, the secretary's son and two others — with an errand: Go, inquire of the LORD for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah ... For great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17 required every king of Israel to write himself a copy of the law and read in it all the days of his life. Verse 2 says Josiah did not turn aside to the right hand or the left, which is the phrase from that same passage — and verse 19 is the first time in his life that he hears it. The statute had been neglected so completely that the book had to be discovered before it could be obeyed.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch how Shaphan delivers it. He does not burst in. He gives the financial report on the repairs, in order, and then mentions almost in passing that the priest has given him a book. Everything that follows in Judah's last good reign comes out of that flat, administrative sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses. Then Hilkiah answered and said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan. Shaphan brought the book to the king, and further reported to the king, "All that was committed to your servants they are doing. They have emptied out the money that was found in the house of the LORD and have given it into the hand of the overseers and the workmen." Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read from it before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses.

Found it.

Sit with that word for a moment, because of what it takes for granted. The Book of the Law of the LORD, given through Moses — the covenant document, the charter of the nation, the thing the ark was built to hold — was lost. Inside the temple. In the building whose entire reason for existing was to house it.

And it did not turn up because anyone went looking. Nobody in Judah had noticed it was missing. It surfaced because a building project was under way and somebody was carrying a chest of money out of a room, and there it was.

That is what two generations can do. Manasseh reigned fifty-five years and Amon two, and by the end of it a high priest could walk through the house of God every day of his working life and not know where the Bible was. The idols in chapter 33 are more spectacular; this verse is more frightening. A nation does not usually decide to abandon the word of God. It mislays it.

What follows is a masterpiece of understatement, and it repays reading in sequence.

Hilkiah tells Shaphan: I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD, and hands it over. Shaphan goes to the king — and gives him the building report first. All that was committed to your servants they are doing. They have emptied out the money that was found in the house of the LORD and have given it into the hand of the overseers and the workmen.

Accounts in order, contractors paid, works proceeding. And then, as a second item:

Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, Hilkiah the priest has given me a book. And Shaphan read from it before the king.

A book. Not the law of God; not the covenant; a book. Whether Shaphan was being careful or simply had no idea what he was holding, the flattest sentence in the chapter is the one everything turns on. And then he read it aloud, because that is what a secretary does with a document, and the reign of Judah's last good king split in two while a civil servant read.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes. And the king commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying, "Go, inquire of the LORD for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD, to do according to all that is written in this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes.

He heard it. He did not study it, or take it away to consider, or ask for a summary. It was read to him and he tore his clothes in the room.

Understand what he had done up to this point. He had been seeking God for ten years. He had purged Judah of its high places, ground its idols to powder, walked the ruins of the north pulling down altars, cleansed the land and the house, and put a major restoration in hand. By any measure available to him he was the best king Judah had seen in a century.

Then somebody read him the Bible, and he tore his clothes.

Such is the effect of the word of God genuinely heard rather than merely handled. It did not confirm him in his reforms; it showed him a gap he had not known was there. And this was a man doing everything he knew, which is precisely why the moment matters. The book does not measure us against the previous generation, or against our own past, or against what our friends think. It measures us against God, and there is no reading of it that leaves an honest man comfortable.

Anyone who can sit through the reading of Scripture week after week entirely at ease should ask whether they have been hearing it at all.

Go, inquire of the LORD for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that has been found.

The five men are named: Hilkiah, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant. Two of them are from one family — Shaphan, who had just read the book aloud, and his son Ahikam, standing beside him on the errand it produced.

Follow that family and it runs to the end of the story. Ahikam is the man who later put himself between Jeremiah and a mob that wanted him dead (Jer 26:24). And when everything is finally over, when the city has fallen and the temple is ash and the king is blinded and gone, the man Nebuchadnezzar leaves in charge of whoever is still alive in Judah is Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan (2 Kgs 25:22). A secretary read a scroll out loud in a throne room, and his son and grandson spent their lives protecting what was left of the people that scroll belonged to.

Five men are sent, and the phrase he uses for his people is those who are left. He knows what he is king of: a remnant, in a small hill country, with the north in ruins and empires on both horizons.

For great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD.

Our fathers. He takes the family guilt onto himself, exactly as Hezekiah did in the eastern square a century earlier (29:6). His grandfather filled the temple with idols and his great-grandfather burned children, and he does not say they. He says ours, and he says it in the first sentence of the most important errand of his reign.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–28 — Because Your Heart Was Tender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The delegation goes to Huldah the prophetess, wife of the keeper of the wardrobe, living in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem (v. 22). Her word has two halves. To the nation: I will bring disaster upon this place, all the curses written in the book, because they have forsaken me, and the wrath will not be quenched (vv. 23-25). To the king: because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God ... and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you (vv. 26-27) — you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Both halves are spoken by the same prophet in the same breath, and neither softens the other. The judgment on Judah is settled and will not be recalled; the mercy to this one man is equally settled. Reform could no longer save the nation, and it was still worth every year Josiah gave it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 28 promises he will go to his grave in peace, and the next chapter has him shot by archers at Megiddo (35:23-24). The promise is not about the manner of his death. It is that he would be buried in his fathers' tombs, in his own land, mourned by his own people, and would not live to watch the city burn.

verseByVerse.quote: So Hilkiah and those whom the king had sent went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter) and spoke to her to that effect. And she said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: 'Tell the man who sent you to me, Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the curses that are written in the book that was read before the king of Judah. Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands, therefore my wrath will be poured out on this place and will not be quenched.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Hilkiah and those whom the king had sent went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter) and spoke to her to that effect.

Israel's high priest and four senior officials of the crown walk across Jerusalem to a house in the Second Quarter to ask a woman what God is saying.

The Chronicler gives her address and her husband's job — he looked after the royal wardrobe — and no explanation whatever of why she was the one they went to. Jeremiah had been prophesying in Judah since Josiah's thirteenth year, five years before this (Jer 1:2), and the text does not tell us why the delegation went to Huldah instead. Presumably because she was the prophet God was speaking through, and everyone in Jerusalem knew it.

Her first words set the tone. Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you to me.

The man. Not the king, not your master, not his majesty. A delegation arrives from the throne of David with the high priest at its head, and the prophetess sends back a message addressed to the man who sent you. She is not being rude; she is speaking for someone in whose presence there are no kings, only men. Two verses later she does use the title — to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire — and by then it is clear which of the two words is the load-bearing one.

The word she gives is not softened by a syllable, and the men who wrote it down were the men it condemned.

I will bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the curses that are written in the book that was read before the king of Judah.

All the curses in the book. Deuteronomy ends with a long chapter of them — siege, famine, exile, a nation scattered — read out to Israel before it ever entered the land, so that nobody could say afterwards that they had not been told. Huldah's message is not new information. It is the delivery notice on a warning that had been sitting in the archive for eight hundred years.

Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods ... therefore my wrath will be poured out on this place and will not be quenched.

Forsaken. It is the verb this book has been laying on king after king since Rehoboam, and here it arrives at the nation and the sentence is final. Will not be quenched — meaning the reform now in progress, the best reform Judah would ever see, was not going to stop it.

Face that honestly rather than hurrying past it. Josiah's reformation was real, thorough and God-honouring, and it did not save the country. Some things, given long enough, become consequences rather than choices. It does not follow that the reform was pointless: God sent the word, the king obeyed it, a generation heard the Scriptures read aloud, and the mercy in the second half of Huldah's oracle exists precisely because he did.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Regarding the words that you have heard, because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD. Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place and its inhabitants.'" And they brought back word to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus shall you say to him.

But. The same prophet, the same sitting, the same breath — and now a word addressed to one man.

Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD.

Four things are named, and God names them in the order they happened. His heart was tender. He humbled himself. He tore his clothes. He wept. None of those is an achievement; not one is a reform, a demolition, a building programme or a policy. God's commendation of the most energetic king in the book says nothing at all about what he built.

A tender heart is the ancient word for a soft one — the opposite of the stiff neck Hezekiah warned the northerners about (30:8), and the opposite of a heart of stone. Which raises the question of where Josiah got his, in that palace, in that family. Ezekiel would answer it within a lifetime: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek 36:26). The tenderness God commends in verse 27 is the tenderness God gives, and it is the one item on that list that a man cannot manufacture.

I also have heard you. Judah would not be spared and Josiah was heard, and both sentences came out of the same mouth in the same afternoon.

Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place.

The reader who goes on to the next chapter will hit a difficulty here, so it is better to meet it now: Josiah is killed by archers in a battle at Megiddo (35:23-24). That is not usually what anyone means by dying in peace, and the text is not embarrassed about it.

What was promised was not a quiet death but this: he would be gathered to his fathers, buried in their tombs in his own city, mourned by his own people, and his eyes would not see the disaster. All four of those happened. He died before Pharaoh Neco's puppets, before Nebuchadnezzar, before the walls came down and the house he had repaired was burned. God's mercy to him was not a long life. It was that he did not have to watch.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Josiah gathers the elders, and goes up to the house with all Judah, the priests, the Levites and the people both great and small — and reads them the whole Book of the Covenant himself (vv. 29-30). And the king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments ... with all his heart and all his soul (v. 31). He brings everyone present into it (v. 32), removes the abominations from all Israel's territory and makes all who were present serve the LORD — All his days they did not turn away from following the LORD, the God of their fathers (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 31 has the king standing at the royal station in the temple — the pillar where the boy Joash was crowned (23:13) — binding himself to the words that had been read, with all his heart and all his soul, which is the first commandment of the Shema. He does not command the covenant and then watch. He makes it first, out loud, and then brings the nation in.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause of the chapter has the dating running the other way. Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada, and Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah. Here it is the nation that is dated, and the anchor is the king: all his days they did not turn away. Judah's obedience lasted exactly as long as Josiah did.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent and gathered together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. And the king went up to the house of the LORD, with all the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the priests and the Levites, all the people both great and small. And he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. And the king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes, with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant that were written in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king sent and gathered together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. And the king went up to the house of the LORD, with all the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the priests and the Levites, all the people both great and small.

Great and small. Everyone. He has been told that the sentence on the nation will not be revoked, and his response is to call the whole country together.

A lesser man would have taken Huldah's second paragraph and gone quiet. He had a personal guarantee: peace in his lifetime, and his own eyes spared. He could have kept the reforms ticking over, enjoyed thirteen more years of a well-run kingdom, and let the deluge fall on somebody else's watch — which, in almost exactly those words, is what Hezekiah had settled for (2 Kgs 20:19).

Instead he gathers the nation and does the one thing that cannot help him at all.

And he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD.

The king read it. Not the high priest, not Shaphan, not a Levite appointed for the purpose — the man on the throne stood up in front of the whole population and read the Bible aloud, all of it, the curses included. Deuteronomy had said that a king should read in the law all the days of his life (17:19). Judah's last good king found the book at twenty-six and started by reading it to everybody he had.

And the king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes, with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant that were written in this book.

He stood in his place — the royal station at the temple entrance, the pillar where a seven-year-old had been crowned by a priest two centuries before (23:13). And what he committed himself to is the first commandment: with all his heart and all his soul, in the words Moses gave Israel to say every morning.

He binds himself first, in public, and only then turns to the nation. That order has not changed. Nobody has ever been led anywhere by a man who had not gone there first.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he made all who were present in Jerusalem and in Benjamin join in it. And the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers. And Josiah took away all the abominations from all the territory that belonged to the people of Israel and made all who were present in Israel serve the LORD their God. All his days they did not turn away from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he made all who were present in Jerusalem and in Benjamin join in it. And the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers.

He brought them in. The covenant he had just made standing at his pillar was not left as a royal gesture to be admired; he put the whole assembly into it with him, and the next sentence says they kept it.

And Josiah took away all the abominations from all the territory that belonged to the people of Israel and made all who were present in Israel serve the LORD their God.

All the abominations, all the territory — including the northern ruins he had no business in. This is the most complete reform in the book, carried out by a man who had been told in writing that it would not avert the judgment.

And then the last clause of the chapter, and it is a shadow.

All his days they did not turn away from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.

All his days. The Chronicler has used that construction before and it never means anything good about the people it describes. Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest (24:2), and buried him and turned. Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah (26:5), and outlived his teacher and walked into the sanctuary with a censer. Now the dating is applied to a whole nation, and the anchor is one man.

Judah's faithfulness had a lifespan, and it was Josiah's. Thirteen years after this covenant he would be carried home from Megiddo in his second chariot, and within a generation the book he found would be ash and the people who swore that covenant would be walking to Babylon.

Which is the last thing this chapter has to teach, and it is the reason there had to be another King. Josiah did everything a man could do. He sought God as a boy, obeyed the book the day he heard it, tore his clothes over his family's sin, read the Scriptures to a nation with his own mouth and bound himself to them with all his heart and all his soul — and the obedience he generated lasted precisely as long as his heartbeat. The covenant that holds is not one made by a good man at a pillar, but one made by a Son of David whose days do not end, who wrote the law not on a scroll to be mislaid in a storeroom but on the hearts of his people, and who gives to hard men and women the one thing God commended in Josiah and no man can manufacture: a tender heart.

35.title: No Passover Like It
35.text: <sup>1</sup>Josiah kept a Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the first month.<sup>2</sup>He appointed the priests to their offices and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And he said to the Levites who taught all Israel and who were holy to the LORD, "Put the holy ark in the house that Solomon the son of David, king of Israel, built. You need not carry it on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel.<sup>4</sup>Prepare yourselves according to your fathers' houses by your divisions, as prescribed in the writing of David king of Israel and the document of Solomon his son.<sup>5</sup>And stand in the Holy Place according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of your brothers the lay people, and according to the division of the Levites by fathers' household.<sup>6</sup>And slaughter the Passover lamb, and consecrate yourselves, and prepare for your brothers, to do according to the word of the LORD by Moses."<sup>7</sup>Then Josiah contributed to the lay people, as Passover offerings for all who were present, lambs and young goats from the flock to the number of 30,000, and 3,000 bulls; these were from the king's possessions.<sup>8</sup>And his officials contributed willingly to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites.
