Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officers of the house of God, gave to the priests for the Passover offerings 2,600 Passover lambs and 300 bulls.<sup>9</sup>Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethanel his brothers, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, the chiefs of the Levites, gave to the Levites for the Passover offerings 5,000 lambs and young goats and 500 bulls.<sup>10</sup>When the service had been prepared for, the priests stood in their place, and the Levites in their divisions according to the king's command.<sup>11</sup>And they slaughtered the Passover lamb, and the priests threw the blood that they received from them while the Levites flayed the sacrifices.<sup>12</sup>And they set aside the burnt offerings that they might distribute them according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of the lay people, to offer to the LORD, as it is written in the Book of Moses. And so they did with the bulls.<sup>13</sup>And they roasted the Passover lamb with fire according to the rule; and they boiled the holy offerings in pots, in cauldrons, and in pans, and carried them quickly to all the lay people.<sup>14</sup>And afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the sons of Aaron, were offering the burnt offerings and the fat parts until night; so the Levites prepared for themselves and for the priests, the sons of Aaron.<sup>15</sup>The singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place according to the command of David, and Asaph, and Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer; and the gatekeepers were at each gate. They did not need to depart from their service, for their brothers the Levites prepared for them.<sup>16</sup>So all the service of the LORD was prepared that day, to keep the Passover and to offer burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah.<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel who were present kept the Passover at that time, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days.<sup>18</sup>No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover as was kept by Josiah, and the priests and the Levites, and all Judah and Israel who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah this Passover was kept.<sup>20</sup>After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him.<sup>21</sup>But he sent envoys to him, saying, "What have we to do with each other, king of Judah? I am not coming against you this day, but against the house with which I am at war. And God has commanded me to hurry. Cease opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you."<sup>22</sup>Nevertheless, Josiah did not turn away from him, but disguised himself in order to fight with him. He did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God, but came to fight in the plain of Megiddo.<sup>23</sup>And the archers shot King Josiah. And the king said to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded."<sup>24</sup>So his servants took him out of the chariot and carried him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem. And he died and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.<sup>25</sup>Jeremiah also uttered a lament for Josiah; and all the singing men and singing women have spoken of Josiah in their laments to this day. They made these a rule in Israel; behold, they are written in the Laments.<sup>26</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his good deeds according to what is written in the Law of the LORD,<sup>27</sup>and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
35.overview:
Josiah keeps the Passover on the correct date — the fourteenth of the first month, where Hezekiah had needed the second (30:3) — appoints and encourages the priests, and formally retires the Levites' oldest duty: You need not carry it on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel (vv. 1-6). The provisioning runs to 33,000 animals from the king's own estate, with the chief officers of the house paying for the priests and the chiefs of the Levites for the Levites (vv. 7-9).

The service is described in detail: every man in his place, the Passover lamb roasted according to the rule and the other offerings boiled, food carried quickly to the people, the Levites cooking last of all for the priests who were at the altar until night, and the singers and gatekeepers fed where they stood so they need not leave their posts (vv. 10-15). No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet — and all of it in the same eighteenth year in which the book was found (vv. 16-19). Then Neco marches north, sends a warning Josiah will not weigh, and Josiah disguises himself and rides to Megiddo; he did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God (vv. 20-22). The archers shoot him; he dies at thirty-nine and is buried in his fathers' tombs with the whole nation mourning, and Jeremiah's lament for him becomes a permanent rule in Israel (vv. 23-27).
35.theology:
Verse 3 shows how God's people handle a finished task. The carrying of the ark was the Levites' founding work and it was over; David had said so (1 Chr 23:26) and Josiah says it again, supplying the replacement in the same sentence — now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel — while the same verse calls them the Levites who taught all Israel, a role that had begun as one king's initiative two centuries earlier (17:7-9).

Verse 22 is the chapter's hardest sentence, and the narrator states it as fact rather than as Neco's claim: Josiah did not listen to Neco's words from the mouth of God. God is not confined to the channels his people find respectable, and the man in this book who heard Scripture best was deaf when the truth arrived by an unexpected road.

And Huldah's promise is kept in a shape nobody would have chosen (34:28). He was gathered to his fathers' tombs, mourned by his nation, and spared the sight of the disaster — by an Egyptian arrow.
35.examples:
The clergy were ready this time, so the feast fell on the right date.

A tribe was told that the work it had existed for since the wilderness was finished, and given a better job in the same sentence.

The king paid for the ordinary families, the senior priests paid for the priests, and the senior Levites paid for the Levites.

On the busiest day of the year, with tens of thousands of animals to prepare, somebody made sure the one item with a rule attached was roasted and not boiled.

The Levites cooked the priests' dinner after everyone else had eaten, because the priests were at the altar until dark.

The singers never broke off and the gatekeepers never left the doors, because food was brought to them where they stood.

The book was found and the greatest Passover since Samuel was kept inside the same twelve months.

Israel made the grief for Josiah a standing rule, and singers were still performing Jeremiah's lament generations later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — You Need Not Carry It on Your Shoulders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Josiah keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month (v. 1), appoints the priests and encourages them (v. 2), and tells the Levites — who taught all Israel — to put the ark in the house Solomon built: You need not carry it on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel (v. 3). They are to prepare by divisions as David and Solomon prescribed (vv. 4-5), and slaughter the lamb according to the word of the LORD by Moses (v. 6). Then the provisioning: 30,000 lambs and goats and 3,000 bulls from the king's possessions (v. 7), 2,600 lambs and 300 bulls from the chief officers of the house for the priests (v. 8), and 5,000 lambs and 500 bulls from the chiefs of the Levites for the Levites (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 3 formally retires the job the tribe was founded to do. Levites had carried the ark on their shoulders since the wilderness; David had already said the carrying was over (1 Chr 23:26), and Josiah says it again and immediately supplies the replacement — now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel. A ministry whose original task is finished is redeployed, not disbanded.
verseByVerse.examples: Look at who gave to whom. The king gave to the lay people. The chief officers of the temple gave to the priests. The chiefs of the Levites gave to the Levites. Every man in a position of responsibility made sure the people he was responsible for could keep the feast, and paid for it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Josiah kept a Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the first month. He appointed the priests to their offices and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD. And he said to the Levites who taught all Israel and who were holy to the LORD, "Put the holy ark in the house that Solomon the son of David, king of Israel, built. You need not carry it on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel. Prepare yourselves according to your fathers' houses by your divisions, as prescribed in the writing of David king of Israel and the document of Solomon his son. And stand in the Holy Place according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of your brothers the lay people, and according to the division of the Levites by fathers' household. And slaughter the Passover lamb, and consecrate yourselves, and prepare for your brothers, to do according to the word of the LORD by Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah kept a Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the first month.

The fourteenth day of the first month, which is to say on the correct date. A century earlier Hezekiah had to push his Passover back a month because the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number and the people had not gathered (30:3). This time the clergy were ready. That is what six years of clearing and repairing had bought.

He appointed the priests to their offices and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD.

Encouraged them — the expression that means, underneath, spoke to their heart. Hezekiah used it on the temple musicians in a good week (30:22) and on his militia when the Assyrians were coming (32:6). Josiah uses it on the priests before the largest service of his reign. Three kings' worth of leadership in this book, and all of it goes through men who took the trouble to say something personal to the people doing the work.

Then an instruction with a whole history behind it.

Put the holy ark in the house that Solomon the son of David, king of Israel, built. You need not carry it on your shoulders.

We are not told why the ark was out of its place. It may have been moved during the repairs; it may have been shifted at some point in the fifty-seven years when Manasseh and Amon had other things in the house. The Chronicler does not explain, and it is better to leave the gap open than to fill it.

What he does explain is the change of job. Carrying the ark on their shoulders was the founding work of the Levites; it is what the tribe existed for from the wilderness onwards, and men had died over how it was done. David had already said the carrying days were finished once there was a permanent house (1 Chr 23:26), and Josiah says it again — and does not leave them standing there with nothing.

Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel.

The old task ends and a new one is handed over in the same breath. And notice how the same verse describes them: the Levites who taught all Israel. That was not in their original job description either. It started as an initiative of Jehoshaphat's, who sent officials and Levites round the towns with the Book of the Law (17:7-9), and two centuries later it is simply what Levites are: the men who teach the country.

Any church that has ever had to retire a ministry knows how hard this is. The thing that was central for a generation stops being needed, and the people who gave their lives to it have to be told. Josiah tells them, and in the same sentence gives them a better job.

The instructions that follow name three authorities in three verses: the divisions as prescribed in the writing of David king of Israel and the document of Solomon his son, and the killing of the lamb according to the word of the LORD by Moses. Nothing here is being invented on the day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Josiah contributed to the lay people, as Passover offerings for all who were present, lambs and young goats from the flock to the number of 30,000, and 3,000 bulls; these were from the king's possessions. And his officials contributed willingly to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officers of the house of God, gave to the priests for the Passover offerings 2,600 Passover lambs and 300 bulls. Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethanel his brothers, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, the chiefs of the Levites, gave to the Levites for the Passover offerings 5,000 lambs and young goats and 500 bulls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the accounts, and they should be read slowly, because of who gives to whom.

Then Josiah contributed to the lay people, as Passover offerings for all who were present, lambs and young goats from the flock to the number of 30,000, and 3,000 bulls; these were from the king's possessions.

Thirty-three thousand animals out of the royal estate, so that ordinary families who had come up to Jerusalem would have something to sacrifice. Nobody was going to be turned away at this Passover because they were poor.

Set the figures beside Hezekiah's great feast, which was itself the largest thing Jerusalem had seen for two centuries: there the king gave a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep and his princes gave a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep (30:24). Josiah's contribution alone is nearly double the whole of that.

And his officials contributed willingly to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites.

Willingly. Not a levy on the nobility; a subscription they wanted to be part of.

Then the pattern that makes the passage worth the space it takes. Hilkiah, Zechariah and Jehiel, the chief officers of the house of God, gave two thousand six hundred lambs and three hundred bulls — to the priests. Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, the chiefs of the Levites, gave five thousand lambs and five hundred bulls — to the Levites.

Each man provisioned his own people. The king looked after the general public; the senior priests looked after the priests; the senior Levites looked after the Levites. Nobody passed the cost of the feast down to the men who would be working it, and nobody waited for somebody further up to notice.

That is a workable rule almost anywhere. The people directly under your care are your bill before they are anyone else's, and paying it yourself is the difference between leading them and merely being over them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests stand in their place and the Levites in their divisions (v. 10); the lamb is killed, the priests throw the blood, the Levites flay the carcasses (v. 11); the burnt offerings are set aside and distributed by families as it is written in the Book of Moses (v. 12). The Passover lamb is roasted with fire according to the rule and the holy offerings boiled, and both are carried quickly to the people (v. 13). The Levites then cook for themselves and for the priests, who are at the altar until night (v. 14); the singers and the gatekeepers stay at their posts, for their brothers the Levites prepared for them (v. 15). Seven days of unleavened bread follow (vv. 16-17), and the verdict: No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 shows what obedience looks like when nobody is watching the detail. Exodus forbids boiling the Passover lamb and requires it roasted (12:8-9); the other holy offerings were boiled as usual. So the cooks kept two methods going side by side at enormous scale, because one of the two was prescribed and the other was not.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 14 and 15 are the loveliest administrative arrangement in the book. The priests worked at the altar until dark and had no chance to eat, so the Levites cooked for them. The singers and the doorkeepers could not leave their stations, so the Levites fed them where they stood. The whole system was built so that nobody had to abandon his post to look after himself.

verseByVerse.quote: When the service had been prepared for, the priests stood in their place, and the Levites in their divisions according to the king's command. And they slaughtered the Passover lamb, and the priests threw the blood that they received from them while the Levites flayed the sacrifices. And they set aside the burnt offerings that they might distribute them according to the groupings of the fathers' houses of the lay people, to offer to the LORD, as it is written in the Book of Moses. And so they did with the bulls. And they roasted the Passover lamb with fire according to the rule; and they boiled the holy offerings in pots, in cauldrons, and in pans, and carried them quickly to all the lay people. And afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the sons of Aaron, were offering the burnt offerings and the fat parts until night; so the Levites prepared for themselves and for the priests, the sons of Aaron. The singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place according to the command of David, and Asaph, and Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer; and the gatekeepers were at each gate. They did not need to depart from their service, for their brothers the Levites prepared for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is a description of a very large organisation working properly, and the Chronicler evidently enjoys it.

The priests stand in their place, the Levites in their divisions. The lambs are killed; the priests throw the blood they are handed; the Levites do the flaying. The burnt offerings are sorted and distributed family by family as it is written in the Book of Moses. Every man knows where he stands and what is in his hands.

Then a detail that only a careful man would record. And they roasted the Passover lamb with fire according to the rule; and they boiled the holy offerings in pots, in cauldrons, and in pans.

Two cooking methods, deliberately kept apart. Exodus is explicit about the Passover lamb: Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted (12:9). The other holy offerings were normally boiled. So on a day when tens of thousands of animals were being prepared at speed, somebody made sure that the one item with a rule attached was done according to the rule, and the rest were done the usual way.

There is a whole attitude in that. Obedience in the small technical matter that nobody in the crowd would have checked, on the busiest day of the year, with every excuse available for simplifying the kitchen.

And carried them quickly to all the lay people. Hot food, served fast, to families who had walked a long way.

Then two verses that are worth more than they look.

And afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the sons of Aaron, were offering the burnt offerings and the fat parts until night; so the Levites prepared for themselves and for the priests.

The priests were at the altar until dark and had no chance to eat. So the Levites — who had spent the day flaying carcasses — cooked the priests' dinner as well as their own, and did it after everyone else had been fed.

The singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place ... and the gatekeepers were at each gate. They did not need to depart from their service, for their brothers the Levites prepared for them.

The choir sang all day without breaking off, and the men on the doors never left the doors, because other men brought them food where they stood.

That is what a well-ordered body of people looks like, and it is a better picture of a healthy church than most of the ones in circulation. Nobody had to choose between doing his job and eating. Nobody's post was left unmanned because he had needs of his own. The arrangement was designed by somebody who had thought about the singers' stomachs, and the Chronicler thought it worth two verses in the account of the greatest Passover in the nation's history.

verseByVerse.quote: So all the service of the LORD was prepared that day, to keep the Passover and to offer burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah. And the people of Israel who were present kept the Passover at that time, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days. No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover as was kept by Josiah, and the priests and the Levites, and all Judah and Israel who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah this Passover was kept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So all the service of the LORD was prepared that day, to keep the Passover and to offer burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah.

Prepared. It is the word that has been running through these chapters — the ordering of things, the putting in place — and it is what a reformation actually consists of once the shouting is over.

No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover as was kept by Josiah.

The Chronicler chooses his benchmark carefully, and it is a longer reach than the one he used for Hezekiah. That Passover, he said, was unmatched since the time of Solomon (30:26). This one reaches back past Solomon, past David, past the whole institution of the monarchy, to Samuel — the last man to hold Israel together before there were any kings at all.

And then he says it a second way, so that nobody misses it: none of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover. Not one, in four hundred years of them.

In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah this Passover was kept.

The eighteenth year. Turn back one chapter: the eighteenth year is when he sent Shaphan to repair the temple, and the book was found, and it was read aloud, and he tore his clothes, and Huldah answered, and he gathered the nation and made the covenant at his pillar.

All of that is one year. The Bible turned up in a storeroom in the spring and by the end of the same twelve months the nation was keeping the greatest Passover since Samuel. That is what a rediscovered Scripture can do to a country when the man who hears it does not put it down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — From the Mouth of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco of Egypt marches for Carchemish and Josiah goes out to meet him (v. 20). Neco sends word: I am not coming against you this day ... And God has commanded me to hurry. Cease opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you (v. 21). Nevertheless, Josiah did not turn away from him, but disguised himself in order to fight with him. He did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God, and came to Megiddo (v. 22). The archers shoot him; he is carried home in his second chariot, dies, and is buried in the tombs of his fathers with all Judah and Jerusalem mourning (vv. 23-24). Jeremiah makes a lament for him, and the singers keep it as a rule in Israel (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 removes the ambiguity. The narrator does not report that Neco claimed to speak for God; he says Josiah did not listen to Neco's words from the mouth of God. The warning was real, and it came through a pagan king with an army and an agenda of his own. God is not restricted to the channels we approve.
verseByVerse.examples: The best king in the book died doing what the worst king in it had done. Ahab went to Ramoth-gilead against a prophet's word and disguised himself (18:29); Josiah goes to Megiddo against a word from God's own mouth and disguises himself. Neither disguise made any difference to an arrow.

verseByVerse.quote: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him. But he sent envoys to him, saying, "What have we to do with each other, king of Judah? I am not coming against you this day, but against the house with which I am at war. And God has commanded me to hurry. Cease opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you." Nevertheless, Josiah did not turn away from him, but disguised himself in order to fight with him. He did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God, but came to fight in the plain of Megiddo.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him.

After all this. The building work was finished, the book was found and obeyed, the covenant was made, the Passover was kept. Everything a king could do had been done, and the chapter has seven verses left.

Egypt was marching north to prop up the last of Assyria against Babylon, and the road ran past Josiah's border. He went out to stop it — probably for good reasons, since an Egyptian victory would have left a great power on both sides of him.

But he sent envoys to him, saying, What have we to do with each other, king of Judah? I am not coming against you this day, but against the house with which I am at war. And God has commanded me to hurry. Cease opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you.

A pharaoh telling a son of David to stop opposing God. Everything in a reader wants to dismiss it: he is a pagan, he has an army on the move, he has every reason to say whatever gets Judah out of his way, and he would hardly be the first commander to claim heaven's backing for his own schedule.

And then the narrator settles it in a single clause.

Nevertheless, Josiah did not turn away from him, but disguised himself in order to fight with him. He did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God.

From the mouth of God. That is not Neco's claim being repeated; it is the historian's own verdict on it. The warning was genuine, and it came through an Egyptian king with a war to fight and no interest in Israel's God beyond the day's convenience.

Which is the hardest thing in this chapter, and it is aimed at good people. Josiah is the man who tore his clothes the moment a book was read to him. Nobody in this book listens better than Josiah listens. And when God's word came to him through the wrong sort of mouth, from a man whose religion was false and whose motives were mixed, he did not hear it at all.

A believer can become so practised at hearing God through the expected channels — the pulpit, the page, the people who talk the way we do — that a true word arriving by any other route is filtered out before it is weighed. The test is never the messenger's credentials. It is whether the thing said is true, and that has to be asked even when asking it is humiliating.

And he disguised himself. The last king in this book to do that was Ahab, who went up to Ramoth-gilead against a prophet's word, put on somebody else's clothes and was hit by an arrow shot at random (18:29-33). The best king Judah ever had died copying the tactic of the worst king Israel ever had, in the same way, for the same reason, with the same result.

verseByVerse.quote: And the archers shot King Josiah. And the king said to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded." So his servants took him out of the chariot and carried him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem. And he died and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah. Jeremiah also uttered a lament for Josiah; and all the singing men and singing women have spoken of Josiah in their laments to this day. They made these a rule in Israel; behold, they are written in the Laments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the archers shot King Josiah. And the king said to his servants, Take me away, for I am badly wounded.

He was thirty-nine years old. Eight when he came to the throne, thirty-one years on it, and the last thing he says in this book is a request to be lifted out of a chariot.

So his servants took him out of the chariot and carried him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem. And he died and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.

And every word of Huldah's promise is kept, in a form nobody would have chosen. You shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster (34:28). He was gathered to his fathers' tombs. He was mourned by his whole nation. And he did not live to watch Nebuchadnezzar's men break the walls, burn the house he had repaired, and walk the last son of David out of the city in chains.

God's mercies do not always arrive looking like mercies. This one arrived through an Egyptian archer.

Jeremiah also uttered a lament for Josiah; and all the singing men and singing women have spoken of Josiah in their laments to this day. They made these a rule in Israel; behold, they are written in the Laments.

Jeremiah wrote a funeral song for him. It is not the book of Lamentations, which mourns the fall of the city a generation later; it was collected in a book called the Laments that we no longer have. And Israel did something with it that nations rarely do: they made the grief permanent. Singers were still performing it when the Chronicler wrote, generations later, because somebody had decided that this loss should be remembered on purpose, every year, rather than allowed to fade.

There is one more mourning at Megiddo in Scripture. Zechariah, writing after the exile, says that on a coming day Jerusalem will mourn for one they have pierced, and that the mourning will be as great as the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (12:10-11) — which is where they mourned for Josiah, and it is generally taken to be him. The deepest grief Israel could remember became the measure for the grief of a people looking at the one their sins had killed.

And the last Passover in this book, kept better than any since Samuel, was not the last Passover that mattered. Six centuries later a descendant of this same house sat down with twelve men on the fourteenth day of the first month, took the bread of the feast Josiah had spent a kingdom's wealth on, and said that it was his body. The lamb Josiah killed by the thousand was pointing at him the whole time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his good deeds according to what is written in the Law of the LORD, and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: His deeds are filed under a standard: according to what is written in the Law of the LORD. The book that was lost in a storeroom and found while men were carrying out money has become the measure by which his whole life is recorded.
verseByVerse.examples: First and last. The historian keeps the Passover and Megiddo in one file, and does not offer an explanation for the second. Some things in a good man's story are recorded rather than accounted for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his good deeds according to what is written in the Law of the LORD, and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his good deeds according to what is written in the Law of the LORD, and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

Two verses of filing, and one phrase in them is a small monument. His good deeds are recorded according to what is written in the Law of the LORD.

That is the book that was lying forgotten in a storeroom until a workman moved a chest of money. It was found in his eighteenth year, read to him by a secretary who called it a book, and by the end of that same year it had been read aloud to the whole nation and sworn to at the temple gate. And now, at the end of his life, it is the standard his deeds are measured by. He did not merely obey it. He handed it to the historians as the ruler for his own reign.

His acts, first and last. Both are in the file. The Passover that reached back past every king to Samuel, and the ride to Megiddo against a warning he would not weigh. The Chronicler does not reconcile them, and there is no reconciling them; the same man did both, and the second cost him his life and the country its last good reign.

Remember that the next time we are inclined to sort people into the useful and the failed. God's record of a servant keeps first and last together, and the mercy of it is that the account does not end with an average. It ends with a Passover lamb, and a king who came after Josiah and did not put a foot wrong from Nazareth to the cross, whose obedience is what stands in the file where ours should be.

36.title: Let Him Go Up
36.text: <sup>1</sup>The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and made him king in his father's place in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>Then the king of Egypt deposed him in Jerusalem and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.<sup>4</sup>And the king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Jehoahaz his brother and carried him to Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God.<sup>6</sup>Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.<sup>7</sup>Nebuchadnezzar also carried part of the vessels of the house of the LORD to Babylon and put them in his palace in Babylon.<sup>8</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and the abominations that he did, and what was found against him, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. And Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.<sup>9</sup>Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>In the spring of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon, with the precious vessels of the house of the LORD, and made his brother Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>11</sup>Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.<sup>12</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>14</sup>All the officers of the priests and the people likewise were exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations. And they polluted the house of the LORD that he had made holy in Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place.<sup>16</sup>But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy.<sup>17</sup>Therefore he brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged. He gave them all into his hand.<sup>18</sup>And all the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon.<sup>19</sup>And they burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem and burned all its palaces with fire and destroyed all its precious vessels.<sup>20</sup>He took into exile in Babylon those who had escaped from the sword, and they became servants to him and to his sons until the establishment of the kingdom of Persia,<sup>21</sup>to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years.<sup>22</sup>Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing:<sup>23</sup>"Thus says Cyrus king of Persia, 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up.'"
36.overview:
Judah's own people crown Jehoahaz, and three months later Egypt deposes him, fines the country a hundred talents, installs his brother and changes his name (vv. 1-4). Babylon replaces Egypt: Jehoiakim is bound in chains and part of the vessels go east; Jehoiachin lasts three months and ten days and goes east with the precious vessels (vv. 5-10). Zedekiah did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the LORD, broke an oath he had sworn by God, and stiffened his neck — and by now the priests and the people are as unfaithful as the king (vv. 11-14).

Then the explanation of four centuries: God sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place, and they mocked, despised and scoffed until there was no remedy (vv. 15-16). The Chaldeans come, kill the young men in the sanctuary and show no compassion, empty every treasury, burn the house, break the wall and deport the survivors — until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths ... to fulfill seventy years (vv. 17-21). And then Cyrus, stirred up by the LORD, proclaims in speech and in writing that God has charged him to build a house at Jerusalem: Whoever is among you of all his people ... let him go up (vv. 22-23).
36.theology:
Verse 15 gives God's motive for every prophet in this book, and it is compassion — for the people and for the building. The prophets were not the sound of God losing his temper; they were the sound of God putting it off. Two verses later the same word appears, negated, in the hand he finally used: the Chaldean had no compassion.

And no remedy closes the book's longest thread. The word is the healing word of 7:14, where God promised to hear and forgive and heal the land of a people who humbled themselves, and of 30:20, where he heard Hezekiah and healed the people. Judah did not fail to qualify for that offer. Judah laughed at the men who brought it.

Even the emptiness is obedience. Leviticus 26:34-35 had said the land would enjoy the Sabbaths it was denied, and it does, for the number of years Jeremiah named. The exile is not history escaping God's hands; it is the covenant running to its stated terms.

Then the last verb: the LORD stirred up Cyrus — the same word used when he stirred up raiders against Jehoram (21:16) and Assyria to take the north into exile (1 Chr 5:26). The hand that scattered gathers. And the book ends, as the Hebrew Bible ends, not with a ruin but with an open gate: let him go up.
36.examples:
A pharaoh set a son of David on the throne and gave him a different name to be known by, and that is where Judah's independence actually ended.

The temple vessels went to Babylon in three loads over twenty-two years — part of them, then the precious ones, then all of them, great and small.

The last king of Judah broke an oath he had sworn by God to a pagan emperor, and Scripture counts it among his sins without qualification.

By the final generation the chief priests were as unfaithful as the king, and the historian names them both.

They did not argue with the prophets. They laughed at them, which takes less effort and works better.

The destruction of the house that took nine chapters to build is reported in one sentence with four verbs and no adjectives.

The fields got the rest they had been denied for centuries, because there was nobody left to work them.

The last three words of the Old Testament are a permission slip.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — A Foreign King Changed His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people of the land crown Jehoahaz, who lasts three months before Egypt deposes him, fines the country a hundred talents of silver, installs his brother Eliakim and changed his name to Jehoiakim (vv. 1-4). Jehoiakim reigns eleven years and is bound in chains for Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar carries off part of the vessels of the house of the LORD (vv. 5-7). His son Jehoiachin reigns three months and ten days and is fetched to Babylon with the precious vessels of the house of the LORD, and Zedekiah is put on the throne (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 is the whole political situation in one clause. A pharaoh takes a son of David and changes his name. Renaming a man is what an owner does, and Judah's independence ends not with a battle in this account but with a clerk writing a different word on a list.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the vessels. Part of them go in verse 7, the precious ones in verse 10, and in verse 18 all of them, great and small. Solomon had stored those in the treasuries on the day the house was finished (5:1). It took twenty-two years and three deportations to empty the room.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and made him king in his father's place in Jerusalem. Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. Then the king of Egypt deposed him in Jerusalem and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. And the king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Jehoahaz his brother and carried him to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and made him king in his father's place in Jerusalem.

That phrase has now appeared four times in this book. They crowned Ahaziah when a raid had emptied the palace (22:1), and Uzziah after an assassination (26:1), and Josiah after another (33:25), and now they bury Josiah and put his son on the throne. Ordinary Judeans have kept the line of David in place through every emergency of the last two centuries.

This is the last time they will manage it. Every king after this one is appointed by a foreigner.

Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. Then the king of Egypt deposed him in Jerusalem and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.

Three months. Neco has come back down the same road he was on when Josiah rode out to stop him, and this time nobody stops him. He removes a king of Judah inside the walls of Jerusalem and puts the country on a payment schedule.

A hundred talents of silver. That figure has been moving through this book like a coin passed from hand to hand. Amaziah paid a hundred talents for mercenaries he had to send home, and was told the LORD could give him much more than that (25:6-9). Jotham received a hundred talents a year from Ammon for three years running (27:5). Now Judah pays a hundred talents to Egypt as the price of being allowed to keep a king at all.

And the king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim.

He changed his name. A pharaoh takes a son of David, sets him on the throne of David, and gives him a different name to be known by.

Naming is what an owner does. Adam named the animals; God renamed Abram and Jacob; Nebuchadnezzar's chief eunuch will shortly rename four Hebrew boys in Babylon. Judah's independence does not end in this account with a siege or a massacre. It ends with a foreign official writing a different word on a list, and everyone accepting it.

And Jehoahaz is taken to Egypt. The nation that God brought Israel out of has one of David's sons back, four hundred years later, as a prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar also carried part of the vessels of the house of the LORD to Babylon and put them in his palace in Babylon. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and the abominations that he did, and what was found against him, behold, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. And Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place. Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. In the spring of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon, with the precious vessels of the house of the LORD, and made his brother Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrative accelerates now, and the acceleration is the point. Eleven years, then three months and ten days, told in six verses.

Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.

Egypt is finished as the power in the room; Babylon has arrived, and it will not leave until there is nothing left to take. Jehoiakim is put in chains, and then a sentence that should be read with the whole book in mind:

Nebuchadnezzar also carried part of the vessels of the house of the LORD to Babylon and put them in his palace in Babylon.

Part of the vessels. Not all — part. Watch that word, because the Chronicler is counting.

In verse 10, when Jehoiachin is taken, it is the precious vessels of the house of the LORD. In verse 18, when the city falls, it is all the vessels of the house of God, great and small. Three visits, three loads, twenty-two years.

Now turn back to the day the house was finished. Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, and stored the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God (5:1). David saved for them, Solomon carried them in, Joash's chest at the gate paid to replace what Athaliah's sons had stolen, Hezekiah's Levites cleaned the ones Ahaz threw out and set them before the altar. Now they go onto carts, in three instalments, and end up as ornaments in a Babylonian palace.

Nothing in a house of God is safe because it is old, or beautiful, or was given at cost. Vessels are not the point of a temple. They were never the point.

Jehoiachin was eighteen, and reigned three months and ten days, and the Chronicler gives him one line of verdict and one of removal. These are not kings any more; they are men being moved about a board by somebody else's hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — He Did Not Humble Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah reigns eleven years and does evil, and he did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the LORD (vv. 11-12). He rebels against Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God, and stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD (v. 13). And it is no longer only the king: All the officers of the priests and the people likewise were exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations. And they polluted the house of the LORD (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb the whole book turns on appears one last time, in the negative, on the last king of Judah. Rehoboam humbled himself under Shishak; Hezekiah humbled himself over his pride; Manasseh humbled himself greatly in a foreign prison and was brought home. Zedekiah would not, and the door that had stood open since 7:14 closes on the man who refused to walk through it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 charges him with breaking an oath he had sworn by God to a pagan emperor. Scripture does not treat that as a technicality or a piece of clever statecraft. A promise made in God's name to a man who does not know God is still made in God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the LORD. He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel. All the officers of the priests and the people likewise were exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations. And they polluted the house of the LORD that he had made holy in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD his God. He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the LORD.

There it is, one last time, and in the negative.

Humble himself is the verb this entire book was built on. It was God's own word at the dedication of the temple: if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven (7:14). And it has been answered again and again by the least likely people. Rehoboam humbled himself with Shishak at the gate and the destruction was cut down. Hezekiah humbled himself over his own pride and the wrath was turned aside. Men of Asher and Zebulun humbled themselves and walked two hundred miles to a Passover. Manasseh, who had put an idol in the sanctuary and burned his sons, humbled himself greatly in an Assyrian prison and was carried home.

Zedekiah would not. And the man he would not humble himself before was Jeremiah, speaking from the mouth of the LORD — which is the exact phrase used of Neco's warning to Josiah one chapter ago (35:22). Josiah could not hear God in a pagan's mouth. His son could not hear him in a prophet's. The problem was never the quality of the messenger.

He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God.

He had sworn an oath, in the name of the LORD, to a Babylonian emperor, and he broke it. The Chronicler lists that among his sins without a word of qualification, and there is no hint anywhere that an oath to a pagan is less binding than an oath to a brother. A promise made in God's name is made before God whoever is standing on the other side of the table, and a man who breaks one has not outwitted an enemy. He has lied about God.

He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel.

Both pictures come from the letter Hezekiah sent north a hundred years earlier: Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the LORD (30:8). The neck that will not turn under the rein, and the heart gone hard. Neither happens in a day. They are what a man ends up with after a long career of small refusals.

All the officers of the priests and the people likewise were exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations. And they polluted the house of the LORD that he had made holy in Jerusalem.

Likewise. For twenty-six chapters this book has hung the fortunes of a nation on its kings, and at the end it will not let anybody stand outside the verdict. The chief priests are named. The people are named. It is not merely that Judah had bad leaders; Judah had the leaders it was content with, and by the last generation the men in the temple were as unfaithful as the man on the throne.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Until There Was No Remedy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place (v. 15). But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy (v. 16). So the king of the Chaldeans comes, kills the young men in the sanctuary itself and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged (v. 17); every vessel and every treasury goes to Babylon (v. 18); the house is burned, the wall broken down, the palaces burned (v. 19); the survivors are deported (v. 20) until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths ... to fulfill seventy years (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 gives God's motive for four centuries of prophets, and it is compassion — for the people and for the building. He did not send them because he wanted a case on record. He sent them because he did not want to do what he finally did. And the same word comes back two verses later, negated, in the hand he used: the Chaldean had no compassion.
verseByVerse.examples: No remedy. The word underneath is the healing word of this book. At the dedication God promised that if his people humbled themselves he would hear and forgive and HEAL their land (7:14); when a crowd of half-instructed northerners ate the Passover wrongly, he heard Hezekiah and HEALED the people (30:20). Here the book that has been about healing since chapter 7 says there was none left.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place. But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now comes the sentence that explains four hundred years, and it is not about wrath.

The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place.

Persistently. Every prophet in this book, and dozens more the book does not name. Shemaiah to Rehoboam, Azariah to Asa, Hanani to Asa, Jehu to Jehoshaphat, Eliezer about the ships, Micaiah at the gate of Samaria, Zechariah stoned in the courtyard, Oded at the gates of Samaria, Elijah's letter, the seers who came to Manasseh, Huldah in the Second Quarter, Jeremiah at the end. Four centuries of men walking into throne rooms with unwelcome information, and the historian tells us at last why they were sent.

Because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place.

Not because a case had to be built. Not so that nobody could complain afterwards. He kept sending them because he loved them and loved the building, and because every messenger was an attempt to avoid what he finally had to do.

Hold on to that, anyone who thinks of the Old Testament as the volume where God is angry. The prophets are not the sound of God losing his temper. They are the sound of God putting it off.

But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy.

Three verbs, and all three are about contempt rather than disagreement. They mocked the men, despised the words, and scoffed at the office. Nobody in that account argues with the message. They laugh at it, which is a much more effective defence and requires no thought at all.

And then four words that close the book's longest thread. Until there was no remedy.

The word underneath remedy is the healing word. It is the promise God made in this very city, in the courtyard of the house they have just polluted: if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and HEAL their land (7:14). It is what happened when Hezekiah prayed for a crowd of unclean northerners at the Passover: and the LORD heard Hezekiah and HEALED the people (30:20).

The offer had been open since chapter seven. It was taken up by a fool, a coward, a proud man and a murderer, and every one of them was healed. Judah at the end did not fail to qualify for it. Judah laughed at the men who brought it, one after another, for four hundred years, until there was nothing left to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged. He gave them all into his hand. And all the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon. And they burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem and burned all its palaces with fire and destroyed all its precious vessels. He took into exile in Babylon those who had escaped from the sword, and they became servants to him and to his sons until the establishment of the kingdom of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore he brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged.

Had no compassion. It is the same word that was used of God two verses earlier — because he had compassion on his people — and here it is, negated, in the hand he used. God's pity had held the sword back for centuries. The man who finally carried it had none.

And they were killed in the house of their sanctuary. The building that had been cleansed by Hezekiah, repaired by Josiah, filled with glory in Solomon's day and defended by an angel in Hezekiah's, is where the young men of Jerusalem were cut down.

Verse 18 empties it. All the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon. All. The counting that began in verse 7 finishes here.

Then four verbs, one after another, with nothing between them. And they burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem and burned all its palaces with fire and destroyed all its precious vessels.

Burned. Broke down. Burned. Destroyed. The Chronicler has spent nine chapters on the building of that house — the cedar from Lebanon, the gold on the walls, the cherubim facing outward, the veil made to the tabernacle's exact pattern, the fire that came down and the glory that filled it so that the priests could not stand to minister. He gives its destruction one sentence and no adjectives at all.

Sometimes that is the only decent way to report a thing.

He took into exile in Babylon those who had escaped from the sword, and they became servants to him and to his sons until the establishment of the kingdom of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years.

And here the Chronicler does the strangest and most characteristic thing in the whole book. He looks at a burned city and an empty country and reaches for a passage in Leviticus.

Moses had written it eight hundred years earlier: Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths as long as it lies desolate ... the rest that it did not have on your Sabbaths when you were dwelling in it (Lev 26:34-35). Israel was commanded to let the fields lie fallow every seventh year, and for centuries had not done it. So the land takes what it was owed while there is nobody there to work it.

Which means that even in the emptiness the commandment is being kept — just not by the people. The exile is not chaos and it is not God losing control of his own history. It is the covenant running to its stated terms, down to the arithmetic, for the exact number of years Jeremiah had said.

Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up (v. 23).

The same hand that moved empires to take Israel away moves an empire to send it home.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing: "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia, 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia.

Stirred up. That verb has been used twice already in these two books, and both times it went the other way.

God stirred up the Philistines and the Arabians against Jehoram, and they emptied his palace and carried off his wives and sons (21:16). God stirred up the spirit of the kings of Assyria, and they took the northern tribes into exile and settled them by a river a thousand miles from home (1 Chr 5:26). The same hand that moved empires to take Israel away now moves an empire to send it back.

Isaiah had said this would happen, and had said the man's name, long before there was any such man: who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose (Isa 44:28). And Jeremiah had put a number on the years. The return is not an accident of Persian foreign policy, and Cyrus is not being generous. He is being used, and the historian says so in the same sentence that names him.

So that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing. Spoken and written, all through the empire, so that a Jewish family in a provincial town could hold the document in their hands.

Thus says Cyrus king of Persia, The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.

A house at Jerusalem. The last thing said about that building in this book was that it had been burned; the next thing said about it is that a foreign emperor has been charged to build it again. Between those two sentences lie seventy years, and the Chronicler does not fill them.

Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up.

And that is the end of the book.

In the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles stands last of all, which makes let him go up the final sentence of the Old Testament. Consider where the two volumes started. The first word of 1 Chronicles is Adam. Nine chapters of names follow, then Saul's death, David's reign, the ark, the temple, the division, twenty kings, a locked door, an open door, a boy with a crown and a law book, a man in chains who prayed, a scroll found in a storeroom, and a fire.

And it ends without a period of grand summary, without a moral, and without telling us whether anyone went. It ends with a gate standing open and three words of permission.

Which is exactly right, because the story was never finished. The house Cyrus authorised was built, and it was smaller, and the glory did not fall on it as it fell on Solomon's. The line of David came home and never sat on a throne again. Something was still owing.

Five centuries later a descendant of that line stood in the courts of the second temple and said that if they destroyed this house he would raise it in three days, and he was speaking of his own body. He went up to Jerusalem to be killed, and went down into an exile deeper than Babylon, and came up out of it on the third day, and then went up where no one could follow him yet — and left behind him the same three words, addressed now to anyone at all. The captivity is over. The gate is open. Whoever is among you of all his people: let him go up.
